title: Integrated assessment of tritium releases from fission and fusion energy systems and their environmental implications
summary: Tritium is a naturally occurring radioactive isotope of hydrogen; a low-energy beta emitter with its health significance through internal exposure. The anticipated deployment of fusion energy systems is expected to increase tritium production significantly. Here we present an integrated assessment of tritium generation, release pathways, and resulting environmental concentrations across existing and emerging nuclear technologies. We first compile a comprehensive database of tritium production and releases from monitoring reports and literature. Analysis of light-water-reactor operating data shows that tritium discharge levels and release pathways are governed mainly by plant-specific strategies rather than reactor power or design parameters. This pattern reflects industry operating practices and efforts, with releases remaining well below regulatory limits. Our synthesis further indicates that FLiBe-based (Li2BeF4) systems may increase tritium production and mobility through enhanced permeation of tritiated hydrogen, although mitigation strategies are available to further limit emissions. Environmental transport modeling suggests that, under appropriate siting conditions, resulting tritium concentrations remain below regulatory thresholds. Furthermore, comparative risk analysis indicates that the associated carcinogenic impacts are expected to be lower than those from fossil-fuel-based power generation. Together, these findings demonstrate the importance of a comprehensive monitoring framework for contextualizing and managing routine effluent releases across energy systems.

AI.tldr: This study integrates a tritium production/release database with transport and risk modeling to show that light-water-reactor tritium discharges are driven by plant-specific strategies rather than design or power, that FLiBe-based fusion systems may raise tritium production and mobility but can be mitigated, and that resulting environmental concentrations and carcinogenic risks stay below regulatory thresholds and below those of fossil-fuel power.
AI.motivation: Tritium is a low-energy beta emitter whose health significance arises from internal exposure, and the anticipated deployment of fusion energy systems is expected to significantly increase tritium production. This creates a need to understand tritium generation, release pathways, and resulting environmental concentrations across both existing and emerging nuclear technologies.
AI.method: The authors compile a comprehensive database of tritium production and releases from monitoring reports and literature. They analyze light-water-reactor operating data to identify determinants of discharge levels and release pathways. They assess FLiBe-based (Li2BeF4) systems for tritium production and mobility via permeation of tritiated hydrogen and evaluate mitigation strategies. Environmental transport modeling is used to estimate resulting tritium concentrations, and a comparative risk analysis is conducted for carcinogenic impacts relative to fossil-fuel-based power generation.
AI.result: Light-water-reactor tritium discharge levels and release pathways are governed mainly by plant-specific strategies rather than reactor power or design parameters, reflecting industry operating practices, with releases remaining well below regulatory limits. FLiBe-based systems may increase tritium production and mobility through enhanced permeation of tritiated hydrogen, although mitigation strategies are available to limit emissions. Under appropriate siting conditions, modeled tritium concentrations remain below regulatory thresholds, and comparative risk analysis indicates carcinogenic impacts lower than those from fossil-fuel-based power generation.
AI.conclusion: The findings demonstrate the importance of a comprehensive monitoring framework for contextualizing and managing routine effluent releases across energy systems.

title: Study of LAGP coating on polyethylene separator for polysulfide suppression in thin Li-S batteries
summary: The use of a thin solid electrolyte layer on polyethylene (PE) separators has been explored as a potential strategy to mitigate the polysulfide shuttle effect in lithium-sulfur (Li-S) batteries, a phenomenon responsible for significantly reducing their lifespan. While some solid electrolytes, such as LAGP , have demonstrated the ability to effectively suppress the shuttle effect, their brittle ceramic nature limits their application, particularly in flexible electronics. Coating PE separators with LAGP nanofilms offers a promising solution by combining the mechanical flexibility and thinness of polymer separators with the electrochemical advantages of LAGP, due to its NASICON-like structure and high ionic conductivity. In this study, PE separators were coated with LAGP nanofilms using the ion sputtering technique and further modified with ferroic elements such as Ni and Co. The surface morphology of the coated separators was analyzed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and staircase voltammetry was employed to evaluate the electrochemical performance and modifications induced by the coatings. The results demonstrate that the use of PE separators with a thin LAGP layer significantly influences polysulfide diffusion and suppresses the shuttle effect, thereby reducing unwanted processes in Li-S batteries.

AI.tldr: Coating PE separators with thin LAGP nanofilms via ion sputtering—optionally modified with Ni and Co—suppresses the polysulfide shuttle effect in Li-S batteries while retaining the flexibility of the polymer separator.
AI.motivation: The polysulfide shuttle effect severely shortens the lifespan of lithium-sulfur batteries. Solid electrolytes like LAGP can suppress this shuttle effect, but their brittle ceramic nature restricts their use, especially in flexible electronics. A hybrid approach is therefore needed that combines the mechanical flexibility and thinness of polymer separators with the electrochemical benefits of LAGP.
AI.method: Polyethylene (PE) separators were coated with LAGP nanofilms using the ion sputtering technique and further modified with ferroic elements such as Ni and Co. Surface morphology of the coated separators was characterized by scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and staircase voltammetry was used to evaluate electrochemical performance and the modifications induced by the coatings.
AI.result: PE separators with a thin LAGP layer significantly influence polysulfide diffusion and suppress the shuttle effect, thereby reducing unwanted processes in Li-S batteries. The LAGP coating combines the flexibility and thinness of the polymer separator with the electrochemical advantages of LAGP, whose NASICON-like structure and high ionic conductivity are beneficial.
AI.conclusion: Thin LAGP nanofilm coatings on PE separators, applied by ion sputtering and optionally modified with Ni and Co, offer a promising route to mitigate the polysulfide shuttle effect in Li-S batteries while preserving suitability for flexible electronics.

title: PIN-Diode-Controlled X-/Ku-Band Frequency Reconfiguration of a CPW-Fed Quasi-Yagi Antenna
summary: A PIN-diode-reconfigurable quasi-Yagi antenna fed by a coplanar waveguide (CPW) is presented for X-band and Ku-band frequency reconfiguration. PIN diodes are strategically introduced between the driven and parasitic elements to control the effective surface-current paths and thereby modify the operating frequency characteristics. By optimizing the diode locations, number, and switching states, two distinct operating modes are achieved. In Mode I, dual-band operation covering the X-band and Ku-band is obtained, with simulated impedance bandwidths of 9-11 GHz and 12.2-18.8 GHz. In Mode II, a simulated continuous impedance bandwidth from 10 to 14.2 GHz is achieved. The corresponding simulated peak gains are approximately 8 and 7 dBi for Mode I and Mode II, respectively. A prototype is fabricated and experimentally characterized in terms of its S-parameters, and the measured results confirm the frequency-reconfiguration behavior of the proposed antenna. The effects of the number and placement of the PIN diodes on the impedance characteristics are further investigated to clarify their roles in frequency reconfiguration and design complexity. The proposed antenna provides a compact CPW-fed quasi-Yagi configuration with PIN-controlled X-band and Ku-band frequency reconfiguration.

AI.tldr: A compact CPW-fed quasi-Yagi antenna with PIN diodes placed between driven and parasitic elements achieves switchable X-band/Ku-band operation, offering dual-band (Mode I) and continuous wideband (Mode II) reconfiguration.
AI.motivation: To realize frequency reconfiguration across X-band and Ku-band using a compact CPW-fed quasi-Yagi configuration, where PIN diodes control surface-current paths to reconfigure the operating frequency without complex feeding structures.
AI.method: PIN diodes are strategically inserted between the driven and parasitic elements to alter effective surface-current paths. Diode locations, number, and switching states are optimized to produce two operating modes. A prototype is fabricated and characterized via S-parameters, and the influence of diode count and placement on impedance characteristics is examined.
AI.result: Mode I yields dual-band operation with simulated impedance bandwidths of 9-11 GHz (X-band) and 12.2-18.8 GHz (Ku-band). Mode II yields a simulated continuous impedance bandwidth from 10 to 14.2 GHz. Simulated peak gains are about 8 dBi (Mode I) and 7 dBi (Mode II). Measured results confirm the frequency-reconfiguration behavior.
AI.conclusion: The proposed antenna provides a compact CPW-fed quasi-Yagi design with PIN-controlled X-band and Ku-band frequency reconfiguration, and clarifies the roles of diode number and placement in reconfiguration and design complexity.

title: Combined photoluminescence and electrical characterization of valley photovoltaic devices explained with an equivalent circuit
summary: We present an equivalent-circuit analysis that simultaneously considers the photoluminescence and electrical responses of valley photovoltaic devices. Valley photovoltaics (VPV) are a novel concept for hot-carrier solar cells, where intervalley scattering of electrons in the absorbing material helps maintain the conduction-band electron populations at metastable satellite valleys, which are at energies higher than the conduction-band minimum. We measure intensity- and voltage-dependent photoluminescence and electrical signals of a VPV device, which has previously shown S-shaped current-voltage characteristics and thus low efficiency. We present an equivalent circuit that captures the S-shaped current-voltage curves and simultaneously describes our photoluminescence and electric measurements. The equivalent-circuit model indicates that a reverse diode causes inefficient extraction of electrons and thus the S shape. We use a Poisson/drift-diffusion model to demonstrate that the reverse diode can be either explained by the valley-scattering process itself or a heterojunction barrier. The reverse diode must be eliminated before VPV devices can achieve high efficiency.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes valley photovoltaic (VPV) devices using an equivalent-circuit model that jointly explains their photoluminescence and electrical responses, identifying a reverse diode as the cause of the S-shaped current-voltage curve and low efficiency.
AI.motivation: VPV devices are a novel hot-carrier solar cell concept relying on intervalley scattering, but prior devices show S-shaped current-voltage characteristics and low efficiency. The underlying mechanism limiting performance needed clarification through combined optical and electrical analysis.
AI.method: The authors measure intensity- and voltage-dependent photoluminescence and electrical signals of a VPV device, then construct an equivalent circuit capturing the S-shaped current-voltage curves while simultaneously describing both photoluminescence and electrical measurements. A Poisson/drift-diffusion model is used to interpret the reverse diode.
AI.result: The equivalent-circuit model shows a reverse diode causes inefficient electron extraction, producing the S shape. The Poisson/drift-diffusion model indicates the reverse diode can be attributed either to the valley-scattering process itself or to a heterojunction barrier.
AI.conclusion: The reverse diode must be eliminated before VPV devices can achieve high efficiency.

title: A partially linearized mapping approach to surface hopping (MASH-PLDM) for nonadiabatic dynamics and nonlinear spectroscopy
summary: We derive a partially linearized version of the mapping approach to surface hopping (MASH) that provides a new method for simulating nonadiabatic dynamics in molecular systems. As in the original MASH formalism, trajectories travel on adiabatic surfaces with hops determined by the dynamics of a spin vector on the Bloch sphere. However, because the new approach is based on the partially linearized density matrix (PLDM), it has two spin vectors, which may be in the same or different hemispheres of the Bloch sphere. The former scenario describes an electronic population moving on a single adiabatic surface, whereas the latter describes a coherence moving on the average surface. We show that this new method, called MASH-PLDM, leads to improved results over the original MASH dynamics for a variety of scattering problems and spin-boson models, especially in cases where coherences play an important role. A further benefit of the new methodology is that it can treat multi-time correlation functions such as those required for nonlinear spectroscopy. We demonstrate this capability with a proof-of-principle simulation of time-resolved pump-probe spectroscopy.

AI.tldr: MASH-PLDM, a partially linearized extension of the mapping approach to surface hopping based on the partially linearized density matrix, improves nonadiabatic dynamics accuracy and enables multi-time correlation functions for nonlinear spectroscopy.
AI.motivation: Original MASH simulates nonadiabatic dynamics via trajectories on adiabatic surfaces with hops governed by a single spin vector, but it struggles in regimes where electronic coherences matter and cannot straightforwardly treat multi-time correlation functions needed for nonlinear spectroscopy.
AI.method: Derive a partially linearized version of MASH starting from the partially linearized density matrix (PLDM) formalism. The resulting method, MASH-PLDM, employs two spin vectors that may reside in the same hemisphere (electronic population on a single adiabatic surface) or different hemispheres (coherence evolving on the average surface) of the Bloch sphere.
AI.result: MASH-PLDM yields improved results over original MASH across a variety of scattering problems and spin-boson models, particularly when coherences are important. It also enables treatment of multi-time correlation functions, demonstrated by a proof-of-principle simulation of time-resolved pump-probe spectroscopy.
AI.conclusion: MASH-PLDM offers a more accurate and more versatile approach to nonadiabatic molecular dynamics, extending trajectory-based surface hopping to coherence-dominated regimes and to spectroscopic observables requiring multi-time correlation functions.

title: Discrete Scale Invariance of Ising Mesons
summary: Discrete scale invariance often arises from resonant few-body or singular scale-invariant dynamics. We show that it can instead emerge in the internal motion of a composite excitation in an ordered quantum magnet. In the marginal $1/r^4$ transverse-field Ising chain, long-range bonds generate an asymptotic inverse-square attraction between dressed domain walls, with strength fixed by the spontaneous magnetization. The dressed two-kink threshold curvature sets the relative kinetic scale. Together, these independently accessible quantities determine the scale-anomaly exponent and hence the meson hierarchy. In the supercritical regime, the same exponent governs geometric binding-energy and size ratios, logarithmic level accumulation, and log-periodic threshold scattering. Full-spin exact diagonalization and a fourth-order weak-field Hamiltonian support the coupled energy--size scaling in the finite window between core and ring effects. This provides a microscopic many-body realization of quantum limit-cycle physics, with its universal scaling fixed by magnetic order and kink mobility.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that discrete scale invariance (DSI) can emerge from the internal motion of a composite excitation—a meson formed by two dressed domain walls—in the marginal 1/r^4 transverse-field Ising chain, rather than from resonant few-body or singular scale-invariant dynamics.
AI.motivation: Discrete scale invariance typically originates from resonant few-body physics or singular scale-invariant dynamics. The authors seek a many-body realization of this phenomenon, showing it can arise naturally in the internal motion of composite excitations in ordered quantum magnets.
AI.method: The authors study the marginal 1/r^4 transverse-field Ising chain, where long-range bonds produce an asymptotic inverse-square attraction between dressed domain walls whose strength is set by the spontaneous magnetization. The dressed two-kink threshold curvature defines the relative kinetic scale. These independently accessible quantities fix the scale-anomaly exponent and the meson hierarchy. The analysis is supported by full-spin exact diagonalization and a fourth-order weak-field effective Hamiltonian.
AI.result: In the supercritical regime, a single exponent governs geometric binding-energy and size ratios, logarithmic level accumulation, and log-periodic threshold scattering. Exact diagonalization and the fourth-order weak-field Hamiltonian confirm the coupled energy–size scaling within the finite window between core and ring effects.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a microscopic many-body realization of quantum limit-cycle physics, in which the universal scaling is fixed by magnetic order and kink mobility, establishing DSI as an emergent property of composite-excitation internal motion in ordered quantum magnets.

title: Permeability and microcrack geometry: Dynamic loading induced evolution
comment: 55 pages, 13 figures, includes a Supplementary Material
summary:
We propose a crack-geometry-based model for permeability evolution in rocks under dynamic loading. Accurate representation of permeability is important for fluid extraction and containment in geological formations, but remains challenging because low-porosity brittle rocks are highly sensitive to changes in pore geometry and connectivity, while dynamic permeability measurements are limited.
  Rock void space is represented as an evolving network of penny-shaped cracks with prescribed orientations. Permeability changes are described through crack microvariables including aperture, length, and crack distance. The model accounts for crack opening and closure, fracture-energy-driven propagation, plastic-strain-driven nucleation, coalescence after full connectivity is reached, and strain-rate-dependent fracture toughening. The evolving crack network directly modifies connectivity, fluid conductance, and preferential flow paths.
  The formulation is implemented in the GeoDyn hydrocode and evaluated under tension, shear, compression, and symmetric impact loading. Results show a strong relation between permeability and crack length, with crack propagation playing a major role in permeability enhancement. Permeability growth can nevertheless be limited by poor connectivity and crack closure. The model captures changes of several orders of magnitude depending on stress state, strain rate, crack orientation, and connectivity, consistent with observed behavior of brittle rocks under high strain-rate loading.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a crack-geometry-based permeability model for rocks under dynamic loading, representing void space as an evolving network of penny-shaped cracks, and validates it across tension, shear, compression, and impact loading scenarios.
AI.motivation: Accurate permeability representation is critical for fluid extraction and containment in geological formations, yet it remains challenging: low-porosity brittle rocks are highly sensitive to pore geometry and connectivity changes, and dynamic permeability measurements are scarce.
AI.method: Rock void space is modeled as an evolving network of penny-shaped cracks with prescribed orientations. Permeability evolution is tracked via crack microvariables—aperture, length, and crack distance. The model incorporates crack opening/closure, fracture-energy-driven propagation, plastic-strain-driven nucleation, coalescence after full connectivity, and strain-rate-dependent fracture toughening. The evolving crack network updates connectivity, fluid conductance, and preferential flow paths. The formulation is implemented in the GeoDyn hydrocode.
AI.result: Under tension, shear, compression, and symmetric impact loading, permeability correlates strongly with crack length, with crack propagation dominating permeability enhancement. Permeability growth can be constrained by poor connectivity and crack closure. The model reproduces permeability changes of several orders of magnitude depending on stress state, strain rate, crack orientation, and connectivity, consistent with observed brittle-rock behavior under high strain-rate loading.
AI.conclusion: The crack-geometry-based approach captures the dynamic permeability response of brittle rocks across varied loading conditions, offering a physically grounded tool for predicting permeability evolution where direct dynamic measurements are limited.

title: Topological Band Theory for High-Dimensional Parameter Spaces
summary: We study the topological band theory of quantum Hall systems in which the adiabatic flux parameters of an external gauge potential form a high-dimensional manifold. This situation arises both for strongly correlated matter on spatial Riemann surfaces of genus $g > 1$, as well as in the formal study of matter on compact oriented manifolds of dimension $4\ell+2 = 2p$ coupled to $p$-form gauge potentials. In these cases, the underlying topological invariants defined over the parameter space are significantly richer than the low-dimensional (i.e., two-dimensional) case and involve both the curvature (i.e., first Chern class) as well as higher order curvature invariants. These higher curvature invariants correspond to topologically protected contributions to Kubo-like formulae, constructed from correlation functions of the physical current operators. We illustrate these general considerations with an explicit example from hyperbolic band theory based on the genus-two Bolza Riemann surface, a case which has recently been simulated on a synthetic-dimension platform.

AI.tldr: A topological band-theory framework for quantum Hall systems whose adiabatic flux parameters form a high-dimensional manifold, revealing richer invariants (first Chern class plus higher curvature invariants) that correspond to topologically protected Kubo-like contributions, illustrated via genus-two hyperbolic band theory.
AI.motivation: Quantum Hall topological band theory is well understood for two-dimensional parameter spaces, but situations arise where the adiabatic flux parameters of an external gauge potential live on a higher-dimensional manifold. These occur both for strongly correlated matter on spatial Riemann surfaces of genus g > 1 and for matter on compact oriented manifolds of dimension 4ℓ+2 = 2p coupled to p-form gauge potentials. In such cases the standard low-dimensional topological classification is insufficient, and a richer characterization is needed.
AI.method: The authors develop a topological band theory defined over the high-dimensional adiabatic parameter space of the external gauge potential. They analyze the underlying topological invariants, showing they involve not only the curvature (first Chern class) but also higher-order curvature invariants. These higher curvature invariants are linked to topologically protected contributions to Kubo-like formulae built from correlation functions of the physical current operators. The general framework is illustrated with an explicit example from hyperbolic band theory on the genus-two Bolza Riemann surface.
AI.result: The topological invariants over the high-dimensional parameter space are shown to be significantly richer than in the two-dimensional case, comprising both the first Chern class and higher-order curvature invariants. These higher curvature invariants translate into topologically protected contributions to Kubo-like formulae derived from current-current correlation functions. The genus-two Bolza Riemann surface example, recently realized on a synthetic-dimension platform, provides an explicit demonstration.
AI.conclusion: Quantum Hall systems with high-dimensional adiabatic flux parameter spaces exhibit a richer topological band structure than the standard two-dimensional case, characterized by first Chern class and higher curvature invariants that correspond to topologically protected Kubo-like contributions. The genus-two hyperbolic band theory example, relevant to synthetic-dimension experiments, confirms the general construction.

title: Enhanced Critical Currents and Irreversibility Fields in YBa$_2$Cu$_4$O$_8$ Films through Ca-Substitution
summary: The intrinsic carrier concentration of superconducting materials may not be optimal, and different superconducting properties may have distinct optimal doping levels. Here, we show that Ca substitution increases the hole concentration in intrinsically underdoped epitaxial (Y$_{1-x}$Ca$_x$)Ba$_2$Cu$_4$O$_8$ (YCa124) films with $x \leq 0.10$, driving YCa124 toward optimal doping, increasing $T_c$ and $J_c$. At 40 K, 10% Ca doping increases $J_c$ by factors of 2.4 and 10 at 0.03 and 6 T, respectively, compared with the undoped film. The field dependence of $J_c$ follows $J_c \propto B^{-0.5}$, independent of Ca content, indicating that Ca substitution does not alter the dominant pinning mechanism. This field dependence is consistent with pinning by planar Y-125 stacking-fault intergrowths observed by electron microscopy. In addition, Ca substitution slows thermally activated vortex motion (creep) at $T \gtrsim 15$ K, while at lower temperatures the creep rate $S$ shows an unusual decrease with increasing field. Finally, we consider how doping tunes the upper bound on $J_c$, set by the depairing current density $J_d$, and the lower bound on creep, set by the Ginzburg parameter $G_i$. We find positive correlations between $J_c$ and $J_d$, and between $S$ and $G_i$, and compare them with trends across a broad range of superconductors.

AI.tldr: Ca substitution in underdoped YBa2Cu4O8 films raises hole concentration toward optimal doping, enhancing Tc and Jc without changing the dominant vortex pinning mechanism, while also suppressing creep at higher temperatures.
AI.motivation: Superconducting materials often have non-optimal intrinsic carrier concentrations, and distinct superconducting properties (Tc, Jc, creep) may peak at different doping levels. The study aims to tune carrier concentration via Ca substitution and understand how doping affects current-carrying capacity and vortex dynamics.
AI.method: Epitaxial (Y1-xCax)Ba2Cu4O8 (YCa124) films with x <= 0.10 were grown, Ca substituting for Y to increase hole concentration. Transport measurements of Tc, Jc(B,T) and creep rate S were performed; pinning mechanisms were assessed via Jc field dependence and electron microscopy; results were compared with depairing current density Jd and Ginzburg parameter Gi across a broad range of superconductors.
AI.result: 10% Ca doping increases Jc by factors of 2.4 at 0.03 T and 10 at 6 T (40 K) versus undoped films. Jc follows Jc proportional to B^-0.5 independent of Ca content, matching pinning by planar Y-125 stacking-fault intergrowths seen by microscopy. Ca substitution slows thermally activated vortex creep at T >= 15 K, while at lower temperatures S decreases unusually with increasing field. Positive correlations appear between Jc and Jd, and between S and Gi.
AI.conclusion: Ca substitution drives underdoped YCa124 toward optimal doping, enhancing Tc and Jc and slowing creep at higher temperatures without altering the dominant pinning mechanism. Doping tunes both the upper bound on Jc (set by Jd) and the lower bound on creep (set by Gi), revealing correlations that hold across diverse superconductors.

title: Advancing Fuzzy-Sphere CFTs: $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-Rotation-Resolving Exact Diagonalization, 3D Ising Heavy Primaries, and Quasi-Hole-Space Projection
summary: Fuzzy-sphere regularization has recently emerged as a powerful framework for studying three-dimensional conformal field theories (CFTs). In this work, we exploit symmetry and Hilbert-space structures to substantially advance this framework. We develop an exact-diagonalization algorithm that resolves the full $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ rotational symmetry, reducing computational costs by factors of several hundred. For the three-dimensional Ising CFT, we identify around 100 primary operators, including a large number of previously unknown heavy scalar primaries up to scaling dimension $Δ\approx16.5$. We also resolve the tension between previous fuzzy-sphere and bootstrap results regarding the parity-odd scalar primary. Furthermore, we identify a branch of scalar primaries associated with $φ^n$ operators in the $φ^4$ Lagrangian description, beginning with the identity, $σ$, $ε$, $ε'$, and $σ'$. Their wave functions exhibit a semi-classical structure closely related to states invariant under area-preserving diffeomorphisms of the sphere. Finally, we show that critical points involving fractional quantum Hall states can be studied within a substantially reduced Hilbert space spanned by quasi-hole states of the corresponding model quantum Hall wave functions like the Laughlin state. This suggests a general strategy for exploring CFTs intertwined with topologically ordered phases.

AI.tldr: The authors advance the fuzzy-sphere regularization framework for 3D CFTs by developing an exact-diagonalization algorithm that fully resolves SO(3) rotational symmetry, cutting computational cost by hundreds of times, and apply it to identify ~100 primary operators in the 3D Ising CFT up to Δ≈16.5.
AI.motivation: Fuzzy-sphere regularization is a powerful framework for studying 3D CFTs, but prior work faced high computational costs and an unresolved tension with bootstrap results (notably regarding the parity-odd scalar primary). The authors aim to exploit symmetry and Hilbert-space structure to overcome these limitations and extend the framework's reach.
AI.method: They develop an exact-diagonalization algorithm that resolves the full SO(3) rotational symmetry, dramatically reducing computational cost. They apply it to the 3D Ising CFT and also show that critical points involving fractional quantum Hall states can be studied in a reduced Hilbert space spanned by quasi-hole states of quantum Hall wave functions such as the Laughlin state.
AI.result: For the 3D Ising CFT they identify ~100 primary operators, including many previously unknown heavy scalar primaries up to Δ≈16.5, resolve the tension with bootstrap results on the parity-odd scalar primary, and identify a branch of scalar primaries associated with φ^n operators (starting with identity, σ, ε, ε', σ') whose wave functions show a semi-classical structure tied to area-preserving diffeomorphism-invariant states on the sphere.
AI.conclusion: The symmetry-resolved exact-diagonalization approach substantially improves the fuzzy-sphere framework, yields rich new operator data for the 3D Ising CFT, clarifies prior discrepancies, and suggests a general strategy for exploring CFTs intertwined with topologically ordered phases.

title: Attributing extreme-event probability to a source variable
comment: 19 pages, 7 figures, research article to be submitted
summary: Information-flow theory quantifies directional coupling through the rate of change of a target's Shannon entropy, a bulk functional insensitive to the tail of the distribution. We ask instead how a source variable contributes to the probability that the target exceeds a threshold. For source-additive drift the source's share of the marginal probability current is exact, and it separates into a mean-forcing part and a conditional-excess part that vanishes under independence. An identity links the two descriptions: the Liang information flow is the density-weighted mean of the derivative of the specific source current, whereas the exceedance current is its level at the threshold. This explains why entropy-based coupling collapses in saturated regimes where the source contributes most to the extreme; the Rényi information flow, a higher-order expansion and a Fisher-normalised response fail for the same reason. The flux decomposition, although exact, does not attribute: its terms are gross transports that nearly cancel. The quantity that does attribute is an adjoint response built from the backward generator which, read as a relative change, is uniformly accurate across two decades of event probability. We map the operating envelope of the estimator under omitted drivers, hidden slow memory, state-dependent coupling and multiplicative noise. Under correct specification the attribution carries a reproducible shortfall of ten to twenty-five per cent; the misspecifications we test bias it upward by up to ninety per cent. Applied to the 2003 European and 2010 Russian heatwaves in reanalysis, the attributed contribution of soil moisture is strongly threshold dependent, rising from the per cent level at moderate thresholds to a factor of two at the rarest, so a contribution quoted without its threshold is underspecified.

AI.tldr: The paper reframes directional coupling attribution from entropy-based information flow to a threshold-exceedance probability current, showing entropy methods collapse in saturated (extreme) regimes, and proposes an adjoint response estimator that remains accurate across two decades of event probability, then applies it to the 2003 European and 2010 Russian heatwaves.
AI.motivation: Information-flow theory quantifies directional coupling via the rate of change of a target's Shannon entropy, which is a bulk functional insensitive to the distribution tail. This makes it inadequate for questions about extreme events, i.e. how a source contributes to the probability that a target exceeds a threshold. The authors seek a coupling measure that attributes contributions specifically in the tail/saturated regime where extremes live.
AI.method: They formulate a threshold-exceedance probability current. For source-additive drift, the source's share of the marginal probability current is exact and decomposes into a mean-forcing part and a conditional-excess part that vanishes under independence. They derive an identity linking Liang information flow (the density-weighted mean of the derivative of the specific source current) to the exceedance current (its level at the threshold). They propose an adjoint response built from the backward generator, read as a relative change, and map its operating envelope under omitted drivers, hidden slow memory, state-dependent coupling, and multiplicative noise.
AI.result: Entropy-based coupling collapses in saturated regimes; the Rényi information flow and a Fisher-normalised response also fail for the same reason. The flux decomposition, though exact, does not attribute because its terms are gross transports that nearly cancel. The adjoint response is uniformly accurate across two decades of event probability. Under correct specification the attribution carries a reproducible shortfall of 10–25%; tested misspecifications bias it upward by up to 90%. In reanalysis of the 2003 European and 2010 Russian heatwaves, the attributed soil-moisture contribution is strongly threshold dependent, rising from the per cent level at moderate thresholds to a factor of two at the rarest.
AI.conclusion: Threshold-exceedance attribution via the adjoint backward-generator response outperforms entropy-based information flow for extreme events, which collapse precisely where sources matter most. A contribution quoted without its threshold is underspecified, since attributed soil-moisture effects vary by orders of magnitude across thresholds. The estimator has a bounded shortfall under correct specification and upward bias under misspecification.

title: Attosecond circular-dichroism spectroscopy of hole ring currents
summary: Ultrafast ionization of atoms by circularly polarized few-cycle laser pulses generates a hole ring currents, offering a route for ultrafast manipulation of magnetism. Here we explore the subcycle formation of these currents whose circulation direction is determined by the driving-field helicity, whereas their magnitude is governed by the quantum coherence of the residual ion. We show that the correlated ion-photoelectron dynamics can be probed with attosecond transient-absorption circular dichroism. Using the Wigner-Eckart theorem, we derive a linear relation between state-resolved dichroic absorption and the orbital and spin angular-momentum projections of the hole, thereby extending the Thole-Carra magnetic CD sum rules from static X-ray spectroscopy to attosecond electron dynamics. The modulation depth of the dichroic signal provides a direct optical measure of the coherence injected by ionization, and its dependence on the pump-pulse duration reveals a competition between coherence build-up and ionization-induced dephasing. These findings demonstrate the potential of attosecond circular dichroism for probing ionic coherence and highlight the role of quantum coherence in ultrafast angular momentum exchange between light and matter.

AI.tldr: This paper studies subcycle formation of hole ring currents generated by circularly polarized few-cycle laser pulses and shows that correlated ion-photoelectron dynamics can be probed via attosecond transient-absorption circular dichroism, extending Thole-Carra magnetic CD sum rules to attosecond timescales.
AI.motivation: Ultrafast ionization by circularly polarized few-cycle pulses can create hole ring currents useful for ultrafast magnetism control, but the subcycle formation dynamics and the role of quantum coherence of the residual ion remain unclear, motivating a probe of these coherence-driven angular momentum processes.
AI.method: The authors analyze subcycle hole ring current formation, using the Wigner-Eckart theorem to derive a linear relation between state-resolved dichroic absorption and the orbital and spin angular-momentum projections of the hole, and employ attosecond transient-absorption circular dichroism to probe ion-photoelectron dynamics.
AI.result: Current circulation direction is set by driving-field helicity while magnitude is governed by residual-ion quantum coherence. Dichroic absorption scales linearly with hole orbital/spin angular-momentum projections, extending Thole-Carra magnetic CD sum rules from static X-ray spectroscopy to attosecond electron dynamics. Dichroic modulation depth provides a direct optical measure of ionization-injected coherence, and its pump-duration dependence reveals competition between coherence build-up and ionization-induced dephasing.
AI.conclusion: Attosecond circular dichroism can probe ionic coherence, highlighting the key role of quantum coherence in ultrafast angular momentum exchange between light and matter.

title: Memory-induced optimal switching in a dynamic Ising-Kuramoto model
summary: We study a globally coupled stochastic system in which each unit carries an Ising spin and a continuous phase. The spins undergo Glauber switching with relaxation rate $γ$, while the phases are driven by Ornstein-Uhlenbeck noise with correlation time $τ$. A spin-dependent phase interaction supports a composite coherent mode, $Z_m=N^{-1}\sum_jσ_j e^{iθ_j}$, that can order even when the ordinary phase coherence is small. Linear response about the nonmagnetic incoherent state gives the synchronization threshold $K_{\mathrm c}=[(μ+β_sγ)χ_γ]^{-1}$, where $χ_γ$ is a memory-weighted Laplace transform of the free phase correlation function. The competition between the increasing Glauber response and the decreasing memory susceptibility produces a finite switching rate at which $K_{\mathrm c}$ is minimized. We derive a general sufficient condition for such an interior optimum and show that finite-time Ornstein-Uhlenbeck correlations satisfy the required fast-switching asymptotics, whereas the white-noise limit need not. Finite-size simulations reproduce the nonmonotonic threshold, its shift toward slower switching as $τ$ increases, antiphase composite order in a nonmagnetic state, and mode mixing on a magnetized background.

AI.tldr: A globally coupled spin-phase system exhibits a composite coherent mode whose synchronization threshold becomes nonmonotonic in the Glauber switching rate, minimized at a finite rate due to competition between increasing spin response and decreasing memory susceptibility.
AI.motivation: The paper seeks to understand how a composite order parameter combining Ising spins and continuous phases can synchronize, even when ordinary phase coherence is weak, and how the interplay of spin switching and phase memory controls the synchronization threshold.
AI.method: The authors analyze a globally coupled stochastic system of Ising spins (Glauber dynamics, rate γ) and phases (Ornstein-Uhlenbeck noise, correlation time τ) with spin-dependent phase interaction. Linear response about the nonmagnetic incoherent state yields the threshold K_c, and a sufficient condition for an interior optimum is derived and checked against finite-time OU correlations and the white-noise limit, supported by finite-size simulations.
AI.result: The synchronization threshold is K_c = [(μ+β_sγ)χ_γ]^{-1}, where χ_γ is a memory-weighted Laplace transform of the free phase correlation function. Increasing Glauber response versus decreasing memory susceptibility yields a finite switching rate minimizing K_c. Simulations reproduce the nonmonotonic threshold, its shift to slower switching with larger τ, antiphase composite order in a nonmagnetic state, and mode mixing on a magnetized background.
AI.conclusion: The composite spin-phase mode can order below ordinary phase coherence, and its synchronization threshold is nonmonotonic in the switching rate, with a finite optimal rate guaranteed by finite-time phase correlations. The findings clarify how memory and switching jointly govern collective coherence in mixed spin-phase systems.

title: Linking Topological Medium Range Order and Density-Wave Coherence to Metallic Glass Ductility
summary: Metallic glasses exhibit pronounced composition-dependent mechanical properties, yet identifying the structural origins of these changes remains difficult. An outstanding issue is how to correlate different forms of medium range order (MRO), defined at different length scales and accessed through different experimental observables, and to understand their connection to properties. We combine synchrotron reduced density function, G(r), with machine-learning-assisted four dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (4D-STEM) to examine geometric and topological MRO in five Zr-based metallic glasses. Density wave analysis of G(r) provides a geometric MRO descriptor through the coherence length of atomic density correlations, while 4D-STEM reveals nanoscale topological and chemical MRO motifs, including crystal-like local ordering with distinct rotational symmetries. We show that the G(r)-derived coherence length captures an important baseline tendency for cooperative ductile relaxation, while composition-dependent topological MRO provides an additional structural contribution that helps explain the observed mechanical responses. In particular, increasing Zr content suppresses Cu-rich FCC-like MRO, increases the cooperative coherence volume, and promotes fine Zr-rich HCP-like local order associated with enhanced ductility. These results identify the combined structural influence of geometric and topological MRO as a key basis for composition-dependent mechanical response in metallic glasses.

AI.motivation: Metallic glasses show pronounced composition-dependent mechanical properties, but the structural origins of these changes remain poorly understood. A key open problem is how to correlate different forms of medium-range order defined at different length scales and measured by different experimental observables, and to relate them to macroscopic properties.
AI.method: The authors combine synchrotron reduced density function, G(r), with machine-learning-assisted four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (4D-STEM) to probe geometric and topological MRO in five Zr-based metallic glasses. Density wave analysis of G(r) yields a geometric MRO descriptor via the coherence length of atomic density correlations, while 4D-STEM resolves nanoscale topological and chemical MRO motifs, including crystal-like local ordering with distinct rotational symmetries.
AI.result: The G(r)-derived coherence length captures a baseline tendency for cooperative ductile relaxation, whereas composition-dependent topological MRO provides an additional structural contribution explaining the mechanical responses. Increasing Zr content suppresses Cu-rich FCC-like MRO, enlarges the cooperative coherence volume, and promotes fine Zr-rich HCP-like local order associated with enhanced ductility.
AI.conclusion: The combined structural influence of geometric and topological MRO constitutes a key basis for the composition-dependent mechanical response of metallic glasses.

title: Directional strain control of magnetism in MnBi$_2$Se$_4$, MnSb$_2$Se$_4$, and MnSb$_2$Te$_4$ freestanding monolayers
summary: MnBi$_2$Se$_4$, MnSb$_2$Se$_4$, and MnSb$_2$Te$4$ are layered magnetic quantum materials of interest for spintronic and topological electronic applications, where control of magnetic order at the atomic scale is essential. These materials are particularly sensitive to strain. We investigate their strain-dependent magnetism in the monolayer limit using first-principles calculations across the full two-dimensional strain space spanned by independent variations of the two in-plane strain components. Our results show that the Mn-projected local moments depend primarily on the volumetric strain, whereas the magnetic ground state, exchange interactions, magnetocrystalline anisotropy, and ordering temperature show pronounced directional and composition-dependent responses. We also observe strain-induced competition between the phases, with MnBi$_2$Se$_4$, and MnSb$_2$Se$_4$ monolayers exhibiting a more diverse range of competing magnetic states, while MnSb$_2$Te$_4$ monolayer remains ferromagnetic over a larger portion of strain space. MnSb$_2$Te$_4$ also exhibits a substantially larger out-of-plane magnetocrystalline anisotropy, while showing a weaker dependence on strain than the Se-based materials. The calculated magnetic ordering temperature maps further highlight the role of two-dimensional strain to tune thermal magnetic stability in these materials. These results establish magnetoelastic trends across this family of Mn-based chalcogenide monolayers.

AI.tldr: First-principles study of strain-dependent magnetism in MnBi2Se4, MnSb2Se4, and MnSb2Te4 monolayers across full 2D strain space reveals composition- and direction-dependent magnetoelastic trends.
AI.motivation: These layered magnetic quantum materials are promising for spintronic and topological electronic applications, where atomic-scale control of magnetic order is essential. They are highly strain-sensitive, yet magnetism under arbitrary 2D strain (independent variation of both in-plane components) remained underexplored.
AI.method: First-principles (DFT) calculations in the monolayer limit, systematically varying the two independent in-plane strain components to span the full 2D strain space; computed local moments, magnetic ground states, exchange interactions, magnetocrystalline anisotropy, and magnetic ordering temperatures.
AI.result: Mn-projected local moments depend mainly on volumetric strain, whereas the magnetic ground state, exchange interactions, magnetocrystalline anisotropy, and ordering temperature show pronounced directional and composition-dependent responses. Strain induces phase competition: MnBi2Se4 and MnSb2Se4 monolayers display more diverse competing magnetic states, while MnSb2Te4 remains ferromagnetic over a larger strain region. MnSb2Te4 shows substantially larger out-of-plane magnetocrystalline anisotropy but weaker strain dependence than the Se-based compounds. Ordering-temperature maps demonstrate 2D strain control of thermal magnetic stability.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes magnetoelastic trends across the Mn-based chalcogenide monolayer family, highlighting 2D strain as a tool to tune their magnetic order, anisotropy, and thermal stability for spintronic and topological applications.

title: Minor Structural Differences Tune Functional Specialization of Antenna Subunits in the PSII Energy Transfer Network
summary: Photosystem II (PSII) contains a diverse array of pigment-protein subunits with specialized roles in the antenna network. We investigate the functional significance of this subunit diversity in two structurally similar yet functionally distinct PSII subunits: minor light-harvesting complex CP29 and major light-harvesting complex LHCII. We combine two-dimensional electronic-vibrational spectroscopy with lifetime density analysis and structure-based kinetic modeling to assign spectral features to exciton states, providing molecular detail to probed spectral features. We show how the distinct pigment compositions of CP29 and Lhcb1, a monomeric subunit of the major LHCII trimer, reshape excitonic connectivity and energy transfer pathways in the complexes. Compared to Lhcb1, energy transfer pathways in CP29 are more spatially connected and reversible, suggesting CP29 evolved to distribute excitation between the core and periphery of the PSII antenna. We find that small structural modifications from a common framework tune CP29 and Lhcb1 to complementary roles in the PSII supercomplex.

AI.motivation: PSII contains diverse pigment-protein subunits with specialized antenna roles, but the functional significance of this subunit diversity remains unclear. The study asks how two structurally similar yet functionally distinct subunits, minor LHC CP29 and major LHCII (Lhcb1), differ functionally despite a common structural framework.
AI.method: The authors combine two-dimensional electronic-vibrational spectroscopy with lifetime density analysis and structure-based kinetic modeling. This approach assigns spectral features to specific exciton states, linking spectroscopic observables to molecular detail, and compares excitonic connectivity and energy transfer pathways between CP29 and Lhcb1.

title: Locking transition in coupled disordered systems
summary: When a system of many interacting constituents is extended across space, every region carries the same disordered landscape, and it is unclear whether distant regions settle into the same state. We study copies of the Random Energy Model (REM), sharing one disorder realization, coupled along a chain. A first-order transition separates a phase with short-range correlations, from a locked phase in which the entire chain occupies the lowest-energy state with probability one, even at positive temperature. No intermediate ordering lengths occur. In the Generalized REM the chain locks either to the lowest-energy state or to the lowest free-energy valley.

AI.tldr: The paper studies copies of the Random Energy Model (REM) sharing a single disorder realization and coupled along a chain, finding a first-order transition between a short-range-correlated phase and a "locked" phase where the whole chain occupies one lowest-energy state with probability one, with no intermediate ordering lengths.
AI.motivation: When a many-body system with quenched disorder is extended across space, every region samples the same disordered landscape, and it is unclear whether distant regions settle into identical states. The authors aim to clarify how shared disorder and spatial coupling determine global versus local ordering.
AI.method: The authors construct a chain of coupled copies of the Random Energy Model (REM) that share one common disorder realization. They analyze the phase behavior of this coupled chain, and extend the analysis to the Generalized REM, examining locking to lowest-energy states versus lowest free-energy valleys.
AI.result: A first-order transition separates a phase with only short-range correlations from a locked phase where the entire chain occupies the lowest-energy state with probability one, even at positive temperature. No intermediate ordering lengths appear. In the Generalized REM, the chain locks either to the lowest-energy state or to the lowest free-energy valley.
AI.conclusion: Shared disorder combined with spatial coupling induces a sharp, first-order global locking transition with no intermediate length scales, and the Generalized REM exhibits locking to either the lowest-energy state or the lowest free-energy valley.

title: Moment hierarchy and exact steady-state solutions in a Callaway lattice Boltzmann model for phonon hydrodynamics
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures; Supplemental Material included as an ancillary file
summary: We analyze the moment hierarchy of a Callaway lattice Boltzmann model for phonon hydrodynamics and derive exact steady-state solutions for a driven planar channel with diffuse walls. The collision operator decomposes the population space into conserved, heat-flux, and fast kinetic sectors, whose coupling through streaming determines the transport response. For the two-dimensional, eight-velocity (D2Q8) lattice Boltzmann model, we derive a fully discrete closure that relates the heat flux to transverse kinetic moments. The higher-order transverse kinetic moment contains both a second-difference term and an explicit contribution from the imposed energy drop. Diffuse-wall population constraints then determine the heat-flux and kinetic-moment profiles without fitted parameters. The resulting solution reproduces the numerical bulk moment amplitudes and wall slip, while an exact wall relation separates the contribution of the higher-order moment from deviations from the leading gradient approximation. Finite-wave-number analysis further resolves the collision-sector mixing associated with longitudinal propagation. These results provide a unified description of collision relaxation, the moment hierarchy, and boundary response within the specified discrete model.

AI.tldr: Exact steady-state solutions for a driven planar phonon channel with diffuse walls are derived for a Callaway D2Q8 lattice Boltzmann model, yielding a parameter-free closure linking heat flux to transverse kinetic moments and reproducing bulk moments and wall slip.
AI.motivation: Phonon hydrodynamics requires a tractable description of how collision relaxation, the moment hierarchy, and boundary response interact, particularly in confined channels with diffuse walls where fitted parameters are typically needed.
AI.method: The moment hierarchy of a Callaway lattice Boltzmann model is analyzed by decomposing the collision operator into conserved, heat-flux, and fast kinetic sectors coupled through streaming. For the D2Q8 lattice, a fully discrete closure relating heat flux to transverse kinetic moments is derived, with the higher-order moment containing a second-difference term and an explicit imposed-energy-drop contribution. Diffuse-wall population constraints then fix the heat-flux and kinetic-moment profiles, supported by finite-wave-number analysis of collision-sector mixing.
AI.result: The derived solution reproduces numerical bulk moment amplitudes and wall slip without fitted parameters. An exact wall relation separates the higher-order moment contribution from deviations of the leading gradient approximation, and finite-wave-number analysis resolves the collision-sector mixing tied to longitudinal propagation.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a unified, parameter-free description of collision relaxation, the moment hierarchy, and boundary response within the specified discrete Callaway lattice Boltzmann model for phonon hydrodynamics.

title: Magnetoplasmon molecule
summary: We investigate a two-dimensional electron system in an external magnetic field. An intrinsic four-particle excitation of the electron system, which we term a magnetoplasmon molecule, is observed. The molecule comprises two identical electrons and two Fermi holes with opposite spins. Both electrons and one Fermi hole participate in the collective plasma oscillations of the electron system, whereas the second Fermi hole neutralizes the excess electronic charge. We examine the interaction between the magnetoplasmon molecule and a magnetoexciton condensate.

AI.motivation: The study is motivated by the need to understand collective and few-particle excitations in a 2D electron system subject to an external magnetic field, and how a newly identified composite excitation (magnetoplasmon molecule) couples to a magnetoexciton condensate.
AI.method: Theoretical investigation of a two-dimensional electron system in an external magnetic field, identifying an intrinsic four-particle excitation. The composite object consists of two identical electrons and two Fermi holes of opposite spins. Its plasma oscillation character and charge-neutralizing role of the second Fermi hole are analyzed, followed by examination of its interaction with a magnetoexciton condensate.
AI.result: An intrinsic four-particle excitation, the magnetoplasmon molecule, is observed in the 2D electron system. Two electrons plus one Fermi hole participate in the collective plasma oscillations, while the second Fermi hole neutralizes the excess electronic charge, rendering the molecule overall neutral. The interaction between this molecule and a magnetoexciton condensate is examined.
AI.conclusion: The magnetoplasmon molecule represents a distinct charge-neutral composite excitation of the 2D electron system in a magnetic field, and its interplay with a magnetoexciton condensate constitutes a relevant coupled excitation problem.

title: Evanescent-wave Johnson Noise from Superconductors
summary: We compute the evanescent-wave Johnson noise (EWJN) in the vacuum half-space above a superconductor, and the resulting relaxation time ($T_1$) of spin and charge qubits placed at nanometer distances from the surface. The electromagnetic response is described by a single microscopic transverse current-response kernel $Q(q, ω)$ for a BCS superconductor. This is computed for varying densities of both non-magnetic impurities and magnetic impurities, for arbitrary frequency and temperature and for wave vectors $q \ll k_F$ (the Fermi wavevector). When combined with the fluctuation-dissipation theorem and the nonlocal surface impedances of the half-space, this yields the magnetic and electric field noise at any distance $z \gg k_F^{-1}$ from the surface, from which we obtain $T_1$. Just below $T_c$ the magnetic noise is enhanced relative to the normal state by the coherence (Hebel-Slichter-type) peak of the dissipative conductivity and drops exponentially at lower temperatures; the electric noise shows no coherence peak. The theory predicts that there is a zero-temperature noise floor induced by magnetic impurities. In the gapless regime produced by pair breaking, the finite subgap density of states $ν(0)$ yields a temperature-independent noise spectral density and a relaxation rate bounded by $T_1^{-1}(T)\le[ν(0)/ν_F]^{2}\,T_{1,N}^{-1}(T)$ for $T\ll T_c$, with equality in the extreme nonlocal regime. Here $ν(0)$ and $ν_F$ are the superconducting and normal-state densities of states at the Fermi energy, and $T_{1,N}(T)$ is the relaxation time the same electrode would produce in its normal state at the same temperature.

u(0)/
