AI.conclusion: Evanescent-wave Johnson noise above a superconductor, derived from a microscopic BCS current-response kernel, governs qubit $T_1$ and exhibits distinct magnetic versus electric behaviors: a coherence peak near $T_c$, exponential suppression at low temperature, a magnetic-impurity zero-temperature noise floor, and a subgap-density-of-states-bounded relaxation rate in the gapless regime.

title: Spectroscopy of phonon-coupled integer and fractional Chern insulators: emergence of polarons and chirality deficit of graviton mode
summary: Strong electron-phonon coupling can destabilize both Chern insulators (CIs) and fractional Chern insulators (FCIs) in favor of charge order, but whether the instabilities in CI and FCI share a common microscopic mechanism remains unclear. In this paper, we address this question by studying a flat-band Haldane model coupled to dynamical Holstein phonons at integer and fractional fillings using density-matrix renormalization group with local basis optimization. We find that the low-energy effects of phonons are dominated by their dressing of charge-neutral collective modes. In the CI and FCI, phonons dress excitons and magnetorotons into composite modes that we identify as exciton polarons and magnetoroton polarons, respectively. These modes soften strongly upon approaching the transition, while the momenta of their energy minima anticipate the ordering wave vectors of the charge-ordered phases. The phonon spectrum, in turn, acquires dispersive features inherited from the exciton and magnetoroton modes, providing direct lattice signatures of these neutral excitations. Within the FCI phase, electron-phonon coupling also enhances the opposite-chirality spectral weight of the graviton response, thereby resulting in a chirality deficit. Our results provide a unified excitation-based picture of phonon-driven instabilities in CIs and FCIs and establish lattice dynamics as a probe of their neutral collective modes.

AI.tldr: Phonons destabilize both Chern and fractional Chern insulators via a common mechanism: they dress charge-neutral collective modes (excitons/magnetorotons), forming polarons that soften toward charge order, with signatures in lattice dynamics.
AI.motivation: Strong electron-phonon coupling can drive charge order that destroys both Chern insulators (CIs) and fractional Chern insulators (FCIs), but whether these instabilities arise from a shared microscopic mechanism was unknown.
AI.method: The authors study a flat-band Haldane model coupled to dynamical Holstein phonons at integer and fractional fillings, using density-matrix renormalization group with local basis optimization.
AI.result: Phonon low-energy effects are dominated by dressing of charge-neutral collective modes: excitons and magnetorotons become exciton polarons and magnetoroton polarons that soften strongly near the transition, with energy minima momenta anticipating the charge-order wave vectors. The phonon spectrum inherits dispersive features from these modes. In the FCI phase, electron-phonon coupling enhances opposite-chirality spectral weight of the graviton response, producing a chirality deficit.
AI.conclusion: The results offer a unified excitation-based picture of phonon-driven instabilities in CIs and FCIs, and establish lattice dynamics as a probe of their neutral collective modes.

title: Optimization Using Pathwise Algorithmic Derivatives of Electromagnetic Shower Simulations
summary:
Among the well-known methods to approximate derivatives of expectancies computed by Monte-Carlo simulations, averages of pathwise derivatives are often the easiest one to apply. Computing them via algorithmic differentiation typically does not require major manual analysis and rewriting of the code, even for very complex programs like simulations of particle-detector interactions in high-energy physics. However, the pathwise derivative estimator can be biased if there are discontinuities in the program, which may diminish its value for applications.
  This work integrates algorithmic differentiation into the electromagnetic shower simulation code HepEmShow based on G4HepEm, allowing us to study how well pathwise derivatives approximate derivatives of energy depositions in a sampling calorimeter with respect to parameters of the beam and geometry. We found that when multiple scattering is disabled in the simulation, means of pathwise derivatives converge quickly to their expected values, and these are close to the actual derivatives of the energy deposition. Additionally, we demonstrate the applicability of this novel gradient estimator for stochastic gradient-based optimization in a model example.

AI.tldr: This work integrates algorithmic differentiation into the HepEmShow electromagnetic shower simulation (based on G4HepEm) to evaluate pathwise derivative estimators for energy deposition in a sampling calorimeter, and demonstrates their use in stochastic gradient-based optimization.
AI.motivation: Pathwise derivatives (averages of pathwise derivatives via algorithmic differentiation) are the easiest approach to approximate derivatives of Monte-Carlo-computed expectancies, requiring little manual code analysis even for complex simulations like particle-detector interactions. However, the estimator can be biased when the program contains discontinuities, which may limit its practical value; hence its quality needs to be studied in a realistic simulation.
AI.method: Algorithmic differentiation is integrated into the electromagnetic shower simulation code HepEmShow, built on G4HepEm. This enables studying how well pathwise derivatives approximate derivatives of energy depositions in a sampling calorimeter with respect to beam and geometry parameters. The study also examines the effect of disabling multiple scattering on estimator convergence, and applies the resulting gradient estimator in a stochastic gradient-based optimization example.
AI.result: When multiple scattering is disabled in the simulation, means of pathwise derivatives converge quickly to their expected values, and these values are close to the actual derivatives of the energy deposition. The novel gradient estimator is also shown to be applicable to stochastic gradient-based optimization in a model example.
AI.conclusion: Pathwise derivatives computed via algorithmic differentiation can serve as a practical, unbiased-in-practice estimator for derivatives of energy deposition in electromagnetic shower simulations when multiple scattering is disabled, and can be used effectively for stochastic gradient-based optimization.

title: Shortcut to Adiabatic Transfer in a Four-Level N-type System using Counterdiabatic Driving
summary: The stimulated Raman shortcut-to-adiabatic passage (STIRSAP) technique has been demonstrated to accelerate adiabatic population transfer processes. Traditionally applied to three-level atomic systems, this method enables rapid and efficient population transfer in a short interaction time. In this work, we extend this approach to a four-level N -type system driven by three laser fields. Under the three-photon phase matching condition, the first-order Doppler effect can be completely eliminated, making this configuration more suitable for applications in frequency metrology and quantum information processing. By adiabatically eliminating the intermediate state, the four-level system is effectively reduced to a two-level model, enabling the application of counterdiabatic driving without requiring additional couplings. This approach allows for fast and efficient population transfer between metastable states. We analyze the influence of laser intensity peaks and detuning, and we show that the transfer time is significantly shorter than that achieved with the STIRAP technique. Moreover, we also show 1 that an optimal coupling strength between the ground and metastable states further minimizes the operation time.

AI.tldr: The paper extends the STIRSAP technique from three-level to four-level N-type systems driven by three laser fields, using adiabatic elimination to reduce the system to an effective two-level model for counterdiabatic driving, achieving fast population transfer between metastable states with Doppler-free operation.
AI.motivation: Conventional STIRSAP is limited to three-level atomic systems. Extending it to a four-level N-type configuration exploits three-photon phase matching to eliminate the first-order Doppler effect, which is advantageous for frequency metrology and quantum information processing. A key motivation is achieving fast, efficient population transfer between metastable states without requiring additional couplings.
AI.method: The authors consider a four-level N-type system driven by three laser fields. Under the three-photon phase matching condition, the first-order Doppler effect is eliminated. By adiabatically eliminating the intermediate state, the four-level system is reduced to an effective two-level model, to which counterdiabatic driving is applied without extra couplings. They analyze the effects of laser intensity peaks and detuning, and examine the role of ground-metastable coupling strength.
AI.result: Fast and efficient population transfer between metastable states is achieved, with transfer times significantly shorter than those of conventional STIRAP. The analysis of laser intensity peaks and detuning shows their influence on the process, and an optimal coupling strength between the ground and metastable states is found to further minimize the operation time.
AI.conclusion: The STIRSAP approach can be successfully generalized to four-level N-type systems, enabling Doppler-free, rapid population transfer without additional couplings. This makes the scheme promising for frequency metrology and quantum information processing, with an optimal coupling strength further reducing the operation time.

title: Nonreciprocal Chiral Automata
summary: Odd pressure is a parity-odd transport coefficient that gives an isotropic pressure response to vorticity in compressible two-dimensional fluids. By asymmetrically coupling vortical and compressional modes, it provides a direct mechanism for a nonreciprocal hydrodynamic response reminiscent of several biological systems. Yet microscopic models realizing odd pressure as a transport coefficient are relatively scarce. Here, we construct one such model using a lattice-gas cellular automaton based on the Frisch-Hasslacher-Pomeau II model with rest particles and chiral collisions, whose Chapman-Enskog coarse-graining produces a nonzero odd pressure coefficient. The key ingredient is a local parity-breaking collision that weakly rotates moving particles in the presence of a rest particle. At hydrodynamic scales, this microscopic rule acts as an effective magnetic field, converting the model's bulk viscosity into odd pressure. More generally, we derive expressions relating Hall viscosity, odd pressure, and odd torque to their parity-even counterparts in our model.

AI.tldr: The authors construct a lattice-gas cellular automaton (FHP-II with rest particles and chiral collisions) whose Chapman-Enskog coarse-graining yields a nonzero odd pressure, showing a local parity-breaking collision acts as an effective magnetic field that converts bulk viscosity into odd pressure.
AI.motivation: Odd pressure is a parity-odd transport coefficient producing an isotropic pressure response to vorticity in compressible 2D fluids, enabling nonreciprocal hydrodynamic responses reminiscent of biological systems. However, microscopic models realizing odd pressure as a transport coefficient remain scarce.
AI.method: A lattice-gas cellular automaton based on the Frisch-Hasslacher-Pomeau II model, augmented with rest particles and chiral collisions. The key ingredient is a local parity-breaking collision that weakly rotates moving particles in the presence of a rest particle. Chapman-Enskog coarse-graining is applied to extract hydrodynamic transport coefficients, and general expressions relating Hall viscosity, odd pressure, and odd torque to their parity-even counterparts are derived.
AI.result: The model produces a nonzero odd pressure coefficient. At hydrodynamic scales, the local parity-breaking collision rule acts as an effective magnetic field that converts the model's bulk viscosity into odd pressure. Expressions linking Hall viscosity, odd pressure, and odd torque to parity-even counterparts are obtained.
AI.conclusion: A microscopic lattice-gas realization of odd pressure is established, and the mechanism—an effective magnetic field transmuting bulk viscosity into odd pressure—along with general relations connecting parity-odd and parity-even transport coefficients, provides a tractable platform for studying nonreciprocal hydrodynamic responses.

title: Measuring trainable degrees of freedom in materials graph neural networks: a random-subspace intrinsic dimension analysis
summary: Final predictive accuracy is the standard basis for comparing graph neural networks (GNNs) in materials-property prediction, but it does not show how strongly performance depends on access to trainable parameter-space directions. Here, we introduce trainable-degree dependence as a complementary characterization of materials GNN learning. Using random-subspace intrinsic-dimension analysis, we train CGCNN, ALIGNN, and DimeNet++ in randomly oriented parameter subspaces across six prediction tasks and measure how performance recovers as independent trainable degrees of freedom are restored. The resulting recovery curves separate endpoint accuracy from the trainable-dimensional demand required to recover it. They reveal distinctions that final errors alone miss: metallic classification and log-bulk-modulus regression recover near-reference performance from small fractional subspaces, formation-energy and band-gap prediction show stronger architecture dependence, and phonon prediction is most sensitive to dimensional restriction. Dataset-size sweeps show that band-gap models require larger fractional subspaces as training data grows, whereas formation-energy and bulk-modulus responses are more stable. A width sweep shows that fractional thresholds can remain stable while absolute threshold dimensions increase with model size. Random-subspace analysis therefore provides a targeted stress test for how materials GNNs use their optimization space.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces trainable-degree dependence as a complementary characterization of materials GNN learning, using random-subspace intrinsic-dimension analysis to measure how performance recovers as independent trainable degrees of freedom are restored across models and tasks.
AI.motivation: Final predictive accuracy is the standard basis for comparing graph neural networks in materials-property prediction, but it fails to reveal how strongly performance depends on access to trainable parameter-space directions.
AI.method: Random-subspace intrinsic-dimension analysis is applied by training CGCNN, ALIGNN, and DimeNet++ in randomly oriented parameter subspaces across six prediction tasks, measuring performance recovery as independent trainable degrees of freedom are restored, with dataset-size and width sweeps.
AI.result: Recovery curves separate endpoint accuracy from the trainable-dimensional demand required to recover it: metallic classification and log-bulk-modulus regression recover near-reference performance from small fractional subspaces, formation-energy and band-gap prediction show stronger architecture dependence, and phonon prediction is most sensitive to dimensional restriction. Band-gap models require larger fractional subspaces as training data grows, whereas formation-energy and bulk-modulus responses are more stable; fractional thresholds can remain stable while absolute threshold dimensions increase with model size.
AI.conclusion: Random-subspace analysis provides a targeted stress test for how materials GNNs use their optimization space, complementing final-accuracy comparisons.

title: Ohm's law for information revealed by a skyrmion Maxwell's demon
summary: Reducing the energy cost of computation-a pressing issue in the age of AI-requires a framework for circuit design based on information thermodynamics. By extending non-equilibrium statistical mechanics to information thermodynamics, it has been shown that a probability flow carrying information-hereinafter referred to as an 'information current'-is driven by its conjugate thermodynamic force, namely 'information affinity'. Since information affinity plays a role analogous to that of voltage in an electrical circuit, it is suggested that information transport also follows a linear response relationship analogous to Ohm's law. However, despite this theoretical prediction, experimentally establishing an Ohm-like constitutive relation for information transport remains an important unsolved problem. Here, we realise an information engine consisting of two magnetic skyrmions undergoing Brownian motion at room temperature. We demonstrate that the resulting information current is proportional to the information affinity generated by Maxwell's demon over a relatively wide range, establishing Ohm's law for information. Furthermore, we clarify that, in real information circuits, both Ohm's law for information and Kirchhoff's voltage law must be slightly modified to account for interactions between information carriers and the scattering of the information current.

AI.tldr: The authors experimentally establish an Ohm-like linear constitutive relation between information current and information affinity using an information engine of two magnetic skyrmions at room temperature, and show that Ohm's law for information and Kirchhoff's voltage law require slight modifications in real information circuits.
AI.motivation: Reducing computation energy cost in the AI era demands a circuit-design framework grounded in information thermodynamics. Theory predicts an information current driven by a conjugate information affinity, with a linear response analogous to Ohm's law, but this Ohm-like relation for information transport had not been experimentally established.
AI.method: They realize an information engine consisting of two magnetic skyrmions undergoing Brownian motion at room temperature, generating an information affinity via Maxwell's demon, and measure the resulting information current.
AI.result: The information current is proportional to the information affinity over a relatively wide range, establishing Ohm's law for information. They further show that in real information circuits both Ohm's law for information and Kirchhoff's voltage law must be slightly modified to account for interactions between information carriers and scattering of the information current.
AI.conclusion: An experimentally verified Ohm-like constitutive relation for information transport is demonstrated, providing a foundation for information-thermodynamic circuit design, while highlighting necessary corrections to ideal-circuit laws in realistic settings.

title: Anomalous pressure-dependent viscosity of basaltic melts and its role in asthenosphere melt accumulation
summary: The asthenosphere's mechanical weakness enables plate tectonics, but its origin is debated. Partial melt has been proposed to cause this softening, yet recent studies suggest that the measured viscosity minimum in basaltic melts, an essential control on melt mobility, is an experimental artifact. Using quantum mechanics-based, machine learning-accelerated molecular dynamics, we extend simulation timescales by more than a factor of 1000 and achieve percent-level precision. We show that basaltic melt exhibits a robust viscosity minimum (approximately 20% below 1-bar values) at approximately 3 GPa, driven by pressure-induced reorganization of aluminum coordination that facilitates shear relaxation while silicon-oxygen polyhedra remain structurally rigid. Our results reveal a depth-dependent rheological transition: melt mobility peaks below approximately 150 km, promoting efficient extraction, but declines sharply during ascent, causing melt to stagnate beneath the lithosphere. This mechanism provides a physical basis for the dual seismic signatures of a melt-depleted deep asthenosphere and a melt-enriched layer near the lithosphere-asthenosphere boundary.

AI.tldr: Basaltic melt has a genuine viscosity minimum (~20% below 1-bar values) at ~3 GPa, caused by pressure-driven aluminum coordination changes, leading to a depth-dependent melt mobility transition: efficient extraction below ~150 km and stagnation beneath the lithosphere.
AI.motivation: The asthenosphere's mechanical weakness enables plate tectonics, but its origin remains debated. Partial melt has been proposed to cause the softening, yet recent studies suggest that the previously measured viscosity minimum in basaltic melts—an essential control on melt mobility—is merely an experimental artifact, leaving the role of melt in asthenospheric weakening uncertain.
AI.method: Quantum mechanics-based, machine learning-accelerated molecular dynamics simulations, extending simulation timescales by more than a factor of 1000 and achieving percent-level precision.
AI.result: Basaltic melt exhibits a robust viscosity minimum (~20% below 1-bar values) at ~3 GPa, driven by pressure-induced reorganization of aluminum coordination that facilitates shear relaxation while silicon-oxygen polyhedra remain structurally rigid. Melt mobility peaks below ~150 km depth, promoting efficient extraction, but declines sharply during ascent, causing melt to stagnate beneath the lithosphere.
AI.conclusion: The viscosity minimum is real, not an artifact, providing a physical basis for the dual seismic signatures of a melt-depleted deep asthenosphere and a melt-enriched layer near the lithosphere-asthenosphere boundary.

title: Ergodicity in a hole-dopped Anderson spin insulator
summary: An interacting many-body system being localized in the presence of disorder can fail to serve as its own bath. In an electronic system, the charge and spin degrees of freedom can act as thermal baths for each other. In this paper, we study the stability of an Anderson insulator in the spin sector with respect to charge doping. We consider one-dimensional two-component fermions in a lattice with large onsite repulsion ($t-J_{XX}$ model) and with a single hole in a random magnetic field. In the absence of the hole the spin sector is localized in arbitrarily weak random magnetic fields. We argue that a single hole thermalizes the spin chain in the weak disorder limit. In this regime our numerical results indicate ergodicity of the system as a whole and delocalization of the hole. At larger magnetic fields the hole eventually localizes with a finite localization length, and the Anderson spin insulator is restored.

AI.tldr: A single hole can thermalize an otherwise localized spin chain in a $t-J_{XX}$ model with random magnetic field, restoring ergodicity in the weak disorder limit, while at strong fields the hole localizes and the Anderson spin insulator returns.
AI.motivation: In an interacting many-body system, disorder-induced localization can prevent the system from acting as its own thermal bath. Since charge and spin degrees of freedom can serve as mutual baths, the authors investigate whether doping with a charge carrier destabilizes a localized spin (Anderson) insulator.
AI.method: The authors study one-dimensional two-component fermions on a lattice with large onsite repulsion (the $t-J_{XX}$ model) and a single hole subject to a random magnetic field. They combine analytical arguments with numerical simulations.
AI.result: Without the hole, the spin sector is localized for arbitrarily weak random magnetic fields. Adding a single hole thermalizes the spin chain in the weak disorder limit; numerically, the system becomes ergodic as a whole and the hole delocalizes. At larger magnetic fields the hole localizes with a finite localization length, restoring the Anderson spin insulator.
AI.conclusion: Charge doping can melt the localization of a disordered spin chain, but only below a disorder threshold. Beyond that threshold, localization of the hole reestablishes the Anderson spin insulator, showing a competition between spin localization and hole-induced thermalization.

title: TT-FDTD: Tensor Train Accelerated Three-Dimensional FDTD With Logarithmic Cost of Spatial Operators
comment: Submitted to IEEE Transaction on Microwave Theory and Techniques on July 27, 2026
summary: Quantized tensor-train (QTT) compression is incorporated into a full-vector three-dimensional scattered-field finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) formulation on uniform Yee grids. All six electromagnetic-field components, material-dependent update coefficients, equivalent-current sources, and staggered finite-difference operators are represented in compatible QTT form. Gaussian regularization of voxelized material interfaces is used to reduce the coefficient ranks generated by abrupt dielectric and conductivity transitions. The formulation is evaluated for an anatomically heterogeneous human-head model and a homogeneous dielectric sphere on grids containing up to $512^3$ spatial cells. The reported results show that interface smoothing substantially reduces material-coefficient ranks and that the TT--FDTD solution reproduces the full-grid transient fields with pointwise absolute errors on the order of $10^{-4}$ in the examined slices. Compared with conventional FDTD, the tensor representation greatly reduces storage at fine discretizations, although tensor contractions and recompression introduce additional per-step computational cost. These results demonstrate the feasibility and memory--time tradeoff of QTT-accelerated three-dimensional FDTD for large structured-grid simulations.

AI.tldr: This work integrates quantized tensor-train (QTT) compression into a full-vector 3D scattered-field FDTD formulation on uniform Yee grids, using Gaussian interface regularization to lower material-coefficient ranks, and demonstrates accurate transient fields with large storage savings but added per-step cost.
AI.motivation: Conventional full-vector 3D FDTD on fine uniform grids requires prohibitive memory, especially for large anatomically heterogeneous models. A compressed tensor representation could make such large structured-grid simulations feasible.
AI.method: All six electromagnetic-field components, material-dependent update coefficients, equivalent-current sources, and staggered finite-difference operators are cast into compatible QTT form on uniform Yee grids. Gaussian regularization of voxelized material interfaces reduces the ranks induced by abrupt dielectric and conductivity transitions. The formulation is tested on an anatomically heterogeneous human-head model and a homogeneous dielectric sphere with grids up to 512^3 cells.
AI.result: Interface smoothing substantially lowers material-coefficient ranks. The TT-FDTD solution reproduces full-grid transient fields with pointwise absolute errors around 1e-4 in examined slices. Tensor representation greatly reduces storage at fine discretizations, while tensor contractions and recompression add per-step computational cost.
AI.conclusion: QTT-accelerated 3D FDTD is feasible for large structured-grid simulations and exhibits a memory-time tradeoff.

title: Topology Obstructs Nodeless Excitons
summary: Lowest-energy excitons are usually expected to have nodeless $1s$-like envelope wavefunctions. We show that band topology can obstruct this expectation. The exciton envelope wavefunction is a section of the valence-conduction transition bundle, whose topology can enforce momentum-space zeros, with their parity or signed total index fixed by the corresponding characteristic class. We exemplify this behavior in a minimal $PT$-symmetric three-band model with a rank-two transition bundle characterized by Euler number $ν^e=2$. By directly solving the Bethe-Salpeter equation with both contact and Rytova-Keldysh interactions, we find that the lowest exciton contains two zeros, each with index $+1$, and is less strongly bound than its topologically trivial counterpart. We further classify topology-enforced exciton nodal structures for real and complex transition bundles in dimensions $d \leq 3$. Our results establish the topology of the transition bundle as a direct constraint on exciton wavefunctions and spectra.

AI.tldr: Band topology can obstruct nodeless 1s-like exciton envelopes: topology of the valence-conduction transition bundle can enforce momentum-space nodes in the lowest exciton wavefunction, demonstrated in a PT-symmetric three-band model with Euler number 2.
AI.motivation: The lowest-energy excitons are conventionally assumed to have nodeless 1s-like envelope wavefunctions. The paper challenges this expectation, proposing that band topology of the transition bundle can obstruct nodeless envelopes and impose unavoidable momentum-space zeros.
AI.method: The exciton envelope wavefunction is treated as a section of the valence-conduction transition bundle, whose topology enforces momentum-space zeros with parity or signed total index fixed by the corresponding characteristic class. The authors study a minimal PT-symmetric three-band model with a rank-two transition bundle characterized by Euler number ν^e = 2, solving the Bethe-Salpeter equation with both contact and Rytova-Keldysh interactions. They also classify topology-enforced exciton nodal structures for real and complex transition bundles in dimensions d ≤ 3.
AI.result: The lowest exciton contains two zeros, each with index +1, and is less strongly bound than its topologically trivial counterpart. A general classification of topology-enforced nodal structures is obtained for real and complex transition bundles in d ≤ 3.
AI.conclusion: The topology of the transition bundle acts as a direct constraint on exciton wavefunctions and spectra, establishing a link between band topology and exciton nodal structure and binding energies.

title: Reversible field-free superconducting diode effect controlled by an antiferromagnet
summary: The semiconductor diode, which allows current to flow preferentially in one direction, is a fundamental building block of numerous modern electronic circuits. Its superconducting analogue---the superconducting diode effect---enables directional dissipationless current flow and may provide similar functionality in future superconducting quantum circuits. Realization of such a nonreciprocal supercurrent requires broken time-reversal symmetry. At zero applied field, this has been typically associated either with intrinsic unconventional superconductivity or extrinsic spin-split electronic states induced by magnetic proximity. Here we demonstrate a field-free superconducting diode effect in conventional superconducting Al proximitized by collinear antiferromagnetic CuMnAs, whose electronic structure breaks time-reversal symmetry without generating spin splitting. By tuning the proximity effect through an insulating AlAs interlayer and correlating the reversal of the diode polarity with the reversal of the remanent Néel state, we establish that the antiferromagnet controls the superconducting diode effect. Our results show that neither spin-split bands nor net magnetization is required for a magnetically controlled field-free superconducting diode effect, extending superconducting nonreciprocity to a broader class of collinear compensated magnets.

AI.tldr: The authors demonstrate a field-free superconducting diode effect in conventional Al proximitized by the collinear antiferromagnet CuMnAs, showing that neither spin-split bands nor net magnetization are required for magnetic control of nonreciprocal supercurrent.
AI.motivation: The superconducting diode effect enables directional dissipationless current flow, useful for future superconducting quantum circuits, but its zero-field realization has typically required either intrinsic unconventional superconductivity or extrinsic spin-split electronic states from magnetic proximity. The work aims to test whether a compensated collinear antiferromagnet, which breaks time-reversal symmetry without spin splitting, can instead drive this effect.
AI.method: Conventional superconducting Al is proximitized by collinear antiferromagnetic CuMnAs, with an insulating AlAs interlayer used to tune the proximity coupling. The diode polarity reversal is correlated with the reversal of the remanent Néel state.
AI.result: A field-free superconducting diode effect is observed. Its polarity reverses in correspondence with reversal of the remanent Néel state, and the effect is tunable via the AlAs interlayer, establishing that the antiferromagnet controls the diode effect.
AI.conclusion: Magnetically controlled field-free superconducting diode effect does not require spin-split bands or net magnetization. This extends superconducting nonreciprocity to a broader class of collinear compensated magnets.

title: Excitonic Stripe Order in the Two-Orbital Hubbard-Kanamori Model
summary: Excitonic condensation and stripe formation are two distinct manifestations of electronic correlations. While excitonic order naturally arises in multi-orbital systems, stripe order is a prominent feature of doped correlated-electron models. Here, we investigate an excitonic analogue of stripe order in the two--orbital Hubbard-Kanamori model on the square lattice, characterized by a spatial modulation of inter-orbital particle-hole coherence and, in the orbital-parity-symmetric limit, spontaneous breaking of a relative orbital $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry. Using unrestricted real-space Hartree-Fock calculations complemented by random-phase-approximation instability analysis, we determine how the Kanamori interactions select different excitonic channels. The sign of Hund's exchange controls the spin character of the condensate: ferromagnetic Hund coupling favors triplet excitonic order, whereas antiferromagnetic Hund coupling stabilizes singlet excitonic order. Upon doping, commensurate excitonic density waves develop incommensurate textures, including excitonic stripes and, in the triplet sector, spiral excitonic density waves. We further show that crystal-field splitting strongly reorganizes the excitonic instability by modifying inter-orbital nesting and can stabilize triplet excitonic order even in the absence of pair hopping. Our results establish excitonic stripes as a distinct symmetry-broken state of multi-orbital correlated systems and identify microscopic routes for their stabilization.

AI.tldr: This work studies an excitonic analogue of stripe order in the two-orbital Hubbard-Kanamori model on a square lattice, showing how Kanamori interactions, Hund's coupling sign, and crystal-field splitting select distinct excitonic channels and drive incommensurate textures under doping.
AI.motivation: Excitonic condensation and stripe formation are distinct manifestations of electronic correlations; while excitonic order arises naturally in multi-orbital systems and stripe order is prominent in doped correlated models, an excitonic analogue of stripe order and its stabilization mechanisms remain unexplored.
AI.method: Unrestricted real-space Hartree-Fock calculations complemented by random-phase-approximation (RPA) instability analysis applied to the two-orbital Hubbard-Kanamori model on the square lattice.
AI.result: The sign of Hund's exchange controls the condensate's spin character: ferromagnetic Hund coupling favors triplet excitonic order, while antiferromagnetic coupling stabilizes singlet order. Upon doping, commensurate excitonic density waves develop incommensurate textures, including excitonic stripes and, in the triplet sector, spiral excitonic density waves. Crystal-field splitting strongly reorganizes the excitonic instability by modifying inter-orbital nesting and can stabilize triplet order even without pair hopping.
AI.conclusion: Excitonic stripes are established as a distinct symmetry-broken state of multi-orbital correlated systems, with microscopic routes identified for their stabilization, characterized by spatial modulation of inter-orbital particle-hole coherence and, in the orbital-parity-symmetric limit, spontaneous breaking of a relative orbital Z2 symmetry.

title: Autonomous self-harmonic drift in Langevin dynamics causes a compaction of underlying domain for the density of Stochastic Localization
summary: Our recent research on Langevin dynamics with self-harmonic drift and classical spins has revealed a strong connection to ``Stochastic Localization," a concept attracting attention in the fields of mathematical geometry and data science. Roughly speaking, the former can be viewed as a version of the latter in which the $n$-dimensional Euclidean space - the domain of the probability distribution function appearing in the latter - is ``compactified'' to the surface of an $n$-dimensional sphere. By comparing the two frameworks, we argue that this compactification is a consequence of requiring the drift to be autonomous. The relationship between the two approaches may expand the scope of Stochastic Localization.

AI.tldr: The paper connects Langevin dynamics with self-harmonic drift and classical spins to Stochastic Localization, showing that the former corresponds to a compactified (sphere-valued) version of the latter, with compactification arising from requiring an autonomous drift.
AI.motivation: The authors seek to relate their prior research on Langevin dynamics (with self-harmonic drift and classical spins) to Stochastic Localization, a concept of growing interest in mathematical geometry and data science, in order to clarify the relationship between the two frameworks and potentially expand the scope of Stochastic Localization.
AI.method: The authors perform a comparative analysis of the two frameworks: Langevin dynamics with self-harmonic drift and classical spins versus Stochastic Localization (whose probability distribution function is defined on n-dimensional Euclidean space). They interpret the former as a compactified version of the latter, where the Euclidean domain is replaced by the surface of an n-dimensional sphere, and analyze the role of the autonomy requirement on the drift.
AI.result: The comparison shows that the Langevin dynamics formulation can be viewed as a version of Stochastic Localization in which the n-dimensional Euclidean domain is compactified to the surface of an n-dimensional sphere. The compactification is argued to be a consequence of requiring the drift to be autonomous.
AI.conclusion: The relationship identified between the two approaches may serve to expand the scope of Stochastic Localization, offering a new perspective linking Langevin dynamics on spheres with existing Euclidean Stochastic Localization theory.

title: All-optical switching in a trapped ion cavity QED system: a comparative study
summary: We investigate the transient dynamics of cavity-EIT-based all-optical switching in a system of trapped ions coupled to an optical cavity through numerical simulations. In contrast to steady-state analysis, the time-dependent response provides direct insight into the switching speed, transient dynamics, and achievable switching contrast. We consider three distinct switching schemes and systematically compare their performance as a function of the relevant system parameters. The switching contrast is evaluated from the time-dependent cavity output and used to characterize the performance of each scheme. For the four-level N-type system, we find distinct trade-offs between switching through suppression of the cavity-EIT signal and switching through resonance shifting, with the former exhibiting a faster temporal response. The corresponding three-level scheme can achieve near-unity switching contrast with substantially shorter switching pulses, although it does not provide an independent switching control field. These results establish the performance limits and trade-offs of different cavity-EIT-based switching schemes and provide guidelines for optimizing their operation for applications such as high-speed optical gating, frequency-selective photon routing, frequency-multiplexed quantum communication, etc.

AI.tldr: This paper numerically studies the transient dynamics of cavity-EIT-based all-optical switching in trapped-ion cavity systems, comparing three switching schemes by switching contrast and speed to establish performance limits and trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Steady-state analyses of cavity-EIT switching do not reveal switching speed, transient behavior, or achievable contrast, which are essential for practical high-speed applications.
AI.method: Time-dependent numerical simulations of trapped ions coupled to an optical cavity, examining three switching schemes and systematically comparing their performance versus relevant system parameters, with switching contrast extracted from the time-dependent cavity output.
AI.result: For the four-level N-type system, distinct trade-offs arise between switching via suppression of the cavity-EIT signal and switching via resonance shifting, the former giving a faster temporal response. The corresponding three-level scheme achieves near-unity switching contrast with substantially shorter switching pulses, though without an independent switching control field.
AI.conclusion: The results define performance limits and trade-offs of different cavity-EIT-based switching schemes and offer guidelines for optimizing applications such as high-speed optical gating, frequency-selective photon routing, and frequency-multiplexed quantum communication.

title: Accelerating phase-field simulations on exascale computing systems for faster-than-real-time precipitate aging predictions
summary: Three-dimensional phase-field simulations are a gold-standard for microstructure prediction for materials, but their computational cost often limits application-relevant calculations to modest domain sizes and timescales. Here, we present a holistic approach for accelerating Fourier pseudospectral phase-field simulations by combining performance-portable GPU computing, large-scale distributed-memory parallelism, and high-order implicit-explicit time integration within the MEUMAPPS C++ framework. We demonstrate this approach with a 1.5-billion-grid-point simulation of the growth and coarsening of 1,920 gamma'' precipitates in a Ni-Nb-Fe alloy. The simulated seven-hour heat treatment is completed in 5.5 hours, making the calculation faster than real time and an estimated 217-501x faster than a CPU-only, first-order baseline. This performance makes three-dimensional simulations of thousands of interacting precipitates tractable, enabling quantitative studies ocollective microstructural phenomena, large simulation ensembles, and real-time integration into controlling and interpreting experiments. Benchmarking shows single-node GPU speedups of up to 17.5x relative to comparable CPU resources, near-ideal strong scaling to 4096 GPUs for a 12-billion-grid-point problem, and a further 2.6-2.9x acceleration from fourth-order time integration at scientifically relevant error tolerances. These results establish a performance-portable strategy for exploiting leadership-scale GPU systems that is applicable to a broad class of Fourier pseudospectral simulations beyond phase-field models such as fluid dynamics and crystal plasticity simulations.

AI.tldr: A holistic GPU-accelerated framework (MEUMAPPS) combining performance-portable GPU computing, distributed-memory parallelism, and high-order implicit-explicit time integration achieves real-time-scale, trillion-cell phase-field simulations of precipitates in alloys.
AI.motivation: Three-dimensional phase-field simulations are gold-standard for microstructure prediction in materials, but their computational cost restricts application-relevant calculations to modest domain sizes and timescales.
AI.method: The authors combine performance-portable GPU computing, large-scale distributed-memory parallelism, and high-order implicit-explicit time integration within the MEUMAPPS C++ framework to accelerate Fourier pseudospectral phase-field simulations.
AI.result: A 1.5-billion-grid-point simulation of growth and coarsening of 1,920 gamma'' precipitates in a Ni-Nb-Fe alloy completed a simulated seven-hour heat treatment in 5.5 hours—faster than real time and an estimated 217-501x faster than a CPU-only, first-order baseline. Benchmarks showed up to 17.5x single-node GPU speedup, near-ideal strong scaling to 4096 GPUs for a 12-billion-grid-point problem, and 2.6-2.9x further acceleration from fourth-order time integration.
AI.conclusion: The approach makes 3D simulations of thousands of interacting precipitates tractable, enabling quantitative studies of collective microstructural phenomena, large simulation ensembles, and real-time integration into experiments. It establishes a performance-portable strategy for leadership-scale GPU systems applicable to a broad class of Fourier pseudospectral simulations beyond phase-field models, such as fluid dynamics and crystal plasticity.

title: Disentangling octahedral distortion and symmetry breaking in the ordered double perovskite SrLaCoNbO$_6$
summary: We report a comprehensive high temperature structural investigation of the B-site ordered double perovskite SrLaCoNbO$_6$ using combined Raman spectroscopy and x-ray diffraction (XRD) over the range 25--900~$^\circ$C. Two distinct temperature-driven anomalies are identified at $T_\mathrm{OD} = 300\pm 25~^\circ$C and $T_\mathrm{PT} = 750\pm 25~^\circ$C through pronounced renormalizations in the phonon frequency and linewidth, accompanied by the evolution and suppression of characteristic XRD reflections. The low-temperature anomaly at $T_\mathrm{OD}$ is associated with an isostructural octahedral distortion within the monoclinic $P2_1/n$ phase. At $T_\mathrm{OD}$, the radial and angular distortion parameters of the CoO$_6$ and NbO$_6$ octahedra decrease to near-zero values before reversing upon further heating due to an inversion of the in-plane Co--O and Nb--O bond-length hierarchy. The high-temperature anomaly at $T_\mathrm{PT}$ corresponds to a symmetry-breaking structural phase transition from $P2_1/n$ to the monoclinic $I2/m$ phase, confirmed by group-theoretical analysis and Rietveld refinement. These results demonstrate that integrating temperature-dependent Raman spectroscopy with laboratory-based XRD, complemented by quantitative octahedral distortion analysis, provides a robust approach to disentangle isostructural octahedral distortions from symmetry-breaking phase transitions in complex double perovskite oxides without recourse to synchrotron or neutron diffraction facilities.

AI.tldr: A combined high-temperature Raman and XRD study of the B-site ordered double perovskite SrLaCoNbO6 (25–900 °C) reveals two distinct thermal anomalies: an isostructural octahedral distortion at ~300 °C within the monoclinic P2₁/n phase, and a symmetry-breaking P2₁/n → I2/m phase transition at ~750 °C.
AI.motivation: Complex double perovskite oxides can exhibit both isostructural octahedral distortions and symmetry-breaking phase transitions that are difficult to disentangle, typically requiring synchrotron or neutron diffraction. The work aims to distinguish these phenomena using accessible laboratory techniques.
AI.method: Temperature-dependent Raman spectroscopy combined with laboratory-based XRD over 25–900 °C, complemented by quantitative analysis of radial and angular distortion parameters of the CoO6 and NbO6 octahedra, group-theoretical analysis, and Rietveld refinement.
AI.result: Two anomalies were identified at T_OD = 300 ± 25 °C and T_PT = 750 ± 25 °C, marked by renormalizations in phonon frequency and linewidth and by evolution/suppression of characteristic XRD reflections. At T_OD, octahedral distortion parameters decrease to near-zero before reversing due to inversion of the in-plane Co–O and Nb–O bond-length hierarchy (isostructural distortion in P2₁/n). At T_PT, a symmetry-breaking transition from P2₁/n to I2/m occurs.
AI.conclusion: Integrating temperature-dependent Raman spectroscopy with laboratory-based XRD and quantitative octahedral distortion analysis offers a robust means to separate isostructural octahedral distortions from symmetry-breaking phase transitions in complex double perovskite oxides, without needing synchrotron or neutron diffraction facilities.

title: Electronic excitation spectra and recovery of excited states with neural network wave functions
summary: Accurate electronic spectra require both a flexible description of electron correlation and a tractable treatment of the many states contributing to the response. We combine neural network wave functions with the Lorentz integral transform to calculate electronic spectra directly in continuous coordinates, without truncation error from a fixed one-electron basis and with polynomial computational cost per optimization step. Instead of constructing a prescribed set of excited states, the method solves an inhomogeneous Schrödinger equation at a chosen complex energy. This formulation gives access, in principle, to the entire spectrum coupled to a perturbation, including bound excitations and the ionization continuum, without explicitly determining all lower-lying eigenstates. A finite imaginary energy controls the resolution and keeps the response square integrable. Near an isolated bound excitation, the normalized response also recovers the corresponding eigenstate as the width tends to zero. A helium application illustrates the extraction of an excitation energy and oscillator strength. The formulation provides a route from neural descriptions of electronic correlation to spectra beyond a small manifold of low-lying states.

AI.tldr: The paper combines neural network wave functions with the Lorentz integral transform to compute electronic spectra directly in continuous coordinates, solving an inhomogeneous Schrödinger equation at a chosen complex energy to access bound excitations and the ionization continuum without enumerating lower-lying eigenstates.
AI.motivation: Accurate electronic spectra demand both a flexible description of electron correlation and a tractable treatment of the many states contributing to the response. Conventional approaches are limited: fixed one-electron basis sets introduce truncation error, and constructing a prescribed set of excited states becomes intractable when many states (including the continuum) contribute. The work aims to overcome these bottlenecks.
AI.method: The authors combine neural network wave functions with the Lorentz integral transform. Rather than constructing a set of excited states, the method solves an inhomogeneous Schrödinger equation at a chosen complex energy, giving direct access to the spectrum coupled to a perturbation. A finite imaginary energy controls resolution and keeps the response square integrable. Computation proceeds in continuous coordinates with polynomial cost per optimization step. As the width tends to zero, the normalized response recovers the corresponding eigenstate near an isolated bound excitation.
AI.result: A helium application demonstrates extraction of an excitation energy and its oscillator strength, illustrating that the formulation yields spectral quantities without a fixed one-electron basis and without explicitly determining all lower-lying eigenstates.
AI.conclusion: By avoiding basis-set truncation error and the need to enumerate lower-lying states, the formulation provides a route from neural descriptions of electronic correlation to spectra beyond a small manifold of low-lying states, with in-principle access to the entire perturbation-coupled spectrum, including bound excitations and the ionization continuum.

title: From Bellissard's gap labeling to atomistic quasiperiodic bilayers
summary: Bellissard's framework uses covariant observables to describe aperiodic solids. We examine how butterfly-like spectra in twisted bilayers can be related to bulk gap labels and topological response. A bulk gap permits a spectral projector and an integrated density of states. A topological response requires an additional pairing of that projector. In an illustrative finite honeycomb bilayer, an exact second-moment identity isolates the interlayer contribution to spectral variance. Angle-resolved spectra, finite state counts, an uncoupled reference, and size and broadening checks show how coupling redistributes spectral weight without assigning a bulk gap label. We then examine the requirements for atomistic electronic-structure calculations, including nonorthogonal orbitals, projected densities of states, and basis functions that move during relative sliding. The resulting framework specifies the steps needed to connect atomistic spectra with bulk state counting and topological response.

AI.tldr: The paper adapts Bellissard's covariant-observable framework to twisted bilayers, examining how butterfly-like spectra relate to bulk gap labels and topological response, and derives a second-moment identity for the interlayer contribution to spectral variance in a finite honeycomb bilayer.
AI.motivation: Bellissard's framework describes aperiodic solids through covariant observables, but its application to twisted bilayers—where butterfly-like spectra arise—raises open questions about how such spectra connect to bulk gap labels and topological response. Clarifying these connections requires identifying what a bulk gap alone permits (a spectral projector and an integrated density of states) versus what an additional pairing is needed for topological response.
AI.method: The authors analyze spectral projectors and integrated density of states enabled by a bulk gap, and the additional pairing required for topological response. Using an illustrative finite honeycomb bilayer, they derive an exact second-moment identity isolating the interlayer contribution to spectral variance, and employ angle-resolved spectra, finite state counts, an uncoupled reference, and size and broadening checks. They also assess requirements for atomistic electronic-structure calculations, including nonorthogonal orbitals, projected densities of states, and basis functions that move during relative sliding.
AI.result: The exact second-moment identity isolates the interlayer contribution to spectral variance. Angle-resolved spectra, finite state counts, the uncoupled reference, and size and broadening checks demonstrate that coupling redistributes spectral weight without assigning a bulk gap label. The analysis further identifies the conditions needed for atomistic calculations, covering nonorthogonal orbitals, projected densities of states, and sliding basis functions.
AI.conclusion: The resulting framework specifies the steps needed to connect atomistic spectra with bulk state counting and topological response, linking butterfly-like spectral features to gap labels and topological observables in twisted bilayers.

title: Label-Permutation Symmetry and Stability in Oscillator Potts Machines
summary: Oscillator Potts machines (OPMs) provide a physics-inspired, energy-minimization framework for solving combinatorial optimization problems described by the $q$-state Potts Hamiltonian. Although OPMs may be viewed as multistate extensions of oscillator Ising machines (OIMs), here, we show that they exhibit dynamical properties absent in the binary case. Specifically, we derive a configuration-dependent local-stability condition for a recently proposed multiharmonic OPM formulation and show that configurations with the same Potts energy need not be dynamically equivalent. In particular, for $q\geq4$, permutations of the Potts labels can alter the Jacobian spectrum and, consequently, the regularization strength required to locally stabilize a given Potts configuration. Thus, different phase encodings of the same Potts solution can exhibit different local stability properties despite having identical Potts energies.

AI.tldr: Oscillator Potts machines (OPMs) exhibit configuration-dependent local stability: configurations with identical Potts energy are not dynamically equivalent, and for q>=4, label permutations alter the Jacobian spectrum and required regularization strength.
AI.motivation: OPMs are regarded as multistate extensions of oscillator Ising machines (OIMs), but it is unclear whether the binary-case intuition carries over. The paper aims to show that OPMs possess dynamical properties absent in the binary (Ising) case.
AI.method: The authors derive a configuration-dependent local-stability condition for a recently proposed multiharmonic OPM formulation, analyzing the Jacobian spectrum of the system and its dependence on the Potts configuration and label permutations.
AI.result: Configurations with the same Potts energy need not be dynamically equivalent. For q>=4, permutations of the Potts labels can alter the Jacobian spectrum and consequently the regularization strength required to locally stabilize a given Potts configuration.
AI.conclusion: Different phase encodings of the same Potts solution can exhibit different local stability properties despite identical Potts energies, revealing a multistate-specific dynamical effect not present in binary oscillator Ising machines.

title: Unveiling Three-Dimensional Skyrmion Transitions Through Vortices and Monopoles
summary: Magnetic skyrmions represent vortex-like spin configurations that provide a robust platform for next-generation spintronic technologies. Although they are often treated as two-dimensional objects with integer topological charge, their extension into three-dimensional strings realizes other composite structures with unique device functionalities that transcend planar frameworks. Unfortunately, a lack of bulk probes has failed to realize such higher-dimensional topological structures and their implementations. Here, we report the first experimental visualization of three-dimensional topological $Q = 0$ skyrmion structures using neutron scattering tomography techniques across the equilibrium phase of a Co$_8$Zn$_8$Mn$_4$ sample. Disordered skyrmion states reveal metastable skyrmioniums and composite topological objects novel to bulk systems. Vortex-antivortex lattices mediate changes in topology, with unprecedented transition pathways via a coupling of merons and monopoles. The present realization of bulk Q = 0 quasiparticles and meron-mediated dynamics paves the way for higher-dimensional spintronic frameworks through multi-bit encoding architectures, unidirectional transport schemes, and monopole-mediated controls.

AI.tldr: This work reports the first experimental visualization of three-dimensional topological Q = 0 skyrmion structures in bulk Co8Zn8Mn4 using neutron scattering tomography, revealing metastable skyrmioniums, composite topological objects, and meron-monopole-mediated vortex-antivortex lattice transitions.
AI.motivation: Magnetic skyrmions are promising for next-generation spintronics but are typically treated as two-dimensional objects with integer topological charge. Extending them into three-dimensional strings could enable higher-dimensional topological structures with novel device functionalities, yet the absence of bulk probes has prevented their realization and implementation.
AI.method: Neutron scattering tomography techniques were applied to visualize three-dimensional topological Q = 0 skyrmion structures across the equilibrium phase of a Co8Zn8Mn4 sample, probing bulk disordered skyrmion states, vortex-antivortex lattices, and their transition pathways.
AI.result: The experiments provided the first experimental visualization of three-dimensional Q = 0 skyrmion structures in bulk. Disordered skyrmion states revealed metastable skyrmioniums and composite topological objects novel to bulk systems. Vortex-antivortex lattices were found to mediate topology changes, with unprecedented transition pathways arising from coupling of merons and monopoles.
AI.conclusion: The realization of bulk Q = 0 quasiparticles and meron-mediated dynamics establishes a pathway toward higher-dimensional spintronic frameworks, enabling multi-bit encoding architectures, unidirectional transport schemes, and monopole-mediated control.

title: Anisotropic interface-confined superconductivity in FeTe-based heterostructures
summary: Interface-confined superconductivity emerges from the interaction of electronic states across chemically distinct boundaries, providing a route to engineer superconducting phases where magnetism and topology coexist. Determining the intrinsic nature of such superconductivity, however, is challenging because the superconducting layer is only a few nanometers thick and buried beneath several normal layers. Here, we measure the whole-sample Meissner response of six $\mathrm{FeTe}$-based heterostructures in a uniform magnetic field using a frequency-domain tunnel-diode resonator. In the ultrathin limit, the conventional normalization of the measured susceptibility, $χ(T\to0)=-1$, fails by tens of percent. We establish the appropriate calibration and invert $χ(T)$ to determine the London penetration depth $λ(T)$. Two key results emerge. First, the broad transitions observed in $χ(T)$ arise naturally from the extreme geometry and large $λ$, without requiring chemical or structural inhomogeneity; the extracted $λ(T)$ closely tracks the resistive transition. Second, $λ(T)$ and the corresponding superfluid density are inconsistent with a fully gapped isotropic $s$-wave state and instead indicate a strongly anisotropic order parameter possibly with line nodes or deep gap minima. The inferred $λ(0)$ is of order $1\,μ$m, consistent with an independent analysis of the 2D phase stiffness. Despite the distinct chemical, magnetic, and topological character of the three overlayers, all six FeTe heterostructures exhibit similar low-temperature power-law behavior, with no systematic dependence of the superconducting response on overlayer identity. These results point to the interfacial $\mathrm{FeTe}$ layer as the common origin of superconductivity.

AI.tldr: Whole-sample Meissner measurements on six FeTe-based heterostructures reveal that superconductivity originates from the interfacial FeTe layer, with strongly anisotropic gap symmetry and λ(0)~1 μm, independent of overlayer identity.
AI.motivation: Interface-confined superconductivity in few-nanometer-thick layers buried under normal layers is difficult to characterize intrinsically. Standard susceptibility normalization χ(T→0)=-1 fails in the ultrathin limit, obscuring the true superconducting response and its gap symmetry.
AI.method: Frequency-domain tunnel-diode resonator measurements of the whole-sample Meissner response in a uniform magnetic field on six FeTe-based heterostructures. The authors establish an appropriate calibration scheme and invert χ(T) to extract the London penetration depth λ(T), then analyze superfluid density and 2D phase stiffness.
AI.result: Broad χ(T) transitions arise from extreme geometry and large λ, not inhomogeneity. Extracted λ(T) tracks the resistive transition, is inconsistent with fully gapped isotropic s-wave, and indicates a strongly anisotropic order parameter with possible line nodes or deep gap minima. λ(0)~1 μm, consistent with independent 2D phase-stiffness analysis. All six heterostructures show similar low-temperature power-law behavior regardless of overlayer identity.
AI.conclusion: The interfacial FeTe layer is the common origin of superconductivity. The superconducting response is independent of overlayer identity despite distinct chemical, magnetic, and topological characters, supporting a robust, anisotropic interfacial superconducting state.

title: Magnetic excitations of the strongly-anisotropic triangular XXZ model: a projected spin-product state approach
summary: Recent experiments have sparked interest on the ground-state properties and on the excitation spectrum of the spin-$1/2$ triangular XXZ model with strong Ising-like anisotropy. In this work, we introduce and analyze a ``projected'' coherent-state approximation to the model, constructed by projecting spin-product states onto the low-energy configurations of the triangular Ising antiferromagnet. Within this approximation, we discuss the structure of the ground-state ordering and the magnetization curve under a longitudinal field. We then discuss the excitation spectrum by linearizing equations of motion deriving from a time-dependent variational principle. This leads to a natural description of spin-wave-like excitations within the strongly constrained Hilbert space. At zero field, the variational approximation leads to a very flat landscape of quasi-degenerate states, which results in a low-energy pseudo-Goldstone mode in the excitation spectrum. We compare our results to experimental measurements on the cobaltite K$_{2}$Co(SeO$_{3}$)$_{2}$ (KCSO). Our approximation leads to a dramatic improvement as compared to linear spin-wave theory. However, there remain deviations in the value of the pseudo-Goldstone gap and in the dispersion near $M$ points at low field.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce a "projected" coherent-state variational approximation for the spin-1/2 triangular XXZ model with strong Ising-like anisotropy, constructed by projecting spin-product states onto low-energy Ising antiferromagnet configurations, and use it to study ground-state ordering, the magnetization curve, and the excitation spectrum via a time-dependent variational principle.
AI.motivation: Recent experiments have renewed interest in the ground-state properties and excitation spectrum of the spin-1/2 triangular XXZ model with strong Ising-like anisotropy, motivating a theoretical approach capable of capturing physics beyond standard linear spin-wave theory.
AI.method: A "projected" coherent-state approximation is constructed by projecting spin-product states onto the low-energy configurations of the triangular Ising antiferromagnet. Ground-state ordering and the magnetization curve under a longitudinal field are analyzed within this approximation. The excitation spectrum is obtained by linearizing equations of motion derived from a time-dependent variational principle, yielding spin-wave-like excitations within the strongly constrained Hilbert space.
AI.result: At zero field, the variational approximation produces a very flat landscape of quasi-degenerate states, giving rise to a low-energy pseudo-Goldstone mode. Comparison with experimental measurements on the cobaltite K2Co(SeO3)2 (KCSO) shows a dramatic improvement over linear spin-wave theory. Nonetheless, deviations remain in the pseudo-Goldstone gap value and in the dispersion near M points at low field.
AI.conclusion: The projected coherent-state approximation captures the strongly constrained low-energy physics of the Ising-like triangular XXZ antiferromagnet substantially better than linear spin-wave theory, but further refinement is needed to fully reproduce the experimentally observed pseudo-Goldstone gap and low-field dispersion near M points.

title: Spin-exchange interactions between circular Rydberg atoms over long times
summary: Arrays of neutral atoms excited to Rydberg levels have emerged as one of the most promising platforms for quantum computation and simulation. With the hope to outperform classical devices, the number of atoms has been increased by orders of magnitude. However, the interaction time, i.e., the maximum accumulated time during which an atom interacts with its neighbours, has been limited to a few microseconds only. This restrains the number of gates per atom or prevents the simulation of long-time dynamics of quantum many-body systems. Here, we observe the spin-exchange interaction between two spin 1/2s encoded in laser-trapped circular Rydberg atoms over more than $60μs$ and 40 spin-oscillation periods, improving the state of the art by an order of magnitude. These unprecedented timescales allow us to record for weak atomic trapping a collapse and revival of the spin-exchange oscillation contrast induced by spin-motion coupling. Our results constitute the first observation of this coupling with laser-trapped Rydberg atoms. To counteract its detrimental effect for quantum simulation, we demonstrate a novel dynamical decoupling method that prevents the collapse of the spin oscillations. This method exploits the advantages of our recently developed hybrid platform that enables the measurement and the optical manipulation of long-lived circular Rydberg atoms with auxiliary Rydberg atoms. This work opens a direct route to long-duration quantum simulation of strongly-interacting many-body systems.

AI.tldr: Neutral-atom Rydberg arrays are promising quantum platforms, but their interaction time was limited to a few microseconds. This work observes spin-exchange between two laser-trapped circular Rydberg atoms for over 60 μs and 40 oscillation periods, revealing spin-motion coupling via collapse and revival, and demonstrates a dynamic decoupling method to prevent the collapse, enabling long-duration many-body simulation.
AI.motivation: Arrays of neutral atoms excited to Rydberg levels are among the most promising platforms for quantum computation and simulation, and the number of atoms has grown by orders of magnitude. However, the interaction time—the maximum accumulated time an atom interacts with its neighbors—has been limited to only a few microseconds. This severely constrains the number of gates per atom and prevents simulation of long-time dynamics of quantum many-body systems. Extending interaction times is therefore essential to outperform classical devices.
