For weak atomic trapping, they record a collapse and revival of the spin-exchange oscillation contrast induced by spin-motion coupling. To counteract this detrimental effect, they introduce a novel dynamical decoupling method that prevents the collapse of the spin oscillations, exploiting a hybrid platform enabling measurement and optical manipulation of long-lived circular Rydberg atoms with auxiliary Rydberg atoms.
AI.result: Spin-exchange interaction between two laser-trapped circular Rydberg atoms was observed for over 60 μs and 40 spin-oscillation periods, improving the state of the art by an order of magnitude. The authors observed collapse and revival of the spin-exchange oscillation contrast caused by spin-motion coupling—the first observation of this coupling with laser-trapped Rydberg atoms. The demonstrated dynamical decoupling method successfully prevents the collapse of spin oscillations.
AI.conclusion: By extending coherent interaction times by an order of magnitude and mitigating spin-motion-induced decoherence via dynamical decoupling, this work opens a direct route to long-duration quantum simulation of strongly interacting many-body systems using laser-trapped circular Rydberg atoms.

title: Derivation of Fokker-Planck equation and its entropy production
summary: We derive the Fokker-Planck equation and its entropy production from the master equation. To this end we consider a discrete space of states where the master equation is defined and appropriate transition rates are introduced. A transition rate has two parts, one of which is the ordinary term proportional to the inverse of the spacing and the other is inversely proportional to the square of the spacing corresponding to the variance of the independent stochastic variable. In the continuous space limit, we obtain the Fokker-Planck as well as the rate of entropy production and the flux of entropy. We also consider the case where the space of states is the phase space and discuss the equations appropriate for systems in contact with several heat reservoirs and for isolated systems.

AI.tldr: The paper derives the Fokker-Planck equation and its entropy production from a discrete master equation by introducing transition rates with two spacing-dependent parts, then takes the continuous-space limit, and extends the treatment to phase-space systems with several heat reservoirs and isolated systems.
AI.motivation: The work aims to connect the microscopic master-equation description on a discrete state space with the macroscopic Fokker-Planck description, while also obtaining entropy production and entropy flux, which are essential for characterizing irreversibility and thermodynamic behavior.
AI.method: A discrete state space is used where the master equation is defined. Transition rates are constructed with an ordinary term proportional to the inverse of the spacing and a second term inversely proportional to the square of the spacing, corresponding to the variance of the independent stochastic variable. The continuous-space limit is then taken to obtain the Fokker-Planck equation, entropy production rate, and entropy flux. The formalism is also adapted to phase space, with discussion of systems in contact with several heat reservoirs and isolated systems.
AI.result: In the continuous-space limit, the Fokker-Planck equation, the rate of entropy production, and the flux of entropy are obtained. The formulation is further applied to phase-space descriptions for systems coupled to multiple heat reservoirs and for isolated systems.
AI.conclusion: The discrete master equation with appropriately chosen transition rates yields, in the continuous limit, the Fokker-Planck equation together with its entropy production and entropy flux. This framework extends naturally to phase space and to thermodynamic settings such as multiple heat reservoirs and isolated systems.

title: Far-field terahertz spectroscopy across the charge-density-wave transition in 2H-NbSe$_2$
summary: Charge-density-wave (CDW) formation in 2H-NbSe$_2$ modifies the low-energy electronic structure and gives rise to collective excitations coupled to the lattice. Here, we investigate bulk 2H-NbSe$_2$ single crystals using far-field terahertz time-domain spectroscopy (THz-TDS) in reflection geometry across the CDW transition at $T_{\mathrm{CDW}} \approx 33$~K. Below $T_{\mathrm{CDW}}$, the THz response shows a pronounced high-frequency feature near 1.5~THz together with longer-lived sub-THz oscillations. Both responses progressively weaken upon warming and are strongly suppressed across the CDW transition, supporting their association with the CDW state. Using time-dependent Ginzburg--Landau simulations, we reproduce the main features of the experimental THz response, associating the high-frequency response mainly with CDW amplitude dynamics and the sub-THz response with defect-pinned phase dynamics. The $\sim1.5$~THz feature lies close to the frequency range reported for the Raman CDW amplitude mode, while coupling to lattice degrees of freedom may also influence its spectral position. We also performed complementary angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy measurements, which reveal momentum-selective redistribution of near-Fermi-level spectral weight across the transition. Together, these results show that far-field THz spectroscopy provides a sensitive probe of collective CDW dynamics in bulk 2H-NbSe$_2$.

AI.tldr: Far-field THz-TDS on bulk 2H-NbSe2 reveals a ~1.5 THz CDW amplitude mode and sub-THz defect-pinned phase dynamics that vanish across T_CDW ≈ 33 K, supported by time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau simulations and ARPES.
AI.motivation: CDW formation in 2H-NbSe2 alters its low-energy electronic structure and produces collective excitations coupled to the lattice; a sensitive bulk probe of these collective CDW dynamics is needed.
AI.method: Far-field terahertz time-domain spectroscopy (THz-TDS) in reflection geometry on bulk 2H-NbSe2 single crystals across T_CDW ≈ 33 K; time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau simulations; complementary angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES).
AI.result: Below T_CDW, a pronounced ~1.5 THz feature appears along with longer-lived sub-THz oscillations; both weaken on warming and are suppressed across the CDW transition. Simulations assign the high-frequency response mainly to CDW amplitude dynamics and the sub-THz response to defect-pinned phase dynamics. The ~1.5 THz feature lies near the Raman CDW amplitude mode frequency, with possible lattice coupling shifting it. ARPES shows momentum-selective redistribution of near-Fermi-level spectral weight across the transition.
AI.conclusion: Far-field THz spectroscopy is a sensitive probe of collective CDW dynamics in bulk 2H-NbSe2, resolving amplitude and pinned-phase modes consistent with simulations and ARPES.

title: A systematic comparison of hard- and soft-constrained physics-informed molecular machine learning with the Clapeyron equation
summary: In molecular machine learning (ML), significant progress has been made on integrating fundamental thermodynamic relations into ML models. Such physics-informed approaches can be categorized as hard-constrained, where the thermodynamic relations are embedded in the model architecture, and soft-constrained, where relations are included in the training loss. While both approaches have been applied to various property prediction tasks, a systematic comparison on experimental data is lacking. We herein compare hard- and soft-constrained approaches on a numerically challenging case study: the prediction of vapor pressure, saturated liquid and vapor molar volumes, and enthalpy of vaporization as functions of temperature for single-species vapor-liquid equilibrium, related by the exact Clapeyron equation. Furthermore, soft-constrained approaches in molecular ML typically balance data and physics losses with a fixed weighting factor, requiring careful tuning. To overcome this, we investigate the augmented Lagrangian method (ALM), well established in constrained optimization. We find that for the soft-constrained approach, using the ALM improves prediction performance in terms of constraint satisfaction by factor 2 and reduces training epochs compared to using a fixed penalty by 30%. Hence, in the soft-constrained approach, the use of the ALM is always recommended. The hard-constrained approach, which entails additional architectural design choices, can reach on par accuracy with the soft-constrained approach, at even higher thermodynamic consistency, reaching 12 orders of magnitude closer approximation of the Clapeyron equation. Overall, the hard-constrained approach is most promising when thermodynamic consistency is critical, yet requires tailoring the ML model architecture to the respective thermodynamic relation.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically compares hard- and soft-constrained physics-informed ML approaches for predicting vapor-liquid equilibrium properties linked by the Clapeyron equation, and introduces the augmented Lagrangian method (ALM) to improve the soft-constrained approach by removing fixed loss-weighting.
AI.motivation: Physics-informed ML embeds thermodynamic relations either in the model architecture (hard-constrained) or in the training loss (soft-constrained), but a systematic comparison on experimental data is lacking. Additionally, soft-constrained methods typically rely on a fixed weighting factor balancing data and physics losses, which requires careful tuning.
AI.method: Using a numerically challenging case study—predicting vapor pressure, saturated liquid and vapor molar volumes, and enthalpy of vaporization versus temperature for single-species vapor-liquid equilibrium, all related by the exact Clapeyron equation—the authors compare hard- and soft-constrained approaches. For the soft-constrained approach, they replace the fixed penalty with the augmented Lagrangian method (ALM).
AI.result: For the soft-constrained approach, ALM improves constraint satisfaction by a factor of 2 and reduces training epochs by 30% compared to a fixed penalty. The hard-constrained approach, despite requiring additional architectural design, matches the soft-constrained accuracy while achieving 12 orders of magnitude closer approximation of the Clapeyron equation.
AI.conclusion: ALM is always recommended for the soft-constrained approach. The hard-constrained approach is most promising when thermodynamic consistency is critical, but requires tailoring the ML architecture to the specific thermodynamic relation.

title: Neural-quantum-state based downfolding of the three-band Emery model for cuprates and nickelates
summary: Understanding the physics underlying high-temperature superconductivity in cuprates and, more recently, infinite-layer nickelates has remained a central challenge in condensed-matter physics. We establish neural quantum states (NQS), specifically Hidden Fermion Determinant States (HFDS), as a scalable variational approach to the three-band Emery model of the copper- and nickel-oxide layers in these materials. After benchmarking HFDS against matrix product states on width-two geometries, we study ground states of fully two-dimensional (2D) systems of up to $10\times10$ unit cells ($300$ sites). We characterize the momentum-space distribution of dopants and find a pronounced electron-hole dichotomy similar to cuprate experiments. We further downfold the three-band model to effective single-band descriptions by constructing interacting Wannier functions. We consider a wide range of parameters -- from the charge-transfer regime relevant to cuprates to the Hubbard-Mott regime of nickelates, as well as systematic scans of the charge-transfer gap that has been demonstrated to impact the critical superconducting temperatures. Across all regimes, the effective model significantly deviates from the usual Fermi-Hubbard model: The typical ratio $U/t$ is enhanced, some parameters experience a significant doping dependence, and sizable terms beyond the conventional Hubbard model are present, most notably a density-assisted hopping $t_n$. Notably, in all effective models, $t_n$ has the largest contribution to particle-hole asymmetry, rather than next-nearest-neighbor hopping contributions. The effective parameters sensitively depend on the charge-transfer energy, doping, and interaction ratios. Our results establish HFDS as an efficient tool for studying the 2D Emery model and demonstrate that single-band descriptions can require interaction terms generated by the underlying multi-band models.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce Hidden Fermion Determinant States (HFDS), a neural quantum state approach, to variationally solve the three-band Emery model of cuprate and nickelate layers, benchmarking against MPS and scaling to full 2D 10x10 systems, then downfold to effective single-band models.
AI.motivation: Understanding the physics of high-temperature superconductivity in cuprates and infinite-layer nickelates remains a central challenge in condensed-matter physics, requiring scalable variational methods for the multi-band Emery model describing their copper- and nickel-oxide layers.
AI.method: They establish HFDS as a scalable variational approach to the three-band Emery model, benchmark it against matrix product states on width-two geometries, and study ground states of fully 2D systems up to 10x10 unit cells (300 sites). They characterize the momentum-space distribution of dopants and downfold the three-band model to effective single-band descriptions via interacting Wannier functions, scanning parameters from the charge-transfer regime (cuprates) to the Hubbard-Mott regime (nickelates) and systematic charge-transfer gap scans.
AI.result: They find a pronounced electron-hole dichotomy similar to cuprate experiments. Across all regimes, the effective single-band model deviates significantly from the usual Fermi-Hubbard model: U/t is enhanced, some parameters show significant doping dependence, and sizable terms beyond conventional Hubbard are present, most notably density-assisted hopping t_n, which dominates particle-hole asymmetry over next-nearest-neighbor hopping. Effective parameters sensitively depend on charge-transfer energy, doping, and interaction ratios.
AI.conclusion: HFDS is established as an efficient tool for studying the 2D Emery model, and single-band descriptions of these materials can require interaction terms generated by the underlying multi-band models.

title: Effects of Longitudinal Spin Current Density Gradient on Spin-Orbit Torque Switching of Perpendicular Magnetization
summary: It has remained a critical open question as to whether a longitudinal spin current gradient (e.g., due to a gradient in the thickness, composition, or width) can replace the longitudinal magnetic field required for deterministic spin-orbit torque switching of normal metal/ferromagnet heterostructures with perpendicular magnetic anisotropy. Here, we report robust micromagnetic and experimental evidence that any realistic longitudinal spin-current density gradient cannot be an effective replacement for a longitudinal magnetic field to enable deterministic switching of a perpendicular magnetic anisotropy device. Instead, the longitudinal spin current density can only modify the nucleation and pulse-timing-sensitive oscillations of magnetic domains and thus the picosecond-scale strip-like indeterministic switching windows. The same conclusions hold robustly when the transverse effective field associated with the spin-current pulse (the sum of the Oersted field and field-like torque) is taken into account. The indeterministic switching prevents applications in the presence of finite device-to-device variations and drifts in write current pulse and thermal fluctuations of device parameters. We also experimentally show that, instead of a longitudinal spin current density gradient, perpendicular spins are much more effective in deterministic switching of perpendicular spin torque devices.

AI.tldr: This work uses micromagnetic simulations and experiments to show that a longitudinal spin-current density gradient cannot replace the longitudinal magnetic field needed for deterministic spin-orbit torque switching of perpendicular magnetic anisotropy devices; it only affects domain nucleation and gives indeterminate switching, whereas perpendicular spins enable deterministic switching.
AI.motivation: It was an open question whether a longitudinal spin current gradient (from gradients in thickness, composition, or width) could substitute for the longitudinal magnetic field required for deterministic spin-orbit torque switching in normal metal/ferromagnet heterostructures with perpendicular magnetic anisotropy. Resolving this is important for practical, field-free switching applications.
AI.method: The authors combine micromagnetic modeling with experiments to test whether realistic longitudinal spin-current density gradients can replace the longitudinal magnetic field for deterministic switching of a perpendicular magnetic anisotropy device. They also include the transverse effective field arising from the spin-current pulse (the Oersted field plus field-like torque), and experimentally compare perpendicular spins against longitudinal spin-current gradients for deterministic switching of perpendicular spin torque devices.
AI.result: Realistic longitudinal spin-current density gradients fail to replace the longitudinal magnetic field for deterministic switching. Such gradients only modify domain nucleation and pulse-timing-sensitive magnetic domain oscillations, producing picosecond-scale strip-like indeterminate switching windows. These conclusions hold even when the transverse effective field (Oersted plus field-like torque) is included. The indeterminate switching is incompatible with finite device-to-device variations, write-current pulse drifts, and thermal fluctuations of device parameters. Experiments show perpendicular spins are much more effective than longitudinal spin-current gradients for deterministic switching.
AI.conclusion: A longitudinal spin-current density gradient cannot serve as an effective substitute for the longitudinal magnetic field in deterministic spin-orbit torque switching of perpendicular magnetic anisotropy devices. Perpendicular spins, rather than longitudinal spin-current gradients, are far more effective for deterministic switching of perpendicular spin torque devices.

title: Imaging phase winding in topological superconductors with a fork-tip Josephson STM
summary: The complex phase winding in a topological superconductor remains challenging to access by conventional real-space probes. We propose a scheme to probe this winding with a fork-tip Josephson STM near an impurity, where two superconducting tips form an interferometer sensitive to phase differences between two positions. The signal remains accessible even if the relative phase between the fork-tip and sample fluctuates, establishing a route towards a local phase-sensitive STM probe of topological superconductivity. We numerically compute the interference pattern to demonstrate that the magnitude and phase of the order parameter can be reconstructed as a function of angle, providing a route towards resolving the longstanding open experimental problem of directly detecting phase winding in topological superconductors.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using a fork-tip Josephson STM near an impurity to locally probe the phase winding of a topological superconductor, showing the order parameter magnitude and phase can be reconstructed angularly.
AI.motivation: Complex phase winding in topological superconductors is difficult to detect with conventional real-space probes, leaving direct experimental verification of phase winding an open problem.
AI.method: A scheme employing a fork-tip Josephson STM near an impurity, where two superconducting tips form an interferometer sensitive to phase differences between two spatial positions; numerical computation of the interference pattern.
AI.result: The signal remains accessible even when the relative phase between fork-tip and sample fluctuates, and the magnitude and phase of the order parameter can be reconstructed as a function of angle.
AI.conclusion: This establishes a route toward a local phase-sensitive STM probe of topological superconductivity and toward resolving the longstanding open problem of directly detecting phase winding.

title: Magnetic properties and Fermi-surface topology of kagome magnet HoV$_6$Sn$_6$
summary: We report a study of the magnetic properties and Fermi-surface topology of the kagome magnet HoV$_6$Sn$_6$ using magnetization and tunnel-diode-oscillator (TDO) measurements. The temperature-dependent magnetization exhibits Curie-Weiss behavior at high temperatures and reveals long-range magnetic order below $T_c$ $\approx$ 2.4 K. Below Tc, the field-dependent magnetization reveals pronounced magnetic anisotropy, with saturation moments of $\approx$ 9.5 and 7 $μ_B$ /Ho for fields applied along the out-of-plane and in-plane directions, respectively. To probe the Fermi surface, we perform TDO measurements in magnetic fields up to 41.5 T and at temperatures down to 0.35 K. The TDO signal exhibits well-defined quantum oscillations with multiple frequencies extending up to $\sim$ 9 kT. Angular- and temperature-dependent measurements are used to determine the Fermi-surface geometry and cyclotron effective masses, respectively. To elucidate the electronic structure, we perform first-principles calculations of the electronic bands, density of states (DOS), and Fermi surface. The calculated band structure exhibits flat-band features, van Hove singularities, and Dirac-like crossings near the Fermi level. The DOS near the Fermi level is dominated by the V-d orbitals, indicating that the V kagome layers play a major role in determining the low-energy electronic properties of HoV6Sn6. Our calculations further support a ferromagnetic ground state with the Ho moments oriented along the c axis, consistent with neutron-scattering measurements. The calculated quantum-oscillation frequencies from the Fermi-surface pockets of HoV6Sn6 are in overall good agreement with the experimentally observed frequencies. Our combined experimental and theoretical results provide insight into the magnetic anisotropy and electronic structure of HoV$_6$Sn$_6$ and reveal its multiband Fermi-surface topology.

AI.tldr: This study combines magnetization and tunnel-diode-oscillator measurements with first-principles calculations to characterize the magnetic properties and multiband Fermi-surface topology of the kagome magnet HoV₆Sn₆.
AI.motivation: Kagome magnets host nontrivial electronic bands (flat bands, van Hove singularities, Dirac crossings) that govern low-energy physics, but the magnetic anisotropy and Fermi-surface topology of HoV₆Sn₆ remain poorly established, motivating a combined experimental and theoretical investigation.
AI.method: Temperature- and field-dependent magnetization measurements (up to reveal magnetic order and anisotropy), tunnel-diode-oscillator measurements in fields up to 41.5 T and temperatures down to 0.35 K to detect quantum oscillations, angular- and temperature-dependent analyses to extract Fermi-surface geometry and cyclotron effective masses, and first-principles calculations of electronic bands, DOS, Fermi surface, and quantum-oscillation frequencies.
AI.result: Magnetization shows Curie-Weiss behavior at high temperature and long-range order below Tc ≈ 2.4 K, with saturation moments of ≈ 9.5 and 7 μB/Ho for out-of-plane and in-plane fields. TDO reveals well-defined quantum oscillations with multiple frequencies up to ~9 kT. Calculations show flat bands, van Hove singularities, Dirac-like crossings near EF, V-d dominated DOS, a ferromagnetic ground state with Ho moments along c, and oscillation frequencies in good agreement with experiment.
AI.conclusion: The combined results clarify the magnetic anisotropy and electronic structure of HoV₆Sn₆, establishing that the V kagome layers dominate low-energy electronic properties and revealing a multiband Fermi-surface topology.

title: Surface-Induced Spectral Broadening during Efficient Two-Photon Excitation of Cold $^{133}\text{Cs}$ Atoms near an Optical Nanofiber
summary: We report the experimental observation of the $^{\text{133}}$Cs 6S$_{\text{1/2}}$ to 6D$_{\text{5/2}}$ single-frequency two-photon transition at low excitation power using an optical nanofiber embedded in a cold atom cloud. We investigate the 917 nm fluorescence spectra modified by the surface-induced interaction of the nanofiber, which exhibits a pronounced asymmetric broadening with a distinct red-shifted tail. We present a systematic theoretical description of the two-photon transition process of atoms near a nanofiber surface, considering atomic angular momentum coupling, guided-mode decay rate, and surface-induced van der Waals interactions. Owing to the tight spatial confinement provided by the guided evanescent field, efficient nonlinear excitation is realized at excitation powers down to tens of microwatts, corresponding to a reduction of approximately four orders of magnitude relative to typical free-space implementations. Our work reveals the interplay among waveguide-modified radiative dynamics, surface-induced interactions, and the spatial distribution of atoms around the nanofiber, and provides insights into further studies on nonlinear optical transitions and surface-mediated atomic dynamics in waveguide quantum electrodynamics systems.

AI.motivation: To explore nonlinear optical transitions and surface-mediated atomic dynamics in waveguide QED by exploiting the tight spatial confinement of a nanofiber's evanescent field, which enables efficient two-photon excitation at dramatically reduced power.
AI.method: A single-frequency two-photon transition in ¹³³Cs (6S₁/₂ to 6D₅/₂) is driven via an optical nanofiber embedded in a cold atom cloud. title: Localization Transition in Kinetically Deformed one-dimensional Aubry-André Model
summary: We propose a $q$-deformation in the single-particle kinetic energy and investigate how it modifies the localization in the one-dimensional Aubry-André (AA) model. We construct a Hermitian $q$-deformed kinetic operator as a nonlinear function of the lattice translation operator, preserving the uniform lattice and recovering the conventional AA Hamiltonian continuously in the undeformed limit $q\to1$. The deformation generates an infinite set of correlated odd-range kinetic processes, controlled by a single parameter q, rather than phenomenologically involving long-range hopping. Under the dual transformation, this long-range hopping appears as higher harmonics of the dual quasiperiodic potential, providing a controlled route for breaking the exact self-duality of the AA model, with $q$ as the control parameter, consequently modifying the localization structure for $q\neq1$. In contrast to the conventional AA model, where all eigenstates localize simultaneously at $λ_c=2$, the deformed model exhibits a fraction of delocalized states even beyond $λ_c =2$. An intermediate regime also emerges in the $q-λ$ plane where localized and extended eigenstates coexist across the spectrum. We also propose a possible experimental realization of the hierarchy produced in the $q$-deformed kinetic setting in a periodically driven AA model.

AI.tldr: A q-deformed kinetic operator is introduced into the 1D Aubry-André model, breaking exact self-duality and yielding coexisting localized/extended states and a fraction of delocalized states beyond the conventional threshold.
AI.motivation: The conventional Aubry-André model has an exact self-duality and a sharp, simultaneous localization transition at λ_c=2 for all eigenstates. The paper aims to break this exact self-duality in a controlled way and study how the resulting modified kinetic structure reshapes the localization landscape.
AI.method: Construct a Hermitian q-deformed single-particle kinetic operator as a nonlinear function of the lattice translation operator, preserving the uniform lattice and recovering the conventional AA Hamiltonian as q→1. The deformation generates an infinite set of correlated odd-range kinetic processes controlled by a single parameter q (rather than phenomenological long-range hopping). Apply a dual transformation under which the long-range hopping appears as higher harmonics of the dual quasiperiodic potential, using q as the control parameter to break self-duality.
AI.result: For q≠1 the localization structure is modified: a fraction of delocalized states persists even beyond λ_c=2, and an intermediate regime appears in the q–λ plane where localized and extended eigenstates coexist across the spectrum. A possible experimental realization of the hierarchy is proposed via a periodically driven AA model.
AI.conclusion: q-deforming the kinetic energy provides a controlled, single-parameter route to break the AA model's exact self-duality, producing richer localization phenomena—partial delocalization beyond λ_c=2 and spectral coexistence of localized and extended states—with a feasible experimental platform in periodically driven AA systems.

title: Altermagnetism produces pair emission and absorption from dark excitons and magnons in La$_2$O$_3$Mn$_2$Se$_2$
summary: Altermagnets' (AMs) non-relativistic spin splitting enables novel states, spintronic and magneto-optical devices, though their optical signatures remain elusive. Here, we report exciton-magnon emission and absorption: optical sidebands from a spin-forbidden dark exciton, a direct consequence of altermagnetic symmetry. Combined optical spectroscopy and first-principles calculations reveal that La$_2$O$_3$Mn$_2$Se$_2$ is an altermagnetic insulator, hosting a strongly bound, spin-forbidden dark exciton and a higher-energy bright exciton. Photoluminescence (PL) and absorption reveal mirror-image sidebands, Stokes-shifted in emission and anti-Stokes-shifted in absorption, symmetric about the dark exciton, whose energy shifts and spectral shapes match the magnon energy scale and density of states measured independently by inelastic neutron scattering. The PL intensity tracks the full equal-time spin-spin correlator, combining static and dynamical contributions, and rules out alternative processes. This directly couples PL to magnetism, with potential for magneto-optical devices. These results establish exciton-magnon spectroscopy as a new route for optically identifying and exploiting AMs.

AI.tldr: This paper reports the observation of exciton-magnon emission and absorption sidebands from a spin-forbidden dark exciton in the altermagnetic insulator La2O3Mn2Se2, establishing exciton-magnon spectroscopy as a new optical route to identify and exploit altermagnets.
AI.motivation: Altermagnets exhibit non-relativistic spin splitting that could enable novel spintronic and magneto-optical devices, but their optical signatures have remained elusive, limiting optical identification and exploitation of these materials.
AI.method: Combined optical spectroscopy (photoluminescence and absorption) with first-principles calculations, using inelastic neutron scattering to independently measure the magnon energy scale and density of states.
AI.result: La2O3Mn2Se2 is identified as an altermagnetic insulator hosting a strongly bound spin-forbidden dark exciton and a higher-energy bright exciton. PL and absorption show mirror-image sidebands (Stokes-shifted in emission, anti-Stokes in absorption) symmetric about the dark exciton, with energy shifts and spectral shapes matching the magnon energy scale and density of states. PL intensity tracks the full equal-time spin-spin correlator and rules out alternative processes.
AI.conclusion: Exciton-magnon spectroscopy directly couples photoluminescence to magnetism, offering a new route for optically identifying and exploiting altermagnets and holding potential for magneto-optical devices.

title: Adaptive Expansions of the Optimized Effective Potential in Physically Motivated Response Spaces
summary: The optimized effective potential (OEP) method provides an exact framework for incorporating orbital-dependent exchange within Kohn-Sham (KS) density-functional theory (DFT). Its practical implementation requires representing the exchange-response potential in a suitable auxiliary space, yet conventional choices are not necessarily adapted to the physical structure of the OEP response. Here, we introduce a general response-space strategy in which physically motivated response functions from existing model exchange potentials are repurposed as adaptive auxiliary directions for the OEP equation. Specifically, response functions associated with the Becke-Johnson (BJ), R"as"anen-Pittalis-Proetto (RPP), Gritsenko-van Leeuwen-van Lenthe-Baerends (GLLB), Krieger-Li-Iafrate (KLI), and localized Hartree-Fock (LHF) constructions are incorporated into compact auxiliary spaces, while their coefficients are determined directly from the projected OEP equation rather than fixed by the underlying model potentials. This establishes a systematic connection between model exchange potentials and finite-basis OEP: model potentials provide physically informed response directions, while OEP determines their system-dependent amplitudes. The framework encompasses one- and multidimensional response spaces, including occupied-orbital and occupied-pair representations, without modifying the underlying OEP condition. We show that these physically adapted spaces capture the dominant spatial structures of the OEP exchange response with substantially fewer degrees of freedom than conventional auxiliary expansions. The proposed approach therefore provides a general route to compact, adaptive representations of exchange-only OEP potentials and a systematic framework for developing low-dimensional OEP approximations from physically motivated model response functions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a general response-space strategy for the optimized effective potential (OEP) method, repurposing physically motivated response functions from existing model exchange potentials (BJ, RPP, GLLB, KLI, LHF) as adaptive auxiliary directions in the OEP equation, yielding compact representations that capture dominant spatial structures with far fewer degrees of freedom than conventional expansions.
AI.motivation: OEP provides an exact framework for incorporating orbital-dependent exchange in Kohn-Sham DFT, but practical implementation requires representing the exchange-response potential in an auxiliary space. Conventional auxiliary choices are not adapted to the physical structure of the OEP response, motivating the need for physically informed, compact representations.
AI.method: A general response-space strategy is proposed in which response functions derived from existing model exchange potentials (Becke-Johnson, Rasanen-Pittalis-Proetto, Gritsenko-van Leeuwen-van Lenthe-Baerends, Krieger-Li-Iafrate, localized Hartree-Fock) are repurposed as adaptive auxiliary directions for the OEP equation. Their coefficients are determined directly from the projected OEP equation rather than being fixed by the underlying model potentials. The framework supports one- and multidimensional response spaces, including occupied-orbital and occupied-pair representations, without altering the underlying OEP condition.
AI.result: The physically adapted spaces capture the dominant spatial structures of the OEP exchange response with substantially fewer degrees of freedom than conventional auxiliary expansions.
AI.conclusion: The approach provides a general route to compact, adaptive representations of exchange-only OEP potentials and offers a systematic framework for developing low-dimensional OEP approximations from physically motivated model response functions, establishing a systematic connection between model exchange potentials and finite-basis OEP.

title: Geometry-Controlled Chern transfer and Flat Band Reconstruction in distorted kagome lattices
summary: Flat band formation and nontrivial topology are central manifestations of kagome electronic structure, yet they are commonly discussed in idealized lattice geometries. In distorted kagome materials, structural deformation reorganizes electronic propagation pathways, but a microscopic understanding of how such distortions govern flat band dispersion and band topology is still lacking. Using a distorted kagome tight-binding model with rotated angle dependent long-range hopping and intrinsic spin-orbit coupling, we show that distortion reconstructs both the dispersion and topology of the kagome band manifold. The flat band descendant develops distinct bandwidth regimes associated with a redistribution of its extrema in momentum space. Simultaneously, symmetry-related band inversions generate quantized Chern number transfer whose parity is fixed by the multiplicity of the touching points, thereby determining the gap-resolved Z2 topology. The accompanying Berry curvature evolution produces characteristic anomalous Hall and Nernst responses. These results identify geometric deformation as a common microscopic origin of flat band and topological reconstruction in kagome systems.

AI.tldr: Using a distorted kagome tight-binding model with angle-dependent long-range hopping and intrinsic SOC, the authors show that lattice distortion simultaneously reconstructs flat band dispersion and band topology, linking geometric deformation to quantized Chern number transfer, gap-resolved Z2 topology, and anomalous transport responses.
AI.motivation: Flat bands and nontrivial topology are key features of kagome electronic structure, but they are typically studied in idealized lattices. In real distorted kagome materials, structural deformation reorganizes electronic pathways, yet a microscopic understanding of how distortion controls flat band dispersion and band topology remains missing.
AI.method: A distorted kagome tight-binding model is constructed that includes a rotated-angle-dependent long-range hopping term and intrinsic spin-orbit coupling, and its band dispersion, band inversions, Chern number transfer, Z2 topology, and Berry curvature are analyzed.
AI.result: Distortion reconstructs both the dispersion and topology of the kagome band manifold. The flat band descendant shows distinct bandwidth regimes tied to a redistribution of its momentum-space extrema, while symmetry-related band inversions produce quantized Chern number transfer whose parity is fixed by the multiplicity of touching points, setting the gap-resolved Z2 topology. The Berry curvature evolution yields characteristic anomalous Hall and Nernst responses.
AI.conclusion: Geometric deformation acts as a common microscopic origin of flat band and topological reconstruction in kagome systems, providing a unified framework connecting lattice distortion to dispersion, topology, and transport signatures.

title: Magnetic-field-activated transport from band geometry in gapped nodal-line semimetals
summary: We develop a nonperturbative semiclassical theory of magnetotransport in gapped nodal-line semimetals, retaining the full magnetic-field dependence of Berry-curvature and orbital-magnetic-moment corrections. Starting from a minimal two-band model, we derive exact expressions for both the intrinsic Hall response and the dissipative Fermi-surface conductivity, valid to all orders in the magnetic field within the semiclassical regime. We show that the orbital magnetic moment reconstructs the geometrically active Fermi surface, breaking the azimuthal cancellation imposed by the nodal-line geometry and thereby activating an intrinsic Hall current that is absent at zero magnetic field. The Hall response exhibits a pronounced nonmonotonic dependence on the chemical potential and a strongly nonlinear magnetic-field evolution, reflecting the redistribution of geometrically active states around the nodal ring. We further demonstrate that the Fermi-surface conductivities recover the conventional Drude behavior in the weak-field limit, while acquiring quadratic and ultimately nonperturbative magnetic-field corrections together with a field-induced transport anisotropy that gives rise to a measurable planar Hall effect at intermediate fields. Both the intrinsic and dissipative responses are strongly enhanced when the Fermi level lies close to the nodal ring, where Berry curvature and orbital magnetic moment are largest. Our results identify magnetic-field-activated geometric transport as a characteristic signature of nodal-line semimetals and provide a unified framework for describing magnetotransport beyond perturbative magnetic-field expansions, together with experimentally accessible signatures of orbital-magnetic-moment physics.

It derives exact intrinsic Hall and dissipative Fermi-surface conductivities valid to all orders in the field, showing that the orbital magnetic moment activates a field-induced intrinsic Hall current, nonlinear magnetotransport, and a planar Hall effect, with strong enhancements near the nodal ring.
AI.motivation: Conventional perturbative treatments of magnetotransport in nodal-line semimetals do not capture the full magnetic-field dependence of geometric quantities such as Berry curvature and the orbital magnetic moment. A unified, nonperturbative semiclassical framework is needed to reveal how field-activated geometric transport manifests as a characteristic signature of these materials.
AI.method: Starting from a minimal two-band model, the authors construct a nonperturbative semiclassical theory of magnetotransport in gapped nodal-line semimetals. They retain the full magnetic-field dependence of Berry-curvature and orbital-magnetic-moment corrections and derive exact expressions for the intrinsic Hall response and the dissipative Fermi-surface conductivity, valid to all orders in the magnetic field within the semiclassical regime.

The work provides a unified framework for describing magnetotransport beyond perturbative magnetic-field expansions and offers experimentally accessible signatures of orbital-magnetic-moment physics.

title: Tuning the secondary electron yield and electronic conductivity of MgZnO multilayers synthesized by Atomic layer deposition
summary: Secondary electron emission (SEE), arising from the interaction of energetic electrons with material surfaces, can induce deleterious effects in vacuum radio-frequency (RF) systems, notably multipacting, thereby degrading performance and threatening device integrity. Despite extensive efforts, effective and widely adopted mitigation strategies remain limited. Here, we report an approach to simultaneously tailor SEE and electrical conductivity using nanometric multi-element multilayers deposited by atomic layer deposition (ALD). The design and fabrication of these heterostructures are presented, and a range of films is systematically characterized to establish correlations between emission properties, electrical conductivity, chemical and structural features. We demonstrate that such heterostructures enable combinations of total electron emission yield (TEEY) and conductivity unattainable in single-phase materials, including regimes combining high TEEY with relatively high conductivity and low TEEY with low conductivities. These results open new avenues for the rational design of functional surfaces for vacuum electronic applications.

AI.tldr: This paper reports nanometric multi-element multilayers grown by atomic layer deposition (ALD) that allow independent tailoring of secondary electron emission (SEE) and electrical conductivity, achieving TEEY-conductivity combinations impossible in single-phase materials.
AI.motivation: Secondary electron emission from energetic electrons interacting with material surfaces causes deleterious effects in vacuum RF systems, notably multipacting, degrading performance and threatening device integrity. Despite extensive efforts, effective and widely adopted mitigation strategies remain limited.
AI.method: Design and fabrication of nanometric multi-element multilayer heterostructures deposited by atomic layer deposition (ALD). A range of films is systematically characterized to establish correlations between emission properties, electrical conductivity, and chemical and structural features.
AI.result: The heterostructures enable combinations of total electron emission yield (TEEY) and conductivity unattainable in single-phase materials, including regimes combining high TEEY with relatively high conductivity, and low TEEY with low conductivities.
AI.conclusion: ALD-grown multi-element multilayers allow simultaneous tailoring of SEE and electrical conductivity, opening new avenues for the rational design of functional surfaces for vacuum electronic applications.

title: Quantum metric induced nonlinear transport in the hidden loop-current phase of kagome metal RbV$_3$Sb$_5$
summary: A hidden low-temperature phase with possible loop-current order has been proposed in the kagome metals AV$_3$Sb$_5$ (A=K, Rb or Cs), but its experimental signatures remain subtle and indirect. Here, we use third-order nonlinear transport to probe this hidden phase in RbV$_3$Sb$_5$. At ~35 K, the longitudinal cubic response develops a strong kink and pronounced directional anisotropy with a strong departure from common relaxation time scaling, while the transverse cubic response acquires a magnetic field-odd component at the same temperature. Their coincident onset identifies the third-harmonic response as a sensitive marker of the low-temperature electronic reconstruction with time-reversal broken symmetry. Crucially, we find that the quantum metric quadrupole contributes directly to the longitudinal third-order response. In a loop-current charge-density-wave model, its direction selective enhancement captures the observed angular reconstruction. Our work shows how higher-order nonlinear transport translates subtle changes in electronic symmetry and quantum metric into measurable electrical signatures in quantum materials that is important for studying complex electronic phases of matter.

AI.tldr: Third-order nonlinear transport reveals a hidden time-reversal-symmetry-broken phase in RbV$_3$Sb$_5$ at ~35 K, where the quantum metric quadrupole contributes directly to the longitudinal third-order response and its direction-selective enhancement captures the observed angular reconstruction.
AI.motivation: A hidden low-temperature phase with possible loop-current order has been proposed in kagome metals AV$_3$Sb$_5$, but its experimental signatures remain subtle and indirect, motivating a sensitive probe to detect this hidden phase and its symmetry breaking.
AI.method: The authors use third-order nonlinear transport to probe the hidden phase in RbV$_3$Sb$_5$, measuring the longitudinal and transverse cubic (third-harmonic) responses, and analyze their temperature dependence, angular dependence, and magnetic-field symmetry. They further model the results within a loop-current charge-density-wave framework, focusing on the role of the quantum metric quadrupole.
AI.result: At ~35 K, the longitudinal cubic response develops a strong kink and pronounced directional anisotropy with a strong departure from common relaxation time scaling, while the transverse cubic response acquires a magnetic field-odd component at the same temperature. Their coincident onset identifies the third-harmonic response as a sensitive marker of the low-temperature electronic reconstruction with time-reversal broken symmetry. The quantum metric quadrupole contributes directly to the longitudinal third-order response, and in a loop-current charge-density-wave model its direction-selective enhancement captures the observed angular reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: Higher-order nonlinear transport translates subtle changes in electronic symmetry and quantum metric into measurable electrical signatures in quantum materials, offering a valuable tool for studying complex electronic phases of matter.

title: Artificial versus Natural Atoms: The uncanny capability of the many-body Schrödinger equation to produce emergent behavior
comment: Review paper, 100 pages with 50 figures. For related papers, see https://sites.gatech.edu/cyannouleas/
summary: The paper reviews the theoretical and experimental progress achieved in the last 25 years in understanding the novel physics of artificial atoms and molecules as arising from the formation of Wigner molecules (WMs) of localized (to a stronger or lesser extent) fermionic or bosonic particles, which are finite quantum analogs of the more familiar bulk Wigner crystal. The term artificial atoms, as used here, encompasses a broad range of recently fabricated quantum nanodevices and experimental apparatuses consisting of a finite number of mutually repelling confined particles, including two-dimensional semiconductor and moiré transition metal dichalcogenide quantum dots, as well as trapped ultracold neutral atoms or ions. These nano-sized or micro-sized artificial devices and apparatuses (in single well or multi-well of variable-shape arrangements) hold a great promise for technological applications in the field of quantum information and quantum computers, as well as for advances in fundamental many-body physics. Prominent quantum effects of Wigner molecularization are the strong quenching of the spectral energy gaps, the appearance of rovibational spectra (in analogy with natural molecules), entanglement, and pinning due to an external perturbation. In high magnetic fields or at rapid rotation, WMs provide an alternative theory to the fractional quantum Hall effect. The physics of Wigner molecules is shown to derive from the solutions of the many-body Schrödinger equation (MBSE) in the regime of strong interparticle correlations arising from the dominance of the potential over the kinetic energy, or from a high magnetic field, as well as from a rapid rotation... (continues in the paper).

AI.tldr: A review of 25 years of progress on Wigner molecules—finite quantum analogs of bulk Wigner crystals—in artificial atoms and molecules, covering their formation, emergent quantum effects, and applications.
AI.motivation: To consolidate theoretical and experimental progress in understanding the novel physics of artificial atoms and molecules formed from Wigner molecules, driven by interest in quantum information, quantum computing, and fundamental many-body physics.
AI.method: Analysis of the many-body Schrödinger equation in the strong-correlation regime (potential dominant over kinetic energy, or under high magnetic field / rapid rotation) for confined repelling fermionic or bosonic particles in various artificial systems.
AI.result: Wigner molecularization produces strong quenching of spectral energy gaps, rovibrational spectra analogous to natural molecules, entanglement, and pinning due to external perturbation; it also offers an alternative theory to the fractional quantum Hall effect.
AI.conclusion: Wigner molecule physics forms a unifying framework spanning semiconductor, moiré, and cold-atom systems, with promising implications for quantum technologies and many-body physics.

title: Derivation of the General Solution of the Black-Scholes Boundary-Value Problem
summary: There are infinitely many functions that satisfy the Black-Scholes partial differential equation and the terminal condition corresponding to the European call option. This means that the Black-Scholes formula, which led to the award of the 1997 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences, is not the unique solution, as was once assumed. Consequently, it violates the law of one price, one of the fundamental laws of economics and finance. In this article, we present a rigorous derivation of these solutions to the Black-Scholes boundary value problem.

AI.tldr: The Black-Scholes formula is shown to be non-unique: infinitely many functions satisfy the Black-Scholes PDE with the European call terminal condition, implying a violation of the law of one price. The authors give a rigorous derivation of these solutions to the Black-Scholes boundary value problem.
AI.motivation: The Black-Scholes formula is widely treated as the unique solution to its boundary value problem, a premise underpinning its Nobel-recognized status. The authors challenge this assumption by showing that non-uniqueness undermines the law of one price, a fundamental principle of economics and finance.
AI.method: Rigorous mathematical derivation of the family of solutions to the Black-Scholes boundary value problem, i.e., the PDE together with the European call terminal condition.
AI.result: There exist infinitely many functions satisfying both the Black-Scholes PDE and the European call terminal condition; hence the Black-Scholes formula is not the unique solution as previously assumed.
AI.conclusion: Non-uniqueness of solutions to the Black-Scholes boundary value problem implies a violation of the law of one price, and the paper provides a rigorous derivation of these multiple solutions.

title: Facet- and thickness-dependent band-edge alignment at ZrSe\texorpdfstring{$_3$}{3} surfaces: hybrid-functional calculations with spin-orbit coupling
summary: Transition-metal trichalcogenides MX$_3$ are quasi-one-dimensional van der Waals materials whose layers form through lateral chain binding, giving them an interlayer cleavage plane and in-plane electronic anisotropy. Among them, ZrSe$_3$ is stable under ambient conditions and semiconducting. Exfoliated crystals expose four crystallographic planes, and electrocatalytic measurements on an individual crystal assigned the hydrogen evolution activity to the high-energy (210) facet rather than to the basal plane. Those non-basal surfaces remain uncharacterized, since the available calculations treat either the bulk crystal or the free-standing basal monolayer. Here, we compute the surface energies and the equilibrium morphology of these four surfaces with a dispersion-corrected semilocal functional, and their band-edge alignment with the HSE06 hybrid functional including spin-orbit coupling. The surface energies span nearly an order of magnitude, from \SI{0.097}{\joule\per\meter\squared} for (001) to \SI{0.869}{\joule\per\meter\squared} for (010), and the Wulff shape exposes the four observed planes with area fractions of \SI{17.1}{\percent}, \SI{4.4}{\percent}, \SI{71.4}{\percent}, and \SI{7.0}{\percent}. The ionization potential varies by \SI{0.45}{\electronvolt} between facets and the electron affinity by \SI{0.80}{\electronvolt}, the gap of (210) falls from 1.43 to \SI{0.94}{\electronvolt} between 10 and \SI{23}{\angstrom}, and (010) remains metallic. The facets separate according to whether the cut preserves or distorts the Se-Se dimer, and the distorted dimers concentrate the frontier states. Because the same dimer governs the bulk electronic structure of the MX$_3$ family, the criterion transfers to the related trichalcogenides.

AI.tldr: Dispersion-corrected DFT surface energies and HSE06+SOC band-edge alignment for the four crystallographic facets of ZrSe3 reveal an order-of-magnitude anisotropy in surface energy, a Wulff shape reproducing the observed planes, and facet-dependent ionization potentials and gaps controlled by Se-Se dimer distortion.
AI.motivation: Transition-metal trichalcogenides MX3 are quasi-1D van der Waals materials whose exfoliated crystals expose four crystallographic planes, and prior electrocatalytic measurements assigned hydrogen evolution activity to the high-energy (210) facet. However, non-basal surfaces remained uncharacterized because existing calculations treated either the bulk crystal or the free-standing basal monolayer, leaving surface energies, morphology, and band-edge alignment of these facets unknown.
AI.method: Surface energies and equilibrium morphology (Wulff construction) of the four surfaces were computed with a dispersion-corrected semilocal functional; band-edge alignment was obtained with the HSE06 hybrid functional including spin-orbit coupling.
AI.result: Surface energies span nearly an order of magnitude, from 0.097 J/m2 for (001) to 0.869 J/m2 for (010). The Wulff shape exposes all four observed planes with area fractions of 17.1%, 4.4%, 71.4%, and 7.0%. The ionization potential varies by 0.45 eV and the electron affinity by 0.80 eV between facets; the gap of (210) decreases from 1.43 to 0.94 eV between 10 and 23 Angstrom, and (010) remains metallic.
AI.conclusion: Facets separate according to whether the cut preserves or distorts the Se-Se dimer, with distorted dimers concentrating the frontier states. Because the same dimer governs the bulk electronic structure of the MX3 family, this criterion transfers to related trichalcogenides.

title: Ionization-Driven Dehydrogenation and Molecular Growth in Gas-Phase Adamantane Clusters
comment: Article is submitted to "The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters"
summary: We investigate fragmentation and molecular growth induced by keV ions in initially neutral gas-phase adamantane clusters, the simplest diamondoid molecule (Ad, C$_{10}$H$_{16}$). Using time-of-flight mass spectrometry in combination with quantum-chemical calculations, we find that intact cluster cations undergo extensive dehydrogenation. We also observe a distinct distribution of singly charged products with masses predominantly between those of the adamantane monomer and dimer cations. We attribute these species to ion-induced growth products and interpret their formation considering the smallest cluster cation, [Ad]$_2^+$, using quantum-chemical calculations. Our results demonstrate that ionization strongly reorganizes the dimer geometry, facilitating H$_2$ elimination and intermolecular covalent C--C bond formation. Weakly bound adamantane clusters are thereby transformed into covalently bound carbonaceous species with a strong preference for specific molecular structures. These findings provide new insight into ionization-driven molecular growth in saturated hydrocarbon systems contributing to the understanding of molecular complexification, with implications for chemical physics and astrochemistry.

AI.tldr: KeV ion irradiation of neutral adamantane (C10H16) clusters causes extensive dehydrogenation and transforms weakly bound clusters into covalently bonded carbonaceous species via H2 elimination and intermolecular C–C bond formation, revealing ionization-driven molecular growth in saturated hydrocarbons.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to understand how ionization drives molecular growth and complexification in saturated hydrocarbon systems, using adamantane (the simplest diamondoid) as a model. This is relevant to chemical physics and astrochemistry, where molecular complexification in carbonaceous environments is of interest.
AI.method: KeV ion irradiation of initially neutral gas-phase adamantane clusters was studied using time-of-flight mass spectrometry combined with quantum-chemical calculations. The smallest cluster cation, [Ad]2+, was analyzed computationally to interpret the observed product formation.
AI.result: Intact cluster cations undergo extensive dehydrogenation. A distinct distribution of singly charged products appears with masses predominantly between the adamantane monomer and dimer cations, attributed to ion-induced growth products. Calculations show ionization strongly reorganizes the dimer geometry, facilitating H2 elimination and intermolecular covalent C–C bond formation, with a strong preference for specific molecular structures.
AI.conclusion: Ionization transforms weakly bound adamantane clusters into covalently bound carbonaceous species, providing new insight into ionization-driven molecular growth in saturated hydrocarbon systems and contributing to understanding molecular complexification, with implications for chemical physics and astrochemistry.

title: Conservation-Syndrome Quantum Error Correction for Lattice-Boltzmann Quantum Algorithms
summary: Reliable multistep quantum lattice-Boltzmann evolution requires controlling computational faults. When ideal collision preserves encoded mass and momentum exactly, changes in those charges can provide syndromes for selected faults at the post-collision checkpoint. A fault that shifts one population then leaves a unique mass-momentum residual labeled by the lattice velocity. A coherent reference register stores the expected charges, so the same test remains valid while the physical fluid charges vary across the lattice. Single bit flips on population number registers occupy disjoint syndrome sectors and satisfy the Knill-Laflamme condition. A state-vector demonstration on eighteen data qubits of the two-dimensional nine-velocity lattice (D2Q9) recovers that single-bit family to double-precision roundoff. Conservation still leaves a fifteen-dimensional kinetic nullspace on the three-dimensional nineteen-velocity lattice (D3Q19). Exact multiple-relaxation-time (MRT) streaming analysis ranks those charge-preserving modes by the order at which they return to density or momentum. A classical D3Q19 decaying-flow simulation at moderate Reynolds number then injects about $1.75\times10^4$ selected single-population shifts per realization. Recovery of that alphabet returns the trajectory to floating-point roundoff. The quantum statements assume an ideal charge-preserving collision and a reliable reference. The result is an inner recovery map for a stated charge-changing alphabet together with a kinetic classification of the unresolved sector.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a syndrome-based error-detection framework for quantum lattice-Boltzmann evolution, using mass and momentum conservation of the ideal collision as checks. Post-collision charge residuals detect single-population faults, and a coherent reference register keeps the test valid across a varying lattice. A D2Q9 state-vector demonstration recovers the single-bit fault family to double-precision roundoff, while a D3Q19 MRT analysis classifies the remaining charge-preserving nullspace and shows recovery of a $1.75\times10^4$-shift alphabet in a classical decaying-flow simulation.
AI.motivation: Reliable multistep quantum lattice-Boltzmann evolution demands control of computational faults. Because the ideal collision exactly preserves encoded mass and momentum, deviations in these charges can serve as fault syndromes at the post-collision checkpoint, motivating a conservation-based detection and recovery scheme.
AI.method: A coherent reference register stores expected charges so the syndrome test remains valid despite physical fluid-charge variation across the lattice. Single bit flips on population number registers are shown to occupy disjoint syndrome sectors satisfying the Knill-Laflamme condition. A state-vector simulation on eighteen data qubits of the D2Q9 lattice demonstrates recovery of the single-bit fault family. For D3Q19, exact multiple-relaxation-time (MRT) streaming analysis ranks the charge-preserving modes of the fifteen-dimensional kinetic nullspace by the order at which they return to density or momentum. In the D3Q19 decaying-flow simulation, recovery of the selected shift alphabet returns the trajectory to floating-point roundoff. The MRT analysis provides a kinetic classification of the unresolved charge-preserving sector.
AI.conclusion: Conservation-based syndromes enable an inner recovery map for a stated charge-changing alphabet in quantum lattice-Boltzmann evolution, complemented by a kinetic classification of the unresolved sector, under the assumptions of an ideal charge-preserving collision and a reliable reference.

title: Linear and nonlinear transport responses of topological nodal-line semimetals
summary: Topological nodal-line semimetals are three-dimensional quantum materials characterized by band crossings that form closed loops in momentum space. In $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric realizations, these nodal rings are stabilized in the absence of spin-orbit coupling, giving rise to drumhead surface states and unconventional transport responses. In this work, we study charge transport across a nodal-line semimetal containing a finite electrostatic barrier, with both leads described by the same equilibrium material. By solving the corresponding scattering problem, we show that the transmission across the barrier exhibits {Klein-tunneling behavior protected at normal incidence by the nodal topology}, despite the extended nodal-line dispersion, which can be traced back to Berry-curvature-induced momentum locking. Using the Landauer-Büttiker formalism, we derive general expressions for the linear and nonlinear conductances, including both longitudinal and Hall components, and evaluate them at zero and finite temperature. Our analytical and numerical results elucidate the dependence of the conductance on barrier height and width, as well as on a $\mathcal{PT}$-breaking mass term. We identify distinct transport regimes in which nonlinear contributions are strongly enhanced and transverse Hall currents emerge, providing clear transport signatures of nodal-line topology and suggesting potential routes toward device applications.

AI.tldr: This work studies charge transport across a $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric topological nodal-line semimetal with a finite electrostatic barrier between identical leads, showing Klein-tunneling behavior protected at normal incidence by nodal topology and Berry-curvature-induced momentum locking, and deriving linear and nonlinear (longitudinal and Hall) conductances via Landauer-Büttiker formalism.
AI.motivation: Nodal-line semimetals host band crossings forming closed loops and, in $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric realizations, give rise to drumhead surface states and unconventional transport responses. The authors aim to clarify charge transport through such materials in the presence of a finite electrostatic barrier and to establish transport signatures of nodal-line topology, including nonlinear and transverse responses.
AI.method: The authors solve the scattering problem for charge transport across a nodal-line semimetal with a finite electrostatic barrier, with both leads made of the same equilibrium material. They then apply the Landauer-Büttiker formalism to derive general expressions for linear and nonlinear conductances, including longitudinal and Hall components, evaluated at zero and finite temperature. Analytical and numerical calculations examine dependence on barrier height and width and on a $\mathcal{PT}$-breaking mass term.

Conductances depend on barrier height, barrier width, and the $\mathcal{PT}$-breaking mass term. Distinct transport regimes are identified in which nonlinear contributions are strongly enhanced and transverse Hall currents emerge.
AI.conclusion: The derived longitudinal and Hall conductances, including nonlinear contributions, provide clear transport signatures of nodal-line topology and suggest potential routes toward device applications.

title: Uniform-Charge-Density $d$-Wave Superconductivity in the Pure $t$-$J$ Model at $1/8$ Doping on an Infinite Cylinder
comment: 7 pages (incl. references) + 3 pages Supplemental Material; 7 figures
summary: The ground state of the square-lattice $t$-$J$ model at $1/8$ hole doping has been the subject of a long-standing controversy, with conflicting numerical reports of stripe order versus superconductivity. Here, we address this debate using the variational uniform matrix product state (VUMPS) method, which optimizes the wave function directly in the thermodynamic limit along the cylinder axis and eliminates the boundary pinning effects that can arise in finite-cylinder calculations. On an infinite cylinder of circumference $L_y = 8$, we find a uniform-charge-density $d$-wave superconducting ground state with quasi-long-range pairing correlations. The dominant pairing occurs at zero center-of-mass momentum, while no sizable finite-momentum pairing component is detected. Twisted-boundary-condition calculations reveal a finite superconducting phase stiffness, with the order-parameter phase winding smoothly to follow the applied flux, providing an independent probe of the robustness of the superconductivity. Moreover, both charge and spin correlations decay rapidly, with no signatures of long-range stripe or magnetic order, in contrast to an $L_y=6$ cylinder at $1/6$ doping where the same method readily identifies stripe order. Our results provide methodologically distinct evidence in the long-standing stripe--superconductivity debate in the pure $t$-$J$ model and reveal uniform $d$-wave superconductivity in a minimal model of doped Mott insulators.

AI.tldr: VUMPS on infinite cylinders shows that the 1/8-doped square-lattice t-J model hosts a uniform d-wave superconducting ground state with quasi-long-range pairing, no stripe order, and finite phase stiffness.
AI.motivation: The ground state of the square-lattice t-J model at 1/8 hole doping is highly controversial, with conflicting numerical results reporting either stripe order or superconductivity. Finite-cylinder calculations may suffer from boundary pinning effects that bias the outcome, motivating a thermodynamic-limit approach.
AI.method: Variational uniform matrix product state (VUMPS), which optimizes the wave function directly in the thermodynamic limit along the cylinder axis, avoiding boundary pinning. Calculations on an infinite cylinder with circumference L_y=8 and 1/8 doping, including twisted-boundary-condition probes of phase stiffness; compared against an L_y=6 cylinder at 1/6 doping.
AI.result: At L_y=8 and 1/8 doping: a uniform-charge-density d-wave superconducting ground state with quasi-long-range pairing correlations. Dominant pairing at zero center-of-mass momentum, no sizable finite-momentum pairing. Twisted-boundary calculations give finite superconducting phase stiffness with the order-parameter phase winding smoothly with applied flux. Charge and spin correlations decay rapidly, with no long-range stripe or magnetic order. In contrast, the same method identifies stripe order on the L_y=6 cylinder at 1/6 doping.
AI.conclusion: Methodologically distinct evidence in the long-standing stripe-superconductivity debate supports uniform d-wave superconductivity in the pure t-J model at 1/8 doping, revealing a minimal model of doped Mott insulators.

title: Crossover of Scaling Behaviors of Work Cumulants in a Driven Gaussian Field Theory
summary: We derive the finite-temperature characteristic function of work (CFW) for a driven $O(N)$ Gaussian field theory and obtain closed-form expressions for all zero-temperature excess-work cumulants. For gapped protocols, we use adiabatic perturbation theory (APT) to derive the $τ_Q^{-2}$ scaling for protocols with a nonzero first derivative at either boundary, where $τ_Q$ is the protocol duration; smoother boundaries lead to faster decay. For power-law protocols approaching the critical point with exponent $p$, we determine the competition between critical excitations and the regular contribution. The $n$th cumulant's critical contribution follows Kibble--Zurek (KZ) scaling $τ_Q^{-p(d+n)/(p+2)}$ for $d+n<2p+4$, acquires a logarithmic correction $τ_Q^{-2p}\logτ_Q$ at $d+n=2p+4$, and scales as $τ_Q^{-2p}$ above this condition, where $d$ is the spatial dimension. This analytical study of the APT--KZ crossover in a solvable model provides a basis for studying their competition in interacting field theories.

AI.tldr: The paper derives the finite-temperature characteristic function of work (CFW) for a driven O(N) Gaussian field theory and obtains closed-form expressions for all zero-temperature excess-work cumulants, analyzing the adiabatic perturbation theory (APT)–Kibble–Zurek (KZ) crossover in this solvable model.
AI.motivation: Understanding the competition between adiabatic and critical (Kibble–Zurek) excitation mechanisms in driven quantum field theories requires a solvable model to benchmark and clarify the crossover, providing a foundation for studying interacting field theories.
AI.method: The authors derive the finite-temperature characteristic function of work for a driven O(N) Gaussian field theory, use adiabatic perturbation theory (APT) to analyze gapped protocols, and study power-law protocols approaching the critical point to determine the competition between critical excitations and regular contributions, examining cumulant scaling across dimensional conditions.
