For power-law protocols with exponent p near criticality, the nth cumulant's critical contribution follows KZ scaling τ_Q^{-p(d+n)/(p+2)} for d+n<2p+4, acquires a logarithmic correction τ_Q^{-2p}log τ_Q at d+n=2p+4, and scales as τ_Q^{-2p} above this condition, where d is the spatial dimension.
AI.conclusion: The analytical study of the APT–KZ crossover in a solvable O(N) Gaussian field theory provides a basis for studying the competition between adiabatic and critical excitations in interacting field theories.

title: Fracture of Lattice Materials from Low to High Relative Density
summary: Lattice materials have highly tunable mechanical properties that are controlled by their internal geometry and base material behavior. While fracture models for low-density lattices are well-established, the fracture of lattices at relative densities above 30% remains largely unexplored. Here, we present an analytical model that combines homogenization methods and blunt-crack fracture theory to predict the fracture toughness of triangular and hexagonal lattices over a wide range of relative densities. Finite element modeling corroborates the analytical framework and demonstrates a shift in failure mechanisms between low and high relative density regimes. At high relative densities, failure is dominated by nodal stress concentrations, which are strongly influenced by the local crack-tip geometry and the macroscopic crack path. Significant stress redistribution is observed as the relative orientation and lattice fillet radius are varied, resulting in increased fracture toughness relative to baseline geometries. Furthermore, quasi-brittle poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) lattices achieve about a 1.6x enhancement in fracture toughness relative to perfectly brittle lattices as failure is delayed by localized plasticity. Notably, some quasi-brittle lattices are found to exceed the fracture toughness of their base material -- a feature only possible when the cell size is large compared to the base material's plastic radius. Experiments on lattice fracture specimens made from laser-cut PMMA validate the finite element results, but highlight the stochastic nature of failure in brittle lattice materials, especially at higher relative densities.

AI.tldr: The paper develops an analytical fracture model for triangular and hexagonal lattices across a wide range of relative densities (including >30%), combining homogenization with blunt-crack theory. FEM and PMMA experiments reveal a shift to nodal-stress-dominated failure at high density, and quasi-brittle lattices can exceed the toughness of their base material.
AI.motivation: Fracture models for low-density lattices are well established, but the fracture behavior of lattices at relative densities above 30% remains largely unexplored, leaving a gap in understanding and predicting toughness in this regime.
AI.method: An analytical model combining homogenization methods with blunt-crack fracture theory is used to predict fracture toughness of triangular and hexagonal lattices over a wide density range. Finite element modeling is employed to corroborate the framework. Quasi-brittle PMMA lattices fabricated by laser cutting are tested experimentally.
AI.result: FEM confirms the analytical framework and reveals a failure-mechanism shift between low- and high-density regimes. At high relative densities, failure is dominated by nodal stress concentrations sensitive to local crack-tip geometry and macroscopic crack path. Varying relative orientation and lattice fillet radius causes significant stress redistribution, increasing fracture toughness over baseline geometries. Quasi-brittle PMMA lattices show ~1.6x toughness enhancement vs. perfectly brittle ones due to delayed failure from localized plasticity; some exceed their base material's toughness, which requires large cell size relative to the base material's plastic radius. Experiments validate FEM results but highlight the stochastic nature of brittle lattice failure, especially at higher densities.
AI.conclusion: The proposed homogenization plus blunt-crack framework predicts lattice fracture toughness across densities and captures the high-density failure regime governed by nodal stress concentrations. Geometry (orientation, fillet radius) and base-material quasi-brittleness can be exploited to enhance toughness, with quasi-brittle lattices potentially surpassing their base material when cell size greatly exceeds the plastic radius. Brittle lattice failure is stochastic, particularly at high relative density.

title: The NewMag crystal-field code for f-element systems: Implementation for extended active spaces, second-order correlated energies, and generalisation to fn configurations
summary: We report a massive update of the NewMag program, which enables to extract Stevens crystal-field parameters (CFPs) after relativistic and multiconfigurational calculations are performed. The code can now post-treat ORCA and OpenMolcas outputs that contain state-average complete active space self-consistend field (SA-CASSCF) calculations with minimal or extended active spaces, second-order NEVPT2 or CASPT2 calculations, and spin-orbit configuration interaction (SOCI) calculations. Stevens parameters are extracted following the original Stevens convention with the so-called "extended" parameters. Rotation invariant indicators are also computed, after applying a correction of the parameter values to ensure normalization, following Rudowicz. At the SOCI level, the spin-orbit coupling (SOC) constant is also extracted within a spherical approximation of the SOC operator. For all the reference calculation levels, the model spectrum is reconstructed, allowing a direct assessment of its quality. The reported implementation is successfully applicable to f-element systems with a non-void, non-half-filled/empty or non-full f shell, that is for f^n configurations with n != 0, != 7 and != 14. Similarities and differences with the SINGLE_ANISO and AILFT codes are discussed. With selected examples, we showcase the interest of determining CFPs in f-element systems to understand their magnetic and optical properties in general, and more specifically the added value of NewMag. Finally, application of this approach to d-element systems is discussed, to reveal when it readily and successfully applies and when it may fail in reproducing satisfactorily the ab initio energies.

AI.tldr: This paper reports a major update of the NewMag program, which extracts Stevens crystal-field parameters (CFPs) from relativistic multiconfigurational ab initio calculations, now supporting ORCA and OpenMolcas outputs at SA-CASSCF, NEVPT2/CASPT2, and SOCI levels, with validation for f- and d-element systems.
AI.motivation: Crystal-field parameters provide a compact, chemically intuitive description linking ab initio electronic structure to the magnetic and optical properties of f- and d-element systems. Existing tools (e.g., SINGLE_ANISO, AILFT) have limitations in the range of post-treatment levels and the convention/robustness of extracted parameters, motivating a more versatile and standardized implementation.
AI.method: NewMag post-processes ORCA and OpenMolcas outputs from SA-CASSCF (minimal or extended active spaces), NEVPT2/CASPT2, and SOCI calculations. Stevens CFPs are extracted following the original Stevens convention using "extended" parameters. Rotation-invariant indicators are computed after a Rudowicz-type normalization correction of the parameter values. At the SOCI level, the spin-orbit coupling constant is additionally extracted within a spherical approximation of the SOC operator. Model spectra are reconstructed at all reference calculation levels to assess quality.
AI.result: The implementation is successfully applicable to f-element systems with non-void, non-half-filled/empty, and non-full f shells (f^n, n != 0, 7, 14). Similarities and differences with SINGLE_ANISO and AILFT are discussed. Selected examples demonstrate the value of determining CFPs for understanding magnetic and optical properties, and the specific added value of NewMag. Application to d-element systems is also examined, identifying when the approach succeeds and when it fails to reproduce ab initio energies satisfactorily.
AI.conclusion: NewMag provides a generalized, multi-level tool for extracting Stevens CFPs, SOC constants, and rotation-invariant indicators from relativistic multiconfigurational calculations, with broad applicability to f-element systems and a delimited but useful range for d-element systems.

title: GEM: An implementation of the ghost-Gutzwiller approximation for simulating interacting quantum systems
summary: We present GEM (Ghost Embedding Method), an open-source software package written in Python for computing equilibrium properties of strongly correlated electronic systems within the ghost-Gutzwiller approximation method. GEM provides a computationally efficient framework for studying multi-orbital lattice models. It supports zero- and finite-temperature calculations and symmetry broken phases. It is integrated with the TRIQS ecosystem, providing tools for model construction, self-consistent solution, and evaluation of physical observables. We first detail the method's theoretical formulation, then we present the software architecture, and finally we introduce some practical workflow, which also validates the implementation against established results. In particular, we illustrate the capabilities of GEM through multiorbital and finite-temperature applications and discuss its computational cost relative to more demanding quantum embedding approaches.

AI.tldr: GEM is an open-source Python package implementing the ghost-Gutzwiller approximation for efficient computation of equilibrium properties in strongly correlated multi-orbital lattice models, integrated with the TRIQS ecosystem.
AI.motivation: Equilibrium properties of strongly correlated electronic systems are challenging to compute. The ghost-Gutzwiller approximation offers a computationally efficient alternative to more demanding quantum embedding approaches, but lacked a dedicated, integrated software implementation supporting multi-orbital, finite-temperature, and symmetry-broken phases.
AI.method: The authors formulate the theoretical basis of the ghost-Gutzwiller approximation and describe the architecture of GEM, a Python package integrated with TRIQS for model construction, self-consistent solution, and evaluation of physical observables. The implementation is validated via practical workflows against established results, and applied to multiorbital and finite-temperature cases.
AI.result: GEM reproduces established results, validating the implementation. It demonstrates capability for multiorbital and finite-temperature applications, and offers reduced computational cost compared to more demanding quantum embedding approaches.
AI.conclusion: GEM provides an efficient, open-source framework for studying strongly correlated multi-orbital lattice models within the ghost-Gutzwiller approximation, supporting zero- and finite-temperature calculations and symmetry-broken phases, positioned as a lower-cost alternative to heavier quantum embedding methods.

title: Interlayer coupling between twisted graphenes through atomically-precise barriers
summary: Understanding and controlling interlayer coupling in van der Waals (vdW) materials is crucial for engineering novel electronic phenomena, including correlated states, topological phases, and superconductivity. Twisted bilayer graphene (TBG) offers a highly tunable platform to explore how interlayer orientation and separation influence quantum transport and moiré physics. Here, we introduce a method for achieving precise, atomic-scale control of interlayer coupling in TBG using dual-gated devices separated by ultrathin, thickness-tunable hBN spacers. This approach enables systematic control of interlayer interactions, demonstrating that the critical displacement field required for electron-hole bilayer behavior decreases as the layer separation increases at a fixed twist angle. Remarkably, at small twist angles, moiré-related side peaks persist even when layers are separated by tetralayers of hBN (approximately 1.3 nm), indicating robust interlayer band hybridization. By combining atomic-layer-precise control of interlayer coupling with independent twist angle tunability, our platform opens new avenues for discovering novel moiré physics governed by engineered interlayer coupling and moiré patterns.

AI.tldr: A dual-gated TBG device with thickness-tunable ultrathin hBN spacers enables atomic-scale control of interlayer coupling, revealing that the critical displacement field for electron-hole bilayer behavior decreases with layer separation, while moiré side peaks persist even at ~1.3 nm separation for small twist angles.
AI.motivation: Interlayer coupling in van der Waals materials governs emergent electronic phenomena such as correlated states, topological phases, and superconductivity. Twisted bilayer graphene provides a tunable platform for probing how interlayer orientation and separation affect quantum transport and moiré physics, but a method for precisely controlling interlayer coupling at the atomic scale while retaining twist-angle tunability has been lacking.
AI.method: The authors fabricate dual-gated TBG devices separated by ultrathin, thickness-tunable hBN spacers, enabling systematic and atomic-layer-precise control of interlayer separation independently of twist angle.
AI.result: The critical displacement field required for electron-hole bilayer behavior decreases as layer separation increases at fixed twist angle. At small twist angles, moiré-related side peaks persist even with tetralayer hBN spacers (~1.3 nm), indicating robust interlayer band hybridization.
AI.conclusion: Combining atomic-layer-precise control of interlayer coupling with independent twist-angle tunability provides a versatile platform for discovering novel moiré physics governed by engineered interlayer coupling and moiré patterns.

title: Correlation-assisted topological and metamagnetic transitions in Rashba-coupled superconductors: $t$-$J$-$U$ model study
summary: Unconventional superconductivity commonly emerges in systems characterized by strong electronic correlations, with layered copper-oxides serving as a canonical example. Observation of spin-momentum locking within Bi-family of the cuprates, compatible with the presence of non-negligible Rashba-type spin-orbit coupling (RSOC), calls for an investigation of the joint effects of electronic correlations and RSOC on pairing in copper-oxide and related superconductors. Employing statistically-consistent variational approximation (SGA), we carry out such an analysis by constructing the phase diagram for the case of square-lattice \textit{t-J-U} model incorporating RSOC. We also investigate the effects of time-reversal-symmetry breaking by Zeeman field, as well as characterize emergent topological superconducting (TSC) states. Chern number $C = \pm 4$ TSC is found in a broad regime of on-site Coulomb repulsion close to half-filling. The latter is not governed by correlations and emerges also within the weak-coupling Bogoliubov-de Gennes (BdG) scheme. Yet, we identify a distinct $C = \pm 2$ TSC state that is driven specifically by electronic correlations via a topological transition occurring with no bulk quasiparticle gap closure, and is accompanied by discontinuous metamagnetic and Lifshitz transitions. Moreover, a qualitatively distinct doping evolution of the $d$- and $p$-wave components of the underlying mixed-parity SC order parameter above the metal-to-insulator transition is demonstrated. Our work points toward the relevance of joint correlation and RSOC effects beyond BdG scheme to phase diagrams of RSOC-coupled superconductors.

AI.tldr: This work uses a statistically-consistent variational approximation (SGA) to study the square-lattice t-J-U model with Rashba spin-orbit coupling, mapping its phase diagram and identifying topological superconducting states, including a correlation-driven C = ±2 TSC state distinct from the weak-coupling C = ±4 state.
AI.motivation: Spin-momentum locking observed in Bi-family cuprates suggests non-negligible Rashba spin-orbit coupling (RSOC). This motivates investigating the joint effects of strong electronic correlations and RSOC on pairing in copper-oxide and related superconductors, a regime not captured by conventional weak-coupling treatments.
AI.method: The authors employ a statistically-consistent variational approximation (SGA) to construct the phase diagram of the square-lattice t-J-U model incorporating RSOC. They also include a Zeeman field to break time-reversal symmetry and characterize emergent topological superconducting (TSC) states, comparing with a weak-coupling Bogoliubov-de Gennes (BdG) scheme.
AI.result: A Chern number C = ±4 TSC is found in a broad regime of on-site Coulomb repulsion near half-filling; it is not governed by correlations and also appears in the weak-coupling BdG scheme. A distinct C = ±2 TSC state is identified that is driven specifically by electronic correlations via a topological transition occurring without bulk quasiparticle gap closure, accompanied by discontinuous metamagnetic and Lifshitz transitions. A qualitatively distinct doping evolution of the d- and p-wave components of the mixed-parity SC order parameter above the metal-to-insulator transition is also demonstrated.
AI.conclusion: The results highlight the relevance of joint correlation and RSOC effects beyond the BdG scheme for the phase diagrams of RSOC-coupled superconductors, showing that electronic correlations can drive unique topological superconducting states.

title: Probing the electronic structure of $\mathrm{UTe}_2$ with ARPES and high-energy spectroscopy
comment: 38 pages, 17 figures, accepted to Electronic Structure
summary: $\mathrm{UTe}_2$ has emerged as one of the most intensively studied strongly correlated materials in recent years owing to its unconventional superconductivity and the possible realization of a spin-triplet, topologically nontrivial pairing state. A central open issue concerns the nature of the $\mathrm{U}\,5f$ electrons and their participation in low-energy quasiparticle states. In this review, we summarize recent spectroscopic studies of $\mathrm{UTe}_2$ using momentum-resolved angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) and element- and configuration-sensitive X-ray probes, including X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS), X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES), X-ray magnetic circular dichroism (XMCD), resonant X-ray emission spectroscopy (RXES), and resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS). A key finding is the pronounced technique dependence of the inferred electronic structure. We synthesize the present spectroscopic picture by integrating these results with modern electronic-structure calculations such as density functional theory plus dynamical mean-field theory (DFT+DMFT). These findings support an intermediate-valence ground state with significant admixture of $5f^2$ and $5f^3$ configurations in $\mathrm{UTe}_2$, and they delineate key experimental and theoretical benchmarks needed to connect the normal-state electronic structure to the superconducting mechanism.

AI.tldr: This review synthesizes spectroscopic studies (ARPES, XAS/XANES/XMCD, RXES, RIXS) of UTe2, integrated with DFT+DMFT calculations, and finds a pronounced technique dependence of the inferred electronic structure that supports an intermediate-valence ground state with mixed 5f2 and 5f3 configurations.
AI.motivation: UTe2 is a heavily studied strongly correlated material due to its unconventional superconductivity and possible spin-triplet, topologically nontrivial pairing. A central open question is the nature of the U 5f electrons and how they participate in low-energy quasiparticle states.
AI.method: The authors survey recent spectroscopic studies of UTe2, combining momentum-resolved ARPES with element- and configuration-sensitive X-ray probes: XAS, XANES, XMCD, RXES, and RIXS. These experimental results are integrated with modern electronic-structure calculations, notably DFT+DMFT, to form a coherent spectroscopic picture.
AI.result: The inferred electronic structure shows a pronounced dependence on the experimental technique employed. Integrating the spectroscopic data with DFT+DMFT calculations supports an intermediate-valence ground state with significant admixture of 5f2 and 5f3 configurations in UTe2.
AI.conclusion: The review delineates key experimental and theoretical benchmarks needed to connect the normal-state electronic structure to the superconducting mechanism of UTe2, providing a synthesized spectroscopic framework for understanding its 5f electron physics.

title: Static versus dynamic universality in the site-diluted kagome Ising model
summary: We study the site-diluted Ising model on the kagome lattice using the Wolff single-cluster algorithm, focusing on both equilibrium and dynamic critical properties. The equilibrium critical exponents $ν= 1$ and $γ/ν= 7/4$ retain their exact pure Ising values for all spin concentrations $p$ considered, consistent with the marginal irrelevance of disorder at $α= 0$, with the specific heat crossing over from logarithmic to double-logarithmic growth upon dilution. These static results are shared between the kagome and square lattices. On the dynamic side, $z$ decreases upon dilution on both lattice, opposite to what is observed under local dynamics, with evidence of saturation to a $p$-independent value at strong dilution, suggesting a diluted dynamic fixed point. While $z$ is consistent between the two lattices in the pure case, it differs in the diluted regime, an effect we attribute to the two lattices sitting at different positions along the renormalization-group flow between the Ising and percolation fixed points, rather than to a true asymptotic breakdown of dynamic universality.

AI.tldr: Site-diluted Ising model on the kagome lattice (Wolff single-cluster algorithm): equilibrium exponents retain pure Ising values (ν=1, γ/ν=7/4) for all p, static behavior shared with the square lattice; dynamic exponent z decreases upon dilution on both lattices (opposite to local dynamics), saturating to a p-independent value at strong dilution. The kagome/square discrepancy in z is attributed to different positions along the RG flow between Ising and percolation fixed points, not to asymptotic breakdown of dynamic universality.
AI.motivation: Disorder effects on critical behavior at the marginal dimensionality (α=0) are subtle, and dynamic universality under cluster (Wolff) dynamics with dilution is less explored than under local dynamics. Lattice geometry (kagome vs. square) offers a test of whether dynamic universality survives dilution.
AI.method: Monte Carlo simulations of the site-diluted Ising model on the kagome lattice using the Wolff single-cluster algorithm; extraction of equilibrium critical exponents and the dynamic exponent z as functions of spin concentration p, compared against the square lattice. RG-flow interpretation between Ising and percolation fixed points.
AI.result: ν=1 and γ/ν=7/4 hold for all p, matching exact pure Ising values (marginal irrelevance of disorder, α=0); specific heat crosses over from logarithmic to double-logarithmic growth with dilution. Statics are lattice-independent (kagome = square). Dynamically, z decreases with dilution on both lattices, saturating to a p-independent value at strong dilution, indicating a diluted dynamic fixed point. In contrast to local dynamics. z agrees between lattices in the pure case but differs when diluted.
AI.conclusion: Disorder is marginally irrelevant statically, while cluster dynamics reveals a diluted dynamic fixed point. The lattice-dependent z in the diluted regime reflects different positions along the RG flow between Ising and percolation fixed points rather than a genuine violation of dynamic universality.

title: Fundamental concepts of thermal phonon coherence
summary: As scientists seek to transcend traditional material property relationships, novel structures with artificial periodicity, configurational complexity, and disorder are increasingly being explored. For phonons, these architectures can induce significant phase correlations, which strongly shifts lattice heat conduction away from the conventional framework of particle-like scattering. This thermal phonon coherence can develop in space and time separately, resulting in distinct wave-like phenomena. Here we rigorously outline the theories of phonon spatial and temporal coherence. Crucially, this review focuses on demystifying and building conceptual understanding of the fundamental principles linking the various thermal conductivity and phonon property results reported in the literature. Furthermore, we use this understanding to establish a comprehensive physical picture of the wave nature of thermal phonons, unifying the spatial and temporal coherence theories. Altogether, the theoretical dissections in this review provide an extensive knowledge base for understanding and engineering thermal phonons in complex materials.

AI.tldr: This review rigorously outlines theories of phonon spatial and temporal coherence, building conceptual understanding of thermal conductivity and phonon properties in structurally complex materials, and unifying the two coherence theories into a comprehensive physical picture of the wave nature of thermal phonons.
AI.motivation: As scientists seek to transcend traditional material property relationships, novel structures with artificial periodicity, configurational complexity, and disorder are increasingly explored. In these architectures, phonon phase correlations emerge and strongly shift lattice heat conduction away from the conventional particle-like scattering framework. However, the resulting literature on thermal conductivity and phonon properties is fragmented and lacks a unifying conceptual foundation, motivating a rigorous theoretical synthesis.
AI.method: The authors rigorously outline the theories of phonon spatial coherence and temporal coherence, demystifying the fundamental principles that link the various thermal conductivity and phonon property results reported in the literature. They use this understanding to establish a comprehensive physical picture of the wave nature of thermal phonons, thereby unifying the spatial and temporal coherence theories.
AI.result: The review demonstrates that thermal phonon coherence develops in space and time separately, producing distinct wave-like phenomena. It clarifies the conceptual connections among disparate reported thermal conductivity and phonon property results and integrates the separate spatial and temporal coherence frameworks into a single unified picture.
AI.conclusion: The theoretical dissections in this review provide an extensive knowledge base for understanding and engineering thermal phonons in complex materials, offering a unified wave-based framework that moves beyond conventional particle-like descriptions of lattice heat conduction.

title: What Does a Semilocal Machine-Learning Correction Actually Learn? Size-Dependent Errors across Four Parent Functionals
summary: Machine-learning (ML) corrections to density functional approximations (DFAs) offer a route to improving electronic-structure predictions while retaining the efficiency of semilocal functionals. An important question is whether such corrections learn transferable improvements or instead compensate for errors specific to the parent functional. Here, we address this question by applying the semilocal ML correction of Wang \textit{et al.} [J.~Chem.~Phys.~\textbf{158}, 154107 (2023)] to PBE, B3LYP, SCAN, and r$^2$SCAN, while keeping the network architecture, loss function, training set, and optimization protocol unchanged. We find that the learned correction develops a systematic size-dependent contribution to atomization energies for all four parents, with $|r|\geq0.9999$ along the $n$-alkane series, where r is the Pearson coefficient of the linear fit. Its magnitude and sign depend systematically on the parent: the correction partially compensates the size-dependent errors of PBE and B3LYP, but introduces substantial size-dependent contributions for SCAN and r$^2$SCAN, whose parent errors show little size dependence. In contrast, ionization potentials, electron affinities, and isomerization energies are largely unaffected. Spatial decomposition further reveals distinct origins of this extensive contribution, with bonding regions dominating for B3LYP, SCAN, and r$^2$SCAN and core regions dominating for PBE. These results show that the global-energy ML correction is strongly dependent on the error structure of its parent DFA, highlighting size-dependent error accumulation as a critical consideration in the assessment and development of ML-enhanced density functionals.

AI.tldr: A semilocal ML correction applied identically to PBE, B3LYP, SCAN, and r²SCAN learns a strong size-dependent (extensive) contribution to atomization energies that is systematically parent-dependent, rather than a universally transferable improvement.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether ML corrections to density functional approximations learn transferable improvements or merely compensate for errors specific to the parent functional. This matters because transferability determines whether ML-enhanced functionals generalize beyond their training regime.
AI.method: The authors applied the semilocal ML correction of Wang et al. (J. Chem. Phys. 158, 154107, 2023) to four parent functionals—PBE, B3LYP, SCAN, and r²SCAN—while holding the network architecture, loss function, training set, and optimization protocol fixed. They analyzed the learned correction's effect on atomization energies (including the n-alkane series via linear-fit Pearson correlation r), ionization potentials, electron affinities, and isomerization energies, and performed spatial decomposition to localize its origins.

Its magnitude and sign depend systematically on the parent: it partially compensates size-dependent errors for PBE and B3LYP, but introduces substantial size-dependent contributions for SCAN and r²SCAN, whose parent errors show little size dependence. Ionization potentials, electron affinities, and isomerization energies are largely unaffected. Spatial decomposition shows distinct origins: bonding regions dominate for B3LYP, SCAN, and r²SCAN, while core regions dominate for PBE.
AI.conclusion: Global-energy ML corrections are strongly dependent on the error structure of their parent DFA, indicating they are not universally transferable. Size-dependent error accumulation should be treated as a critical consideration in assessing and developing ML-enhanced density functionals.

title: Quantized Hyperfine Field at an Implanted $μ^+$ Site in PrPb$_3$: Interplay between Localized $f$ Electrons and an Interstitial Charged Particle
comment: 5 pages, 4 figures. Archival upload of the author-prepared manuscript and figures as accepted for publication in 2009. Affiliations shown are those at the time of publication
summary: The local effect of an interstitial hydrogen-like particle on localized $f$ electrons was studied in PrPb$_3$ by means of $μ^+$ spin rotation and relaxation. Spontaneous $μ^+$ spin precession with harmonic frequencies was observed for the first time in $f$ electron compounds. We demonstrate that the signal is derived from a coupling between the $μ^+$ spin and the hyperfine-enhanced nuclear spin of nearest neighbor (nn) $^{141}$Pr with Ising-like anisotropy. The signal also suggests a marked suppression of spin dynamics of the nn $^{141}$Pr in comparison with that of the bulk $^{141}$Pr. These facts strongly indicate modification of the $f$ electronic state due to the interstitial charged particle.

AI.tldr: Using μSR, spontaneous μ+ spin precession with harmonic frequencies is observed for the first time in an f-electron compound (PrPb3), attributed to coupling between the μ+ spin and the hyperfine-enhanced nuclear spin of nearest-neighbor 141Pr with Ising-like anisotropy, indicating local modification of the f-electronic state by the interstitial hydrogen-like particle.
AI.motivation: To investigate how an interstitial hydrogen-like particle locally affects localized f electrons, using PrPb3 as a model f-electron compound.
AI.method: μ+ spin rotation and relaxation (μSR) measurements on PrPb3, analyzing spontaneous μ+ spin precession frequencies and comparing nearest-neighbor versus bulk 141Pr spin dynamics.
AI.result: Spontaneous μ+ spin precession with harmonic frequencies was observed for the first time in f-electron compounds. The signal originates from coupling between the μ+ spin and the hyperfine-enhanced nuclear spin of nearest-neighbor 141Pr with Ising-like anisotropy, and indicates a marked suppression of spin dynamics of the nearest-neighbor 141Pr relative to bulk 141Pr.
AI.conclusion: The interstitial charged particle (μ+) locally modifies the f-electronic state of PrPb3, evidenced by the novel harmonic precession and suppressed nearest-neighbor 141Pr spin dynamics.

title: Thermodynamics of the space of trajectories governed by a combination of two additive boundary functionals
comment: 23 pages, 3 figures. This work extends and generalizes the trajectory functional approach introduced in preprints arXiv:2607.24078 and arXiv:2609.08477 by incorporating relative path-space invariants and establishing a modified strong-drift fluctuation theorem
summary: This paper extends the formalism of stochastic path-space thermodynamics by systematically expanding the space of thermodynamic variables with a spectrum of boundary and relative functionals of random processes. Generalizing the approaches introduced in preprints arXiv:2607.24078 and arXiv:2609.08477, we investigate the fluctuation statistics of a one-dimensional Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with an asymmetric linear drift and a step penalty potential at the origin, which models the waiting phase of a molecular Brownian motor. Utilizing the Feynman-Kac formalism and the parabolic cylinder theory, a numerical scheme based on matching logarithmic derivatives via the secant method is constructed. A high-precision eigenvalues of the effective Hamiltonian is obtained, which define the cumulant generating function. We formulate a modified path-space fluctuation theorem of the Gallavotti-Cohen type for the conjugate drift current at a fixed integral occupation time of the system in the dissipative half-plane. The physical and thermodynamic significance of the new variables is elucidated. A combination of "residence time" and "integral current" functionals is applied to describe an ion channel sensitive to mechanical or electrical stimuli.

AI.tldr: The paper generalizes stochastic path-space thermodynamics by expanding the thermodynamic variable space with boundary and relative functionals of random processes, and studies fluctuation statistics of an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with asymmetric linear drift and a step penalty potential at the origin.
AI.motivation: To extend the formalism of stochastic path-space thermodynamics (building on preprints arXiv:2607.24078 and arXiv:2609.08477) by systematically enlarging the space of thermodynamic variables, and to characterize the waiting phase of a molecular Brownian motor modeled via a one-dimensional Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with asymmetric drift and a step penalty at the origin.
AI.method: The Feynman-Kac formalism combined with parabolic cylinder theory is used. A numerical scheme based on matching logarithmic derivatives via the secant method is constructed, yielding high-precision eigenvalues of the effective Hamiltonian that define the cumulant generating function. A modified path-space fluctuation theorem of the Gallavotti-Cohen type is formulated for the conjugate drift current at fixed integral occupation time in the dissipative half-plane.

A modified Gallavotti-Cohen-type path-space fluctuation theorem is formulated for the conjugate drift current at fixed integral occupation time in the dissipative half-plane. title: Foundation Neural-Network Quantum States for Molecular Potential Energy Surfaces in Second Quantization
summary: Second-quantized neural-network quantum states have achieved accurate molecular energies, but extending them across molecular geometries requires a shared representation of the geometry-dependent wavefunction coefficients. We introduce geometry-conditioned foundation neural-network quantum states for molecular electronic structure in second quantization. A single autoregressive model learns a family of ground states from sparse anchor geometries and provides wavefunctions at untrained geometries without further optimization. Orbital alignment matches orbital identities and transports their phases, establishing an aligned orbital basis across geometries. Frozen energies reach chemical accuracy at every untrained query geometry for N$_2$, CO, and H$_4$. On additional molecular paths, the energy-trained wavefunctions yield dipoles, quadrupoles, and natural occupations without property labels. Across three paired N$_2$ training seeds, orbital alignment lowers the mean absolute energy error over all untrained query geometries from 34-37 mHa to 0.049-0.085 mHa. At approximately 1 mHa mean absolute error, frozen evaluation reduces the per-geometry cost by $986\times$ relative to independent optimization, yielding an estimated $25.8\times$ end-to-end GPU-cost reduction on a 161-point N$_2$ grid.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces geometry-conditioned foundation neural-network quantum states in second quantization, using a single autoregressive model plus orbital alignment to predict molecular ground-state wavefunctions at untrained geometries without re-optimization, achieving chemical accuracy and massive cost savings.
AI.motivation: Second-quantized neural-network quantum states give accurate molecular energies but must be re-optimized per geometry. A shared, geometry-dependent representation of wavefunction coefficients is needed to generalize across molecular geometries.
AI.method: Train a single autoregressive foundation model over a family of ground states from sparse anchor geometries. Introduce orbital alignment that matches orbital identities and transports their phases, establishing a consistent aligned orbital basis across geometries for geometry-conditioned coefficients.
AI.result: Frozen energies reach chemical accuracy at every untrained query geometry for N2, CO, and H4. Energy-trained wavefunctions yield dipoles, quadrupoles, and natural occupations without property labels. Orbital alignment reduces mean absolute energy error over untrained geometries from 34-37 mHa to 0.049-0.085 mHa across three N2 seeds. At ~1 mHa MAE, frozen evaluation cuts per-geometry cost 986x vs independent optimization, giving ~25.8x end-to-end GPU-cost reduction on a 161-point N2 grid.
AI.conclusion: Geometry-conditioned foundation NNQS with orbital alignment enable accurate, transferable molecular wavefunctions across geometries, delivering chemical accuracy and large computational savings without per-geometry optimization.

title: Deep Learning GW Quasiparticle Hamiltonians for Many-Body Excited-State Electronic Structure at Scale
summary: Accurate quasiparticle electronic structures are the foundation for understanding excited-state properties of materials and explaining optoelectronic, quantum, and transport phenomena. First-principles GW calculations nevertheless remain computationally intensive for large or configurationally complex systems. Here we introduce DeepH-GW, a deep-learning framework that predicts an effective GW quasiparticle Hamiltonian directly from atomic structure. Building on the local, equivariant message-passing architecture of DeepH, DeepH-GW is trained on high-fidelity plane-wave GW calculations through a real-space Hamiltonian-reconstruction interface. This approach combines the systematic accuracy and broad chemical applicability of plane-wave methods with linear-scaling neural-network inference. Across the systems examined, DeepH-GW reproduces quasiparticle band structures with errors on the order of a few meV. Moreover, we show that, despite the intrinsic nonlocality of many-body interactions, DeepH-GW exhibits strong cross-scale transferability from relatively small training structures to substantially larger supercells. We demonstrate that the framework can accurately capture GW-level electron-phonon band-gap renormalization through predictions in supercells with thermal displacements, illustrating the power of the approach. DeepH-GW therefore provides a practical route toward large-scale many-body simulations and foundation models for excited-state electronic structure.

AI.tldr: DeepH-GW is a deep-learning framework that predicts effective GW quasiparticle Hamiltonians directly from atomic structure, achieving few-meV accuracy and strong cross-scale transferability.
AI.motivation: Accurate quasiparticle electronic structures are essential for understanding excited-state properties and optoelectronic, quantum, and transport phenomena. However, first-principles GW calculations remain computationally intensive for large or configurationally complex systems.
AI.method: DeepH-GW builds on DeepH's local, equivariant message-passing architecture and is trained on high-fidelity plane-wave GW calculations via a real-space Hamiltonian-reconstruction interface, combining plane-wave accuracy with linear-scaling neural-network inference.
AI.result: DeepH-GW reproduces quasiparticle band structures with errors on the order of a few meV, exhibits strong cross-scale transferability from small training structures to much larger supercells, and accurately captures GW-level electron-phonon band-gap renormalization in thermally displaced supercells.
AI.conclusion: DeepH-GW offers a practical route toward large-scale many-body simulations and foundation models for excited-state electronic structure.

title: Weakly interacting Bose-Einstein condensate with stochastic resetting
summary: Stochastic resetting can generate strong correlations in many-body systems through a shared fluctuating environment. Here, we investigate how such dynamically emergent correlations (DEC) coexist with intrinsic (direct) interactions in a weakly repulsive Bose-Einstein condensate described within the Gross-Pitaevskii framework. The condensate undergoes free expansion from an initial Thomas-Fermi state and is stochastically reset to this initial state at a constant rate. We show that the resetting protocol drives the system into a unique nonequilibrium steady state and obtain its density profile, edge statistics, and full counting statistics analytically. The steady-state density retains an inverted-parabolic form within the core, while developing exponentially decaying tails outside it. We further show that resetting induces nontrivial fluctuations of the condensate edge and particle number, yielding exact scaling forms for the edge distribution and the full counting statistics. Our results provide a tractable setting for exploring the interplay between intrinsic repulsive interactions and attractive DEC generated by a common stochastic environment in quantum many-body systems.

AI.tldr: The paper studies a weakly repulsive Bose-Einstein condensate under stochastic resetting, showing that resetting induces a unique nonequilibrium steady state with an inverted-parabolic core and exponential tails, and analytically derives its edge statistics and full counting statistics.
AI.motivation: Stochastic resetting can generate strong correlations in many-body systems via a shared fluctuating environment, but how these dynamically emergent correlations (DEC) coexist with intrinsic direct interactions remains unclear. This work addresses that interplay in a tractable quantum many-body setting.
AI.method: A weakly repulsive Bose-Einstein condensate is described within the Gross-Pitaevskii framework. The condensate freely expands from an initial Thomas-Fermi state and is stochastically reset to this state at a constant rate. The resulting nonequilibrium steady state is analyzed analytically, yielding the density profile, edge statistics, and full counting statistics.
AI.result: The resetting protocol drives the system into a unique nonequilibrium steady state. Its density retains an inverted-parabolic form in the core while developing exponentially decaying tails outside. Resetting induces nontrivial fluctuations of the condensate edge and particle number, with exact scaling forms obtained for the edge distribution and the full counting statistics.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a tractable setting for exploring the interplay between intrinsic repulsive interactions and attractive dynamically emergent correlations generated by a common stochastic environment in quantum many-body systems.

title: Orbital-engineered px,y-kagome lattice in a halogen monolayer
summary: Multi-orbital kagome lattices with explicit orbital degrees of freedom remain largely unexplored, as most experimentally realized systems rely on complex d-electron manifolds that are approximated by isotropic single-orbital models. Here, we overcome this limitation by realizing a px,y-orbital kagome lattice through deposition of a Br monolayer on Ag(111), where orbital filtering selectively suppresses the pz channel. Scanning tunneling microscopy, angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, and density-functional-theory calculations reveal a large-area, highly ordered kagome structure whose band dispersions quantitatively match the anisotropic px,y tight-binding model. To extract the intrinsic manifold from the substrate background, we construct an effective H-passivated model, which uncover the intrinsic electronic structure and reveals nontrivial topological characteristics of the px,y kagome manifold driven by first-order spin-orbit coupling effect. Our work establishes Br/Ag(111) as an experimentally accessible platform for multi-orbital kagome physics, extending the kagome paradigm from the conventional d-orbital regime to an orbitally engineered topological setting.

AI.tldr: A px,y-orbital kagome lattice is realized by depositing a Br monolayer on Ag(111), where orbital filtering suppresses the pz channel, enabling quantitative validation of the anisotropic px,y tight-binding model and revealing nontrivial topology driven by first-order spin-orbit coupling.
AI.motivation: Multi-orbital kagome lattices with explicit orbital degrees of freedom are largely unexplored because most experimentally realized systems rely on complex d-electron manifolds approximated by isotropic single-orbital models, leaving orbital-resolved kagome physics and its topological consequences inaccessible.
AI.method: A Br monolayer is deposited on Ag(111) to form a px,y-orbital kagome lattice, exploiting orbital filtering to selectively suppress the pz channel. Scanning tunneling microscopy, angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, and density-functional-theory calculations characterize the structure and band dispersions. An effective H-passivated model is constructed to isolate the intrinsic manifold from the substrate background.
AI.result: A large-area, highly ordered kagome structure is formed whose band dispersions quantitatively match the anisotropic px,y tight-binding model. The H-passivated model uncovers the intrinsic electronic structure and reveals nontrivial topological characteristics of the px,y kagome manifold, driven by a first-order spin-orbit coupling effect.
AI.conclusion: Br/Ag(111) is established as an experimentally accessible platform for multi-orbital kagome physics, extending the kagome paradigm from the conventional d-orbital regime to an orbitally engineered topological setting.

title: An F12 Correction for Multicomponent MP2
summary: Multicomponent methods treat both electrons and nuclei quantum mechanically using the standard machinery of electronic structure theory. Previous work has demonstrated that quantitatively describing electron-nuclear correlation in multicomponent many-body perturbation theory methods requires large electronic basis sets with high-angular momentum atomic orbitals, and calculations on large systems can therefore become impractical. Similarly, the slow convergence of the electron-electron correlation energy with respect to highest atomic-orbital angular momentum is a well-known issue in standard electronic structure theory in which only the electrons are treated quantum mechanically, and numerous explicitly correlated methods have been introduced to mitigate this poor convergence. Motivated by the success of single-component explicitly correlated methods, we generalize the single-component MP2-F12/3C(FIX) approach for electron-electron correlation to electron-proton correlation to reduce the need for large electronic basis sets in multicomponent calculations. We also implement the complementary auxiliary basis set (CABS) singles correction for the electrons and protons. Our calculations show that the multicomponent MP2-F12 electron-proton correlation energy is within a few percent of the complete-basis-set (CBS) estimate obtained by QZ-5Z inverse-cubic extrapolation with PB4-D held fixed at every electronic basis-set cardinality tested, with the aug-cc-pVDZ basis set recovering 96-98% of the extrapolated CBS electron-proton correlation energy and exceeding the conventional multicomponent MP2 value at the aug-cc-pV5Z level. These results indicate that explicitly correlated methods can substantially reduce the electronic basis-set requirements of multicomponent calculations.

AI.tldr: The paper generalizes single-component MP2-F12/3C(FIX) to treat electron-proton correlation in multicomponent methods, showing that explicitly correlated approaches drastically reduce electronic basis-set requirements.
AI.motivation: Multicomponent methods treat electrons and nuclei quantum mechanically, but describing electron-nuclear correlation requires large electronic basis sets with high-angular-momentum orbitals, making large-system calculations impractical. This mirrors the well-known slow convergence of electron-electron correlation energy with respect to highest angular momentum in standard electronic structure theory, which explicit correlation methods have successfully mitigated. The authors are motivated to bring the same benefit to multicomponent calculations.
AI.method: The authors generalize the single-component MP2-F12/3C(FIX) approach, originally for electron-electron correlation, to electron-proton correlation. They also implement a complementary auxiliary basis set (CABS) singles correction for both electrons and protons.
AI.result: The multicomponent MP2-F12 electron-proton correlation energy lies within a few percent of the complete-basis-set (CBS) estimate from QZ-5Z inverse-cubic extrapolation with PB4-D fixed at every tested electronic basis-set cardinality. The aug-cc-pVDZ basis recovers 96-98% of the extrapolated CBS electron-proton correlation energy and surpasses conventional multicomponent MP2 at the aug-cc-pV5Z level.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly correlated methods can substantially reduce the electronic basis-set requirements of multicomponent calculations, enabling accurate electron-proton correlation energies at much smaller basis-set cost.

title: Spin separation of Dirac electrons by twisted and vector optical beams
summary: We demonstrate that twisted and vector optical beams can spatially separate two-dimensional electrons with opposite spin projections. Spin accumulation arises from diverging spin currents induced by structured light together with spin relaxation and diffusion. We derive analytical expressions for the resulting spin density in the quasi-local and diffusion-controlled regimes and numerically calculate the spin textures for the parameters relevant to transition metal dichalcogenide monolayers. Our results suggest a mechanism by which the twist and vector pattern of optical beams can be imprinted onto the electron spin degree of freedom.

AI.tldr: Structured light (twisted and vector beams) can spatially separate 2D electrons with opposite spin projections, imprinting the beam's polarization/twist pattern onto the electron spin degree of freedom.
AI.motivation: To establish a mechanism for optical control and spatial manipulation of the electron spin degree of freedom using structured light, going beyond conventional uniform illumination, and to enable spin-pattern imprinting from the optical beam onto electrons.
AI.method: Theoretical/analytical modeling: the authors show that twisted and vector optical beams induce diverging (inhomogeneous) spin currents; combined with spin relaxation and diffusion, these produce spin accumulation. They derive analytical expressions for spin density in the quasi-local and diffusion-controlled regimes, and numerically compute the resulting spin textures for parameters relevant to transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) monolayers.
AI.result: Structured optical beams can spatially separate 2D electrons with opposite spin projections, yielding a spatially patterned spin density. Analytical spin-density expressions are obtained for quasi-local and diffusion-controlled regimes, and spin textures are numerically calculated for TMD monolayer parameters.
AI.conclusion: The twist and vector (polarization) pattern of optical beams can be imprinted onto the electron spin degree of freedom, suggesting a mechanism for all-optical, spatially resolved spin control in 2D materials.

title: Evolution of Magnetism in Ce$_4$Ge$_7$ under Magnetic Field and Pressure
summary: We report the magnetic and transport properties of single-crystalline Ce$_4$Ge$_7$, which crystallizes in a non-centrosymmetric orthorhombic structure (space group C222$_1$). It undergoes an antiferromagnetic transition at $T_N$ = 7.3 K. When a magnetic field is applied along the $b$-axis, a metamagnetic transition occurs at 1.3 T (at 2 K). Correspondingly, this transition gives rise to an anomalous Hall effect, which is dominated by the intrinsic Karplus-Luttinger mechanism. Under hydrostatic pressure, $T_N$ of Ce$_4$Ge$_7$ initially increases slightly and is then gradually suppressed. For pressures above $P_c$ = 10.2 GPa, no magnetic order is observed. The divergence of the $A$ coefficient, the maximum of the residual resistivity, and the non-Fermi liquid behavior around $P_c$ indicate the possible existence of an antiferromagnetic quantum critical point in Ce$_4$Ge$_7$.

AI.tldr: Single-crystalline Ce4Ge7 shows an antiferromagnetic transition at 7.3 K, a field-induced metamagnetic transition with an intrinsic anomalous Hall effect, and pressure-driven suppression of magnetic order suggesting a possible antiferromagnetic quantum critical point near 10.2 GPa.
AI.motivation: To explore the interplay between magnetism, transport, and quantum criticality in a non-centrosymmetric Ce-based compound, potentially revealing unconventional electronic/magnetic ground states.
AI.method: Magnetic and transport measurements on single crystals of Ce4Ge7; magnetotransport with field along the b-axis; hydrostatic pressure studies up to and beyond Pc; analysis of A coefficient, residual resistivity, and non-Fermi liquid behavior.
AI.result: Antiferromagnetic ordering at TN = 7.3 K; field-induced metamagnetic transition at 1.3 T (2 K); anomalous Hall effect dominated by intrinsic Karplus-Luttinger mechanism; TN initially increases slightly then is suppressed with pressure; no magnetic order above Pc = 10.2 GPa; signatures of quantum criticality (divergence of A, residual resistivity maximum, non-Fermi liquid behavior) near Pc.
AI.conclusion: Ce4Ge7 exhibits tunable antiferromagnetic order and transport anomalies, with evidence for a possible antiferromagnetic quantum critical point around 10.2 GPa, making it a candidate for studying quantum criticality in non-centrosymmetric Ce compounds.

title: Accurate ground-state entropies from population Monte Carlo: The antiferromagnetic Ising model on the Shastry-Sutherland lattice
summary: We demonstrate how the population annealing Monte Carlo simulation method can be used to compute the ground-state entropy to high precision. This approach is tested for the classical antiferromagnetic Ising model on the Shastry-Sutherland lattice with diagonal couplings chosen twice as strong as the nearest-neighbor interactions. In the absence of an external magnetic field, the model is known to be disordered at all temperatures, with a macroscopically degenerate ground state. We find the ground-state entropy to be $0.458\,777\,78(10)$ per site, which is in good agreement with the estimate of a recent study using the corner transfer matrix renormalization group method. The sampled ground-state configurations are analyzed by considering the bond configurations, the local-energy configurations, and the spin-spin correlations. While all observations are consistent with the disordered nature of the ground state, the numerical data suggest a power-law decay of the size distribution of clusters of sites with local energies different from the ground-state level.

AI.tldr: Population annealing Monte Carlo computes the ground-state entropy of the classical antiferromagnetic Ising model on the Shastry-Sutherland lattice (diagonal couplings twice the nearest-neighbor strength) as 0.45877778(10) per site, matching corner transfer matrix renormalization group results.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to show that population annealing Monte Carlo can compute ground-state entropy to high precision, and to resolve the numerically challenging, macroscopically degenerate ground state of a disordered-at-all-temperatures model.
AI.method: Population annealing Monte Carlo simulation applied to the classical antiferromagnetic Ising model on the Shastry-Sutherland lattice with diagonal couplings twice as strong as nearest-neighbor interactions, in the absence of an external magnetic field.
AI.result: Ground-state entropy found to be 0.45877778(10) per site, in good agreement with recent corner transfer matrix renormalization group estimates; sampled ground-state configurations analyzed via bond configurations, local-energy configurations, and spin-spin correlations, all consistent with a disordered ground state, with data suggesting power-law decay of the size distribution of clusters of sites with local energies different from the ground-state level.
AI.conclusion: Population annealing Monte Carlo is an effective, high-precision method for ground-state entropy computation, and the observed ground state is disordered with a macroscopically degenerate manifold, as supported by the analyzed configurations.

title: From Automated Simulation to Autonomous Discovery: A Hierarchical Framework for Agentic Computational Materials Science
summary: The convergence of large language models, materials-specific foundation models, and agentic artificial intelligence is reshaping the paradigm of computational materials discovery. While high-throughput computation, automated workflows, and data-driven modeling have greatly expanded the scale of materials exploration, the core scientific decision-making loop remains largely human-directed. Agentic AI introduces the possibility of systems that can autonomously reason about materials objectives, execute simulations, and refine strategies. However, the rapid emergence of such systems has created a critical need for a unified and operational framework to define, evaluate, and guide scientific autonomy in computational materials discovery. In this Perspective, we propose the Computational Materials Agent Autonomy Level (CMA-AL) framework, a hierarchical taxonomy defining six levels of autonomous agency in computational materials science: scripted excecutor, LLM-assisted operator, adaptive explorer, experiment-ready modeler, agentic digital twin, and self-extending intelligence. We further map emerging agentic systems onto the framework and identify key scientific and technological challenges toward higher autonomy. CMA-AL provides a common language for characterizing agentic computational materials discovery, evaluating the maturity of emerging systems, and guiding their evolution toward increasingly autonomous materials discovery.

AI.tldr: This Perspective proposes the Computational Materials Agent Autonomy Level (CMA-AL) framework, a six-level taxonomy for characterizing and guiding scientific autonomy in agentic computational materials discovery.
AI.motivation: The convergence of large language models, materials-specific foundation models, and agentic AI is transforming computational materials discovery. Although high-throughput computation, automated workflows, and data-driven modeling have expanded the scale of materials exploration, the core scientific decision-making loop remains largely human-directed. The rapid emergence of agentic systems has created a critical need for a unified, operational framework to define, evaluate, and guide scientific autonomy in this domain.
AI.method: The authors propose the CMA-AL framework, a hierarchical taxonomy defining six levels of autonomous agency in computational materials science: (1) scripted executor, (2) LLM-assisted operator, (3) adaptive explorer, (4) experiment-ready modeler, (5) agentic digital twin, and (6) self-extending intelligence. They then map emerging agentic systems onto this framework and identify key scientific and technological challenges toward higher autonomy.
AI.result: CMA-AL provides a common language for characterizing agentic computational materials discovery, evaluating the maturity of emerging systems, and guiding their evolution toward increasingly autonomous materials discovery.
AI.conclusion: CMA-AL serves as an operational framework to define, evaluate, and guide scientific autonomy in computational materials discovery, offering a shared vocabulary and a roadmap toward higher levels of autonomy.

title: Chiral Temporal Structures in Molecular Rotational Dynamics
summary: We introduce chiral rotational wavepackets: coherent superpositions of a few low-lying rotational states of an achiral molecule for which the expectation value of a molecular axis traces a three-dimensional chiral curve in the laboratory frame. The handedness is a dynamical property of the quantum state rather than of the equilibrium structure, and we show that it can be imprinted on linear rotors as well as on spherical and symmetric tops. We derive the action of space inversion, motion reversal, and their product on such wavepackets in the Wigner $D^J_{MK}$ basis, and define the rotational enantiomers of a given wavepacket. To quantify the handedness of the orientation trajectory we introduce two derivative-based pseudoscalar measures: a geometrical measure built from the curvature and torsion of the trajectory, which is even under motion reversal, and an origin-referenced measure built from the binormal vector, which is odd under motion reversal. The latter is shown to be proportional to the geodesic curvature of the trajectory projected onto the unit sphere, which links it, via the Gauss--Bonnet theorem, to the solid angle enclosed by the projected trajectory and to the parallel-transport holonomy of a molecule-fixed vector. Finally we show that a nonzero geometrical measure is a sufficient condition for the wavepacket to be truly chiral in the sense of Barron, while wavepackets with real expansion coefficients are only falsely chiral.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces chiral rotational wavepackets—coherent superpositions of low-lying rotational states of an achiral molecule whose molecular axis traces a 3D chiral curve—and characterizes their dynamical handedness via two derivative-based pseudoscalar measures.
AI.motivation: Molecular chirality is conventionally tied to equilibrium structure, but handedness can also emerge as a dynamical property of a quantum state. The authors aim to define and quantify chirality arising purely from rotational dynamics of an achiral molecule, independent of its static geometry.
AI.method: The authors construct coherent superpositions of a few low-lying rotational states for linear rotors, spherical tops, and symmetric tops. They derive the action of space inversion, motion reversal, and their product in the Wigner D^J_{MK} basis and define rotational enantiomers. They introduce two pseudoscalar measures: a geometrical one from curvature and torsion (even under motion reversal) and an origin-referenced one from the binormal vector (odd under motion reversal).
AI.result: The origin-referenced measure is shown to be proportional to the geodesic curvature of the trajectory projected onto the unit sphere, linking it via the Gauss–Bonnet theorem to the enclosed solid angle and to the parallel-transport holonomy of a molecule-fixed vector. A nonzero geometrical measure is proven sufficient for true chirality in Barron's sense, whereas wavepackets with real expansion coefficients are only falsely chiral.
AI.conclusion: Chirality can be a dynamical property of rotational quantum states of achiral molecules. The two pseudoscalar measures provide complementary, symmetry-distinct quantifications of handedness, with the geometrical measure giving a sufficient condition for true chirality and connecting wavepacket handedness to geometric and topological quantities such as solid angle and holonomy.

title: Cavity-QED enhancement of quantum entanglement and battery performance in double quantum dots
summary: We theoretically investigate quantum correlations and energy storage in a single-electron silicon double quantum dot (eDQD) coupled to a single-mode microwave cavity. The charge and spin degrees of freedom are hybridized by Rashba spin-orbit coupling (SOC), while the cavity interacts with the eDQD through spin-photon and charge-photon couplings. Using the reduced thermal density matrix, we characterize spin-charge entanglement by concurrence and quantum coherence by the $l_1$ norm. At low temperature, the cavity strongly modifies the spin-charge correlations, producing distinct regimes of enhanced and suppressed entanglement. We identify a nonlinear crossover between an eDQD-dominated regime and a photon-dressed regime. This crossover is revealed independently by two signatures: a rapid change in the concurrence and the onset of finite photon occupation in the cavity. Its boundary exhibits a dominant $G_{\rm c}\propto\sqrtΩ$ dependence and is robust against cavity Hilbert-space truncation. Beyond the Rashba coupling studied in [Ferreira et al., Phys. Rev. A 107, 052408 (2023)], we show that the cavity provides an additional tunable means of controlling quantum correlations and energy storage. We further characterize the eDQD as a quantum battery under coherent charging and evaluate its stored energy and ergotropy. The ergotropy varies markedly across a cavity-dressing crossover resembling that identified from entanglement, connecting cavity-induced modification of the dressed states to extractable work. Optimization over the charge-photon coupling reveals parameter-dependent optimal charging regimes and enhanced maximum ergotropy with increasing Rashba coupling. Our results establish cavity coupling and SOC as complementary controls of quantum correlations and extractable energy in semiconductor eDQD-cavity systems.

AI.tldr: The paper theoretically studies quantum correlations and energy storage in a silicon double quantum dot coupled to a microwave cavity, showing that cavity coupling and spin-orbit coupling act as complementary controls of entanglement, coherence, and extractable work (ergotropy).
AI.motivation: Extending prior work (Ferreira et al.) beyond Rashba spin-orbit coupling, the authors seek an additional tunable handle—cavity coupling—to control quantum correlations and energy storage in a semiconductor double quantum dot, a promising platform for quantum technologies.
AI.method: A single-electron silicon double quantum dot coupled to a single-mode microwave cavity is modeled, with spin-charge hybridization from Rashba SOC and spin-photon plus charge-photon couplings. Using the reduced thermal density matrix, entanglement is quantified by concurrence and coherence by the l1 norm; the dot is analyzed as a quantum battery under coherent charging via stored energy and ergotropy.
AI.result: At low temperature the cavity strongly reshapes spin-charge correlations, yielding regimes of enhanced and suppressed entanglement. A nonlinear crossover between an eDQD-dominated and a photon-dressed regime is identified by a rapid concurrence change and the onset of finite photon occupation, with boundary scaling as G_c ∝ √Ω and robust to Hilbert-space truncation. Ergotropy varies markedly across the cavity-dressing crossover, and optimization reveals parameter-dependent optimal charging regimes with enhanced maximum ergotropy as Rashba coupling increases.
AI.conclusion: Cavity coupling and SOC are complementary controls of quantum correlations and extractable energy in semiconductor eDQD-cavity systems, linking cavity-induced modification of dressed states to extractable work.

title: The Spectral Cost of Detecting Nonequilibrium at Finite Temporal Resolution
summary: A detector that cannot take two snapshots closer than a time $τ_0$ still identifies a fully observed finite Markov generator exactly, provided its gaps are randomized by two clocks. Identification is not detection. For a normal nonequilibrium network, the number of snapshots needed to reject every hidden equilibrium explanation grows as $e^{2γ_{\mathrm{irr}}τ_0}$, where $γ_{\mathrm{irr}}$ is the slowest damping of rotating modes. No adaptive schedule beats this rate, and a test on one dependent trajectory attains it.

AI.tldr: A dead-time-limited detector can still exactly identify a finite Markov generator if its gaps are randomized by two independent clocks. However, identification differs from detection: rejecting all hidden equilibrium explanations requires exponentially many snapshots, scaling as e^{2γ_irr τ_0}, which is provably optimal.
AI.motivation: Detectors have a minimum time resolution τ_0 and cannot take snapshots closer than this. The paper addresses whether such a resolution-limited detector can identify a fully observed finite Markov generator, and how costly it is to distinguish a genuinely nonequilibrium network from any equilibrium explanation.
AI.method: The gaps between snapshots are randomized using two clocks. The analysis formalizes the distinction between identification and detection, and derives the sample complexity for rejecting hidden equilibrium explanations in a normal nonequilibrium network, with γ_irr defined as the slowest damping of rotating modes. The optimality of adaptive schedules is examined, and a test on a single dependent trajectory is constructed.
AI.result: Identification of the finite Markov generator is exact despite the τ_0 dead time, provided the two-clock gap randomization is used. The number of snapshots needed to reject every hidden equilibrium explanation grows as e^{2γ_irr τ_0}. No adaptive schedule achieves a better rate, and a test based on one dependent trajectory attains this rate.
AI.conclusion: Identification is not detection. The exponential sample complexity e^{2γ_irr τ_0} is fundamental and cannot be improved by adaptivity; the proposed trajectory-based test is rate-optimal, establishing a sharp separation between exact generator identification and nonequilibrium detection under finite time resolution.

title: Enabling the Ambient Pressure Growth of ScB2 Crystals for AlGaN Power Electronics
summary: Here we report the growth of single crystalline ScB2, an ultrahigh-temperature ceramic, at ambient pressure in a laser-heated Optical Floating Zone via the travelling solvent method. Crystals have been grown from both Sc-rich (55-65 at% Sc) and B-rich self-flux (80-83 at% B) at growth rates in the range of 0.2-2 mm/hr. The structure of grown crystals is in good agreement with an AlB2-type layered hexagonal phase, space group P6/mmm, with lattice constants a = 3.1423(2) Å (resp. 3.1502(3) Å) and c = 3.5084(3) Å (resp. 3.5041(3) Å) for crystals grown under Sc-rich (resp. B-rich) conditions. Crystals natively grow along the in-plane [100] direction. Electron backscattered diffraction shows that Sc-flux growth results in boules with multiple domains containing Sc inclusions, with the domains highly aligned. In contrast, B-flux boules are single domain after the initial nucleation region. Rocking-curve measurements of B-flux crystals for the (h000) and (000l) reflections show single peaks, establishing that the crystals are free from grain boundaries; the asymmetry in the scattered-intensity tails suggests the presence of point defects. Surface X-ray photoemission spectroscopy shows that the electronic environment in B-flux crystals is superior to that of Sc-flux crystals and produces highly resolved binding-energy peaks for B 1s and Sc 2p. Work-function measurements for the (11-20) plane give a value of approximately 5 eV, consistent with the highly electrically conductive nature of ScB2. These results demonstrate the viable ambient-pressure growth of ScB2, establish it as a lattice-matched substrate candidate for Al-rich AlGaN power microelectronics, and show that this growth route enables scalable manufacturing of ScB2 substrates.
