AI.motivation: ScB2 is an ultrahigh-temperature ceramic whose single-crystal growth is challenging; establishing a viable ambient-pressure growth route is needed to enable scalable manufacturing and to explore its potential as a lattice-matched substrate for Al-rich AlGaN power microelectronics.
AI.method: Single crystals were grown at ambient pressure in a laser-heated Optical Floating Zone using the travelling solvent method, from Sc-rich (55–65 at% Sc) and B-rich (80–83 at% B) self-flux at growth rates of 0.2–2 mm/hr. Characterization included structural analysis (AlB2-type hexagonal phase, space group P6/mmm), electron backscattered diffraction, rocking-curve measurements, surface X-ray photoemission spectroscopy, and work-function measurements.
AI.result: Crystals adopt an AlB2-type layered hexagonal structure (P6/mmm) with lattice constants a = 3.1423(2) Å, c = 3.5084(3) Å for Sc-rich and a = 3.1502(3) Å, c = 3.5041(3) Å for B-rich growth, natively growing along [100]. Sc-flux boules contain multiple highly aligned domains with Sc inclusions, whereas B-flux boules are single domain after initial nucleation. Rocking curves show single peaks for (h000) and (000l) reflections, confirming freedom from grain boundaries with point-defect-related tail asymmetry. B-flux crystals show superior electronic environment with highly resolved B 1s and Sc 2p peaks. Work function of the (11-20) plane is ~5 eV, consistent with high electrical conductivity.
AI.conclusion: Ambient-pressure growth of ScB2 is viable, establishing it as a lattice-matched substrate candidate for Al-rich AlGaN power microelectronics; this growth route enables scalable manufacturing of ScB2 substrates.

title: Vapor phase growth and characterization of van der Waals BiSbTeSe platelets on semiconducting MoS2
summary: Three dimensional topological insulators of the tetradymite family, such as BiSbTeSe (BSTS), are attractive for spintronic and quantum device applications because of their compensated, bulk-insulating character. Nanostructured BSTS platelets are promising for practical TI based devices. However, their growth often requires complex equipment, organometallic precursors, or electrically insulating substrates. Simple growth on technologically relevant semiconducting substrates remains largely unexplored. Here, we report the vapor phase growth of van der Waals BSTS platelets directly on semiconducting MoS2 using a presynthesized BiSbTe1.5Se1.5 crystal as the source material. The grown BSTS platelets exhibit thicknesses ranging from 4 nm to 246 nm, with an average lateral size of 1.4 mkm for individual platelets. Raman spectra of platelets, acquired in correlation with AFM thickness measurements, reveal contributions from both BSTS and the underlying MoS2 substrate. Among the characteristic BSTS modes, A21g mode shows the highest sensitivity to platelet thickness and local composition. EDS analysis reveals a systematic thickness dependence of the platelet composition, with an apparent crossover around 49 nm that coincides with a change in the thickness dependence of the low-wavenumber component of the E2g Raman band. This correlation suggests a composition-related origin of the Raman behavior, with the compositional variations tentatively attributed to the differential volatility of the constituent elements during growth. These results demonstrate that MoS2 is a promising van der Waals platform for BSTS deposition and provide a structural and compositional baseline for future studies of BSTS-MoS2 heterostructures.

AI.tldr: Van der Waals BSTS (BiSbTeSe) topological insulator platelets were grown directly on semiconducting MoS2 via vapor phase growth using a presynthesized BiSbTe1.5Se1.5 crystal source, establishing a structural and compositional baseline for BSTS-MoS2 heterostructures.
AI.motivation: Nanostructured tetradymite topological insulators like BSTS are promising for spintronic and quantum devices due to their compensated, bulk-insulating character, but their growth typically requires complex equipment, organometallic precursors, or insulating substrates, while simple growth on technologically relevant semiconducting substrates remains largely unexplored.
AI.method: Vapor phase growth of van der Waals BSTS platelets directly on semiconducting MoS2, using a presynthesized BiSbTe1.5Se1.5 crystal as the source material, with characterization by AFM, Raman spectroscopy, and EDS.
AI.result: BSTS platelets with thicknesses from 4 nm to 246 nm and average lateral size of 1.4 mkm were obtained. Raman spectra revealed contributions from both BSTS and MoS2, with the A21g mode showing the highest sensitivity to thickness and local composition. EDS showed a systematic thickness dependence of composition with an apparent crossover around 49 nm, coinciding with a change in thickness dependence of the low-wavenumber E2g component.
AI.conclusion: MoS2 is a promising van der Waals platform for BSTS deposition, and the results provide a structural and compositional baseline for future studies of BSTS-MoS2 heterostructures; the composition-related Raman behavior is tentatively attributed to differential volatility of constituent elements during growth.

title: Irreducible Weyl Semimetals
summary: A key objective in Weyl-semimetal (WSM) research is to identify phases built from minimal configurations of Weyl points (WPs), which provide the simplest settings for investigating the intrinsic physics of chiral topological charges. Pang et al. [Phys. Rev. Res. 8, 033304 (2026)] recently established that crystallographically realizable WSMs can be decomposed into linear combinations of 16 minimal "irreducible Weyl molecules" (IWMs). A fundamental question remains unresolved: which of these non-decomposable configurations can themselves form standalone crystalline phases? Here we introduce irreducible Weyl semimetals (IWSMs), in which two bands crossing near the Fermi level form an elementary symmetry-compatible complex whose complete Weyl-node configuration is charge neutral and crystallographically indivisible. Combining all 1651 magnetic space groups with Weyl-orbit multiplicities and band-compatibility relations, we classify IWSMs formed by crystalline-symmetry-protected twofold WPs. Only ten of the sixteen primitive inventories admit one-copy realizations, comprising four Pair, four Split, and two Mixed charge-node architectures. Remarkably, this classification uncovers five unconventional and previously unrecognized topological phases: the charge-three Pair IWSM {3, -3}; the Split IWSMs {3, -1, -1, -1}, and {4, -1, -1, -1, -1}; and the Mixed IWSMs {3, 1, -2, -2} and {3, 3, -2, -2, -2}. For all ten classes, symmetry-constrained lattice models verify the complete node inventories, Chern charges, and surface chiral-flow incidence. Our results establish crystalline irreducibility as a phase-level organizing principle beyond individual Weyl nodes and provide a symmetry-resolved framework for identifying minimal Weyl complexes in electronic, phononic, and photonic systems.

Pang et al. showed that crystallographically realizable WSMs decompose into linear combinations of 16 minimal "irreducible Weyl molecules" (IWMs), but it remained unresolved which of these non-decomposable configurations can themselves form standalone crystalline phases.
AI.method: The authors define irreducible Weyl semimetals (IWSMs), in which two bands crossing near the Fermi level form an elementary symmetry-compatible complex whose full Weyl-node configuration is charge neutral and crystallographically indivisible. They combine all 1651 magnetic space groups with Weyl-orbit multiplicities and band-compatibility relations to classify IWSMs formed by crystalline-symmetry-protected twofold Weyl points, and verify the results with symmetry-constrained lattice models.
AI.result: Only ten of the sixteen primitive inventories admit one-copy realizations: four Pair, four Split, and two Mixed charge-node architectures. The classification uncovers five unconventional, previously unrecognized topological phases: the charge-three Pair IWSM {3, -3}; the Split IWSMs {3, -1, -1, -1} and {4, -1, -1, -1, -1}; and the Mixed IWSMs {3, 1, -2, -2} and {3, 3, -2, -2, -2}. For all ten classes, symmetry-constrained lattice models confirm the complete node inventories, Chern charges, and surface chiral-flow incidence.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes crystalline irreducibility as a phase-level organizing principle that goes beyond individual Weyl nodes, and provides a symmetry-resolved framework for identifying minimal Weyl complexes in electronic, phononic, and photonic systems.

title: Symmetry-enforced topological parity: revisiting $2\mathbb{Z}$ classifications beyond cellwise symmetry actions
summary: Momentum-dependent symmetry actions can turn the even-integer constraint of a $2\mathbb{Z}$ classification of topological insulators and superconductors into an odd-integer constraint without changing the symmetry algebra. For internal and order-two crystalline symmetries in up to four spatial dimensions, we derive parity relations between the Chern or winding number of a gapped Hamiltonian and topological invariants of its momentum-dependent antiunitary symmetry matrices. Whenever the symmetry action enforces odd parity, any symmetry-preserving gapped phase must be topologically nontrivial. Using cellwise actions, which are represented by momentum-independent matrices in a fixed unit-cell basis, as a reference, we determine how locality constrains the realization of odd topological numbers. Explicit model constructions and no-go theorems distinguish three cases: odd values can be realized by finite-range symmetry actions, can be realized by exponentially decaying quasilocal actions but not by finite-range actions, or are impossible in finite-dimensional Bloch systems.

AI.tldr: Momentum-dependent symmetry actions can convert the even-integer ($2\mathbb{Z}$) constraint of topological insulators/superconductors into an odd-integer constraint without altering the symmetry algebra, forcing any symmetry-preserving gapped phase to be nontrivial. The authors derive parity relations linking bulk topological invariants (Chern/winding numbers) to invariants of momentum-dependent antiunitary symmetry matrices, and determine how locality constrains which odd topological numbers are realizable.
AI.motivation: Standard symmetry classifications (e.g., $2\mathbb{Z}$) impose an even-integer constraint that appears rigid under the symmetry algebra. The paper asks whether momentum-dependent symmetry actions can evade this and enforce odd parity, thereby guaranteeing nontrivial topology, and how the locality of such actions restricts their realization.
AI.method: For internal and order-two crystalline symmetries in up to four spatial dimensions, the authors derive parity relations between the Chern or winding number of a gapped Hamiltonian and topological invariants of its momentum-dependent antiunitary symmetry matrices. They use cellwise (momentum-independent in a fixed unit-cell basis) actions as a reference to analyze locality constraints, supported by explicit model constructions and no-go theorems.
AI.result: The analysis distinguishes three cases for realizing odd topological numbers: (i) achievable via finite-range symmetry actions, (ii) achievable via exponentially decaying quasilocal actions but not finite-range ones, and (iii) impossible in finite-dimensional Bloch systems.
AI.conclusion: Momentum-dependent symmetry actions can break the even-integer constraint and enforce odd topological numbers, making triviality impossible for symmetry-preserving gapped phases. However, locality strongly constrains which odd invariants are physically realizable, yielding a threefold classification of realizability.

title: Scale invariance, fractal dynamics, and critical exponents at the phase transition
comment: Doctoral thesis, University of Brasília, Institute of Physics, Brasília, Brazil, 2026. 102 pages
summary: We propose that, at criticality, equilibrium dynamics effectively evolves on a fractal subspace rather than throughout the full Euclidean space. Starting from Fisher's formulation of the order-parameter correlation function, we interpret the anomalous critical exponent $η$ geometrically through a correlation fractal dimension associated with this effective subspace. Using fractional-calculus tools, we derive a form of the correlation function that recovers critical behavior below the upper critical dimension and obtain an explicit relation between $η$ and a fractal dimension $d_R$ linked to the Riesz fractional derivative. We also examine the Rushbrooke scaling relation and investigate critical behavior in non-integer-dimensional and disordered systems. In the disordered case, controlled by a parameter $σ$, we test the range over which the proposed geometric interpretation remains valid. The results connect scaling laws, critical exponents, correlations, and fractal geometry, suggesting that the anomalous behavior observed at criticality can be understood as a consequence of dynamics constrained to an effective fractal subspace.

AI.tldr: Equilibrium critical dynamics is proposed to effectively occur on a fractal subspace, not the full Euclidean space; using fractional calculus, the anomalous exponent η is linked geometrically to a correlation fractal dimension d_R derived from the Riesz fractional derivative, and this interpretation is tested via the Rushbrooke relation, non-integer dimensions, and disordered systems.
AI.motivation: The anomalous critical exponent η is typically treated as an abstract correction to scaling; a physical/geometric origin for it is lacking. The paper seeks a geometric interpretation by asking whether critical fluctuations are effectively confined to a fractal subspace rather than filling Euclidean space.
AI.method: Starting from Fisher's formulation of the order-parameter correlation function, the authors reinterpret η via a correlation fractal dimension of an effective subspace. They employ fractional-calculus tools, specifically the Riesz fractional derivative, to derive a correlation-function form that recovers critical behavior below the upper critical dimension, and obtain an explicit relation between η and the fractal dimension d_R. They then examine the Rushbrooke scaling relation and test critical behavior in non-integer-dimensional and disordered systems controlled by a parameter σ.
AI.result: An explicit relation between η and the fractal dimension d_R is obtained, and the derived correlation function recovers critical behavior below the upper critical dimension. The Rushbrooke scaling relation is examined, and the range over which the geometric interpretation holds is tested in disordered systems as a function of σ.
AI.conclusion: Scaling laws, critical exponents, correlations, and fractal geometry are connected: anomalous critical behavior can be understood as the consequence of dynamics constrained to an effective fractal subspace.

title: Frustrated Gd3+ Double Perovskites as High-Performance Magnetocaloric Materials for Sub-100 mK Adiabatic Demagnetization Refrigeration
summary: Achieving temperatures below 100 mK is essential for advancing quantum technologies and exploring fundamental quantum phenomena. While paramagnetic salts have traditionally enabled adiabatic demagnetization refrigeration (ADR), their limitations have driven the search for more effective alternatives. In this work, we present Gd3+-based double perovskites, Ba2GdSbO6 and Sr2GdSbO6, as high-performance magnetocaloric materials. Starting ADR from 2 K and 5 T, these compounds reach 67 mK and 68 mK in small finite magnetic fields, and 83 mK and 78 mK in zero field, respectively, which are the lowest reported ADR temperatures for Gd3+ magnets (S = 7/2) under these conditions. The frustrated geometry and the complex interplay of exchange and dipolar interactions suppress their antiferromagnetic ordering temperatures to 100 and 166 mK for Ba2GdSbO6 and 190 mK for Sr2GdSbO6, while maintaining an outstanding entropy density of 189 mJ K-1 cm-3 and 201 mJ K-1 cm-3, respectively. Notably, Ba2GdSbO6 sustains sub-100 mK cooling even at finite fields of 0.5 T, making it particularly promising for practical ADR applications.

AI.tldr: Ba2GdSbO6 and Sr2GdSbO6 double perovskites achieve record-low ADR temperatures (67-83 mK) for Gd3+ magnets, enabled by frustrated geometry that suppresses magnetic ordering while maintaining high entropy density.
AI.motivation: Sub-100 mK temperatures are critical for quantum technologies and fundamental physics. Traditional paramagnetic salts used in adiabatic demagnetization refrigeration (ADR) have limitations, motivating the search for superior magnetocaloric materials that can reach ultra-low temperatures efficiently.
AI.method: The authors investigate Gd3+-based double perovskites Ba2GdSbO6 and Sr2GdSbO6 as magnetocaloric candidates. They perform ADR starting from 2 K and 5 T, measuring achievable temperatures in both finite and zero magnetic fields, and characterize the magnetic ordering temperatures, entropy density, and the roles of frustrated geometry, exchange, and dipolar interactions.
AI.result: From 2 K and 5 T, Ba2GdSbO6 and Sr2GdSbO6 reach 67 mK and 68 mK in finite fields, and 83 mK and 78 mK in zero field—the lowest reported ADR temperatures for Gd3+ (S = 7/2) magnets under these conditions. Antiferromagnetic ordering temperatures are suppressed to 100 and 166 mK (Ba2GdSbO6) and 190 mK (Sr2GdSbO6), with entropy densities of 189 and 201 mJ K-1 cm-3. Ba2GdSbO6 sustains sub-100 mK cooling even at 0.5 T.
AI.conclusion: Gd3+-based double perovskites Ba2GdSbO6 and Sr2GdSbO6 are high-performance magnetocaloric materials that set new benchmarks for ADR temperatures among Gd3+ magnets. Their frustrated geometry and suppressed ordering, combined with high entropy density, make them especially promising—particularly Ba2GdSbO6—for practical sub-100 mK ADR applications.

title: Engineering Vacuum Fluctuations in Hyperbolic Heterostructures
summary: Vacuum fluctuations can be engineered using optical cavities, resonators, and surface-polaritonic modes, but extending such control deep inside a material remains challenging.Here we show that the vacuum field inside a hyperbolic material can be reshaped by a much thinner overlayer with opposite hyperbolicity.This effect requires overlap between the hyperbolic bands of the two materials and modifies the coupling between the vacuum field and matter excitations within the bottom material, without changing its intrinsic dielectric properties. As an application, we use Eliashberg theory to study a two-dimensional superconducting layer inside the bottom material, showing that the overlayer can remotely change its critical temperature.Our results may shed light on recent experiments reporting changes in superconductivity arising from a frequency-matched hyperbolic overlayer, and suggest an on-chip route to long-range control of matter excitations and collective material properties.

AI.tldr: A thin hyperbolic overlayer with opposite hyperbolicity can reshape the vacuum field deep inside a bulk hyperbolic material without altering its intrinsic dielectric properties, enabling remote tuning of embedded superconducting layers and their critical temperature.
AI.motivation: Engineering vacuum fluctuations is well established using optical cavities, resonators, and surface-polaritonic modes, but extending such vacuum-field control deep inside a material remains challenging. This work aims to overcome that limitation by reshaping the vacuum field within a bulk material to remotely influence matter excitations.
AI.method: The authors exploit a hyperbolic material covered by a much thinner overlayer with opposite hyperbolicity. This configuration requires spectral overlap between the hyperbolic bands of the two materials, which reshapes the vacuum field inside the bottom material and modifies its coupling to embedded matter excitations without changing its intrinsic dielectric response. Eliashberg theory is then applied to a two-dimensional superconducting layer embedded in the bottom material to quantify the remote effect on its critical temperature.
AI.result: The overlayer remotely reshapes the internal vacuum field and alters the vacuum-field–matter coupling inside the bottom material, while leaving the material's intrinsic dielectric properties unchanged. Applied to an embedded 2D superconducting layer via Eliashberg theory, the overlayer is shown to change the layer's critical temperature remotely.
AI.conclusion: Hyperbolic-band overlap between a bulk hyperbolic material and a thinner oppositely hyperbolic overlayer enables deep, remote control of vacuum fluctuations and matter excitations. This mechanism may explain recent experiments reporting superconductivity changes induced by a frequency-matched hyperbolic overlayer and offers an on-chip route to long-range control of collective material properties.

title: Strong-to-Weak Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking of Dephased Fermions
summary: Strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking (SWSSB) is a novel phase transition in mixed states associated with the loss of global charge information. In this work we study fermions with $U(1)$ symmetry under infinite density dephasing and derive the SWSSB properties of the resulting mixed states. Our central observation is that at infinite dephasing every Renyi correlator is exactly the spin-spin correlator of a compact XY model, whose Boltzmann weight is the squared full-counting-statistics generating function of a classical ensemble built from the parent state. For the Renyi-2 correlator it is the full counting statistics of the parent state itself. We complement the infinite dephasing mapping with a novel diagrammatic expansion for the Renyi-1 correlator, applicable to any diagonal mixed state, which computes the couplings of the Renyi-1 XY model. We also study a replica field theory for even Renyi index quantities, applicable at finite dephasing. Our analysis indicates that fully dephased metals display long-range SWSSB in $d\geq 2$, as confirmed numerically and experimentally in $d=2$, and quasi-long-range SWSSB in $d=1$. For insulating parent states both an SWSSB and a trivial phase are possible at infinite dephasing depending on UV details. Long-range SWSSB in $d\geq 3$, or quasi-long-range SWSSB in $d=2$, survives above a nonuniversal, Renyi-index-dependent threshold and is lost when the parent state is deep in the insulating phase, with the exception of quantum Hall insulators which generically have quasi-long-range SWSSB. For even Renyi indices we also determine the stability of the SWSSB phase away from infinite dephasing and derive the universality class of the SWSSB transition.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a theory of strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking (SWSSB) in dephased fermionic mixed states with U(1) symmetry, mapping infinite-dephasing Renyi correlators onto XY-model correlators and characterizing SWSSB phases across dimensions and parent-state types.
AI.motivation: SWSSB is a novel mixed-state phase transition tied to loss of global charge information, but its behavior for fermions under dephasing was not understood. The authors aim to characterize when and how dephased fermionic states exhibit SWSSB.
AI.method: For infinite density dephasing, they map every Renyi correlator to the spin-spin correlator of a compact XY model whose Boltzmann weight is the squared full-counting-statistics generating function (of the parent state for Renyi-2). They add a diagrammatic expansion for the Renyi-1 correlator valid for any diagonal mixed state, and a replica field theory for even Renyi-index quantities at finite dephasing.
AI.result: Fully dephased metals show long-range SWSSB in d>=2 (confirmed numerically and experimentally in d=2) and quasi-long-range SWSSB in d=1. Insulating parents can yield either SWSSB or a trivial phase depending on UV details. Long-range SWSSB in d>=3, or quasi-long-range SWSSB in d=2, survives above a nonuniversal, Renyi-index-dependent threshold and disappears deep in the insulating phase, except for quantum Hall insulators which generically show quasi-long-range SWSSB.
AI.conclusion: SWSSB in dephased fermionic mixed states is governed by an effective XY-model description, with phase behavior controlled by dimensionality, parent-state nature, and Renyi index. For even Renyi indices the authors determine stability away from infinite dephasing and the universality class of the SWSSB transition.

title: Anomalous transport in periodic systems driven by active fluctuations
comment: Doctoral dissertation in a form of a guidebook through the series of articles (their full versions are available on arXiv). It was prepared under the supervision of Jakub Spiechowicz
summary:
This dissertation investigates the transport of Brownian particles driven by active fluctuations in periodic potential landscapes. Unlike thermal noise, active fluctuations break detailed balance and violate the fluctuation-dissipation theorem. They model self-propulsion mechanisms and active-bath interactions in biological and synthetic micro-systems. By focusing on white Poisson shot noise with non-Gaussian amplitude statistics, this work systematically uncovers the mechanisms governing three major transport anomalies: giant transport enhancement, absolute negative mobility, and the ratchet effect.
  Combining Monte Carlo simulations with analytical modeling, this work demonstrates that active fluctuations adhering to a bidirectional skew-normal amplitude distribution enhance directed velocity compared to the free-particle by several orders of magnitude. This giant transport enhancement is fully quantified via a phenomenological jump-relaxation model that decouples particle displacement into instantaneous stochastic jumps and deterministic relaxation towards potential minimum. Extending this model to inertial dynamics reveals that finite particle mass m acts as a dynamic control parameter capable of strengthening, weakening, constructively inducing, or completely suppressing transport enhancement depending on noise variance.
  Furthermore, an ultra-minimal model for absolute negative mobility is established in a one-dimensional, purely overdamped system, showing that discontinuous shot noise drives transport opposite to an applied bias without requiring particle inertia, nonlinearity of spatially periodic potential, or explicit time-dependent periodic driving. Conversely, under an alternative scaling of the average stochastic force, an asymmetric distribution of fluctuation amplitudes generates net directed transport through a tilting ratchet effect in the zero-bias limit.

AI.tldr: This dissertation studies Brownian transport driven by active fluctuations (white Poisson shot noise) in periodic potentials, uncovering mechanisms for three transport anomalies: giant transport enhancement, absolute negative mobility, and the ratchet effect.
AI.motivation: Active fluctuations, unlike thermal noise, break detailed balance and violate the fluctuation-dissipation theorem, modeling self-propulsion and active-bath interactions in biological and synthetic micro-systems. Understanding how they govern anomalous transport is key.
AI.method: Monte Carlo simulations combined with analytical modeling. A phenomenological jump-relaxation model decouples displacement into instantaneous stochastic jumps and deterministic relaxation toward the potential minimum; extended to inertial dynamics. An ultra-minimal model for absolute negative mobility is also developed.
AI.result: Bidirectional skew-normal amplitude statistics enhance directed velocity by orders of magnitude over free particles. Finite mass acts as a dynamic control parameter that can strengthen, weaken, induce, or suppress enhancement depending on noise variance. Discontinuous shot noise produces absolute negative mobility without inertia, potential nonlinearity, or explicit periodic driving. Under alternative scaling, asymmetric amplitude distributions yield net directed transport via a tilting ratchet at zero bias.
AI.conclusion: Active fluctuations with non-Gaussian amplitude statistics are a rich mechanism for controlling transport, enabling giant enhancement, absolute negative mobility, and ratchet effects even in minimal overdamped one-dimensional systems.

title: Averaging in thermodynamic dislocation theory: general macroscopically uniform stress and strain states
summary: The averaging procedure, developed for polycrystalline bars under axially symmetric tension or compression, is extended to arbitrary macroscopically uniform stress and strain states. Starting from the equal probability hypothesis for grain orientations, the mean resolved shear stress and the mean resolved elastic and plastic shear strains are defined as root-mean-square averages over all slip-system orientations. Two exact identities for isotropic orientation averages show that the mean resolved shear stress is proportional to the von Mises equivalent stress, and that the direction of macroscopic plastic flow, obtained from the hypothesis that the plastic slip rate on a system is proportional to the resolved shear stress acting on it, is the stress deviator. The result is an associated $J_2$ flow theory whose hardening law is not fitted but follows from the kinetics of thermally activated dislocation depinning and the evolution equations for the dislocation density and the effective disorder temperature of thermodynamic dislocation theory, written as rates with respect to time so that arbitrary loading paths can be followed. For torsion the theory yields the torque--twist relation of bars and tubes without the classical reductions to a shear stress--strain curve. The parameters for copper are identified jointly from Hopkinson-bar tension, dynamic compression at room and elevated temperatures, and torque--twist records at several twist rates. One set of material parameters, consistent with the earlier compression-only identification, describes tension, compression and torsion from room temperature to $1173$\,K and from $10$ to $2300$\,s$^{-1}$ to $6$\,\% rms over 142 data points; the tension--torsion discrepancy noted by Johnson and Cook is traced to the initial dislocation state of their torsion specimens.

AI.tldr: The paper extends the averaging procedure for polycrystalline bars to arbitrary macroscopic stress/strain states, deriving an associated J2 flow theory whose hardening law follows from thermodynamic dislocation theory kinetics rather than being fitted. It predicts tension, compression, and torsion responses across wide temperature and strain-rate ranges with a single parameter set.
AI.motivation: Earlier averaging procedures were limited to polycrystalline bars under axially symmetric tension or compression. There was a need to generalize this framework to arbitrary macroscopically uniform stress and strain states, and to obtain a flow theory whose hardening law is physically derived rather than empirically fitted, enabling prediction of arbitrary loading paths including torsion.
AI.method: Starting from the equal probability hypothesis for grain orientations, mean resolved shear stress and mean resolved elastic/plastic shear strains are defined as root-mean-square averages over all slip-system orientations. Two exact identities for isotropic orientation averages are used to relate mean resolved shear stress to von Mises equivalent stress and to show that macroscopic plastic flow direction is the stress deviator. This yields an associated J2 flow theory whose hardening law follows from thermally activated dislocation depinning kinetics and evolution equations for dislocation density and effective disorder temperature in thermodynamic dislocation theory, written as time rates to follow arbitrary loading paths. For torsion, the torque-twist relation is derived without classical shear stress-strain reductions. Parameters for copper are identified jointly from Hopkinson-bar tension, dynamic compression at room and elevated temperatures, and torque-twist records at several twist rates.
AI.result: One set of material parameters, consistent with an earlier compression-only identification, describes tension, compression, and torsion from room temperature to 1173 K and from 10 to 2300 s^-1 to 6% rms over 142 data points. The tension-torsion discrepancy noted by Johnson and Cook is traced to the initial dislocation state of their torsion specimens.
AI.conclusion: The generalized orientation-averaging framework yields an associated J2 flow theory with physically derived hardening from thermodynamic dislocation theory. A single parameter set captures tension, compression, and torsion across broad temperature and strain-rate ranges, and the noted tension-torsion discrepancy is explained by initial dislocation state rather than model failure.

title: Atomic-scale control of spin transport in exchange-coupled molecules
summary: Spin transport between coupled spins is governed by tunneling and exchange interactions, yet their microscopic relation in real space has remained experimentally elusive. To address this, we functionalize the tip of a scanning tunneling microscope with a single molecule and use it as a movable spin sensor positioned above a second molecule on a ferromagnetic surface, forming an exchange-coupled molecular junction. From the same spectroscopic dataset, we independently extract the junction conductance, exchange coupling, and spin polarization with atomic-scale resolution. Conductance and exchange display nearly identical spatial dependences, consistent with a minimal Hubbard description in which both are governed by the same hopping matrix between the molecular frontier orbitals. In contrast, the spin polarization depends on the orbital composition and the relative weight of the resulting transport channels. These results establish a real-space connection between tunneling, exchange, and spin transport in magnetically coupled molecules.

AI.tldr: By using a single molecule on an STM tip as a movable spin sensor above another molecule on a ferromagnetic surface, the authors simultaneously extract junction conductance, exchange coupling, and spin polarization with atomic-scale resolution, revealing that conductance and exchange share a common hopping-matrix origin while spin polarization depends on orbital composition and transport-channel weights.
AI.motivation: The microscopic real-space relation between tunneling and exchange interactions governing spin transport between coupled spins has remained experimentally elusive; the paper aims to establish this connection directly at the atomic scale.
AI.method: A scanning tunneling microscope tip is functionalized with a single molecule and used as a movable spin sensor positioned above a second molecule adsorbed on a ferromagnetic surface, forming an exchange-coupled molecular junction. From a single spectroscopic dataset, the junction conductance, exchange coupling, and spin polarization are extracted independently with atomic-scale spatial resolution, and the results are interpreted with a minimal Hubbard model.
AI.result: Conductance and exchange coupling exhibit nearly identical spatial dependences, consistent with both being governed by the same hopping matrix element between the molecular frontier orbitals in the minimal Hubbard description. In contrast, the spin polarization depends on the orbital composition and the relative weight of the resulting transport channels.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a real-space connection between tunneling, exchange, and spin transport in magnetically coupled molecules, showing that conductance and exchange share a common microscopic origin while spin polarization is governed by orbital and channel-dependent factors.

title: Variational Monte Carlo for the Hubbard model
summary: In these lecture notes, we introduce the variational Monte Carlo method for the Hubbard model. First, we briefly introduce the single-orbital Hubbard model and its multi-orbital extension, focusing only on electronic models. Then, we introduce the general scheme under which variational Monte Carlo works and we present the variational wave functions that can properly describe superconductive and magnetic states in single-orbital and multi-orbital Hubbard models. We also detail how to perform Monte Carlo calculations for the given wave functions. We also describe how to optimize a variational wave function with the stochastic reconfiguration method. Finally, we present a few results for correlation functions that can be computed in variational Monte Carlo, to determine, for instance, the presence of charge or spin order and superconductivity.

AI.tldr: These lecture notes provide an introduction to the variational Monte Carlo method for the single-orbital and multi-orbital Hubbard model, covering wave functions for superconductive and magnetic states, Monte Carlo sampling, stochastic-reconfiguration optimization, and computation of correlation functions.
AI.motivation: To offer a pedagogical, self-contained introduction to variational Monte Carlo applied to the Hubbard model, enabling the description and identification of superconductive and magnetic states in both single-orbital and multi-orbital electronic models.
AI.method: The notes first introduce the single-orbital Hubbard model and its multi-orbital extension, then present the general variational Monte Carlo scheme, variational wave functions describing superconductive and magnetic states, procedures for Monte Carlo evaluation of these wave functions, and optimization via the stochastic reconfiguration method.
AI.result: Selected results for correlation functions computable in variational Monte Carlo are presented, allowing determination of charge order, spin order, and superconductivity.
AI.conclusion: Variational Monte Carlo, combined with appropriate variational wave functions and stochastic reconfiguration optimization, provides a practical framework for studying superconductivity and magnetic ordering in Hubbard-type models through measurable correlation functions.

title: Phase separation, morphology, and metastability in the three-dimensional active Potts model
summary: We study the three-dimensional active Potts model (APM) on a cubic lattice with 2, 4, and 6 orientational states. The steady-state phase diagrams exhibit low-density gaseous, high-density polar liquid, and liquid--gas coexistence phases, with the phase behavior controlled by density, temperature, and propulsion speed and retaining the main features of the previously studied two-dimensional APM. At weak propulsion, the dense phase forms a slab perpendicular to its direction of motion. With increasing propulsion speed, this morphology persists for the 2-state model, whereas the dense phases for 4 and 6 states reorient and propagate along their longitudinal direction. For the 6-state model, the reoriented dense phase further develops a cylindrical morphology. We also examine the stability of polar liquids against artificially introduced droplets using microscopic simulations and coarse-grained hydrodynamic equations. At high propulsion speeds, counter-propagating droplets can partially modify the initial polar state, while transverse droplets can completely alter it, demonstrating the metastable nature of polar liquids in the three-dimensional active Potts model.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the 3D active Potts model on a cubic lattice with 2, 4, and 6 orientational states, mapping its phase diagram (gas, polar liquid, coexistence) and showing how propulsion speed drives distinct dense-phase morphologies and reorientation, with polar liquids being metastable against transverse perturbations.
AI.motivation: The 2D active Potts model was previously characterized; the authors aim to extend this framework to three dimensions to determine whether the phase behavior and emergent morphologies of the 2D APM persist, and to probe the stability of the resulting polar ordered phases.
AI.method: Microscopic simulations of the 3D APM on a cubic lattice with 2, 4, and 6 orientational states, combined with coarse-grained hydrodynamic equations. Stability is tested by artificially introducing counter-propagating and transverse droplets into the polar liquid.
AI.result: Steady-state phase diagrams show low-density gas, high-density polar liquid, and liquid-gas coexistence, controlled by density, temperature, and propulsion speed, retaining key 2D features. At weak propulsion the dense phase forms a slab perpendicular to its motion. Increasing propulsion, the 2-state slab persists, while 4- and 6-state dense phases reorient and propagate longitudinally; the 6-state case further develops a cylindrical morphology. Transverse droplets can completely alter the polar state, while counter-propagating droplets only partially modify it.
AI.conclusion: Polar liquids in the 3D active Potts model are metastable: their stability depends on perturbation geometry, with transverse droplets fully disrupting order and counter-propagating ones partially modifying it. The results generalize the 2D APM to three dimensions, revealing propulsion-controlled morphology selection and reorientation.

title: Polar-Domain Volume as a Unified Descriptor of Transport in Ionic Liquids
summary: Developing molecular scale structural descriptors that can quantitatively predict the macroscopic transport properties of ionic liquids remains a longstanding question, owing to the complex interplay between molecular interactions, nanoscale organization, and collective ion dynamics. Here, we use all atom molecular dynamics simulations to establish quantitative structure property relationships between the equilibrium microstructure and two key transport properties viscosity and ionic conductivity in a series of imidazolium based ILs with chemically distinct anions and varying alkyl chain lengths. While viscosity and ionic conductivity exhibit distinct dependencies on alkyl chain length and anion chemistry, these seemingly different trends largely collapse onto unified correlations when expressed in terms of the mean polar-domain volume. In particular, both transport properties exhibit systematic power-law scaling with the mean polar domain volume fraction, revealing a common structural origin underlying the variations in ion and momentum transport across chemically distinct ILs. These results establish polar-domain volume as a physically motivated molecular-scale descriptor and provide a general structure property framework for connecting nanoscale organization to macroscopic transport properties in ILs.

AI.tldr: Polar-domain volume is identified via all-atom MD as a unified molecular-scale descriptor that collapses viscosity and ionic conductivity trends onto common power-law scaling for imidazolium-based ionic liquids.
AI.motivation: Predicting macroscopic transport properties of ionic liquids from molecular-scale structure remains unresolved due to the complex coupling of molecular interactions, nanoscale organization, and collective ion dynamics. A physically motivated structural descriptor linking equilibrium microstructure to viscosity and conductivity is needed.
AI.method: All-atom molecular dynamics simulations of a series of imidazolium-based ionic liquids with chemically distinct anions and varying alkyl chain lengths; computation of equilibrium microstructural quantities (mean polar-domain volume and polar-domain volume fraction) and correlation against viscosity and ionic conductivity.
AI.result: Viscosity and ionic conductivity show distinct dependencies on alkyl chain length and anion chemistry, yet these trends largely collapse onto unified correlations when expressed through mean polar-domain volume. Both transport properties exhibit systematic power-law scaling with mean polar-domain volume fraction, indicating a common structural origin for ion and momentum transport across chemically distinct ILs.
AI.conclusion: Polar-domain volume is established as a physically motivated molecular-scale descriptor and provides a general structure-property framework connecting nanoscale organization to macroscopic transport properties in ionic liquids.

title: Nonlinear optical responses of semiconducting graphene nanoribbons: Strong constraint from a hidden symmetry
summary: Nonlinear optical (NLO) responses are powerful tools for probing material structures, as they are highly sensitive to spatial symmetries. For instance, it is well known that having inversion symmetry forbids even-order NLO effects. Here, we show that nonspatial symmetries can also significantly constrain NLO responses. In graphene nanoribbons (GNRs) with bipartite-lattice structures, we identify the approximate bipartite-lattice particle-hole (BLPH) symmetry strongly suppresses even-order NLO effects, even for systems with no inversion symmetry. Importantly, we demonstrate that this approximate symmetry enables the optical generation of nearly pure spin shift currents in ferromagnetic GNRs, with the charge shift currents strongly suppressed. The spin orientation of these photo-induced DC spin currents can be easily tuned by an external magnetic field, providing distinct advantages over previous schemes for generating pure spin shift currents in antiferromagnetic systems. We illustrate our findings using a recently synthesized ferromagnetic Janus GNR. Our results underscore the significance of an overlooked symmetry aspect of NLO responses and highlight magnetic GNRs as promising candidates for spintronic devices.

AI.tldr: Nonspatial symmetries (specifically an approximate bipartite-lattice particle-hole symmetry) strongly constrain nonlinear optical responses, enabling nearly pure photo-induced DC spin shift currents in ferromagnetic graphene nanoribbons.
AI.motivation: NLO responses are known to be governed by spatial symmetries (e.g., inversion symmetry forbids even-order NLO effects), but the role of nonspatial symmetries in constraining NLO responses has been largely overlooked. The authors aim to reveal this overlooked symmetry aspect and exploit it to generate pure spin currents.
AI.method: The authors analyze bipartite-lattice graphene nanoribbons (GNRs) and identify an approximate bipartite-lattice particle-hole (BLPH) symmetry. They theoretically demonstrate that this approximate symmetry suppresses even-order NLO effects even without inversion symmetry, and use it to generate nearly pure spin shift currents in ferromagnetic GNRs, illustrating the findings with a recently synthesized ferromagnetic Janus GNR.
AI.result: The approximate BLPH symmetry strongly suppresses even-order NLO effects and charge shift currents, while enabling nearly pure spin shift currents in ferromagnetic GNRs. The spin orientation of these photo-induced DC spin currents can be easily tuned by an external magnetic field.
AI.conclusion: The work highlights the significance of a previously overlooked symmetry aspect of NLO responses and identifies magnetic GNRs as promising candidates for spintronic devices, offering distinct advantages over previous schemes for generating pure spin shift currents in antiferromagnetic systems.

title: Boundary Criticality in (2+1)-dimensional U(1) Dirac Quantum Spin Liquid
summary: An emergent gauge field can control boundary critical behavior without changing the bulk quantum spin liquid. We investigate the boundary criticality in $(2+1)$-dimensional $U(1)$ Dirac spin liquid, whose low-energy physics is described by massless quantum electrodynamics. Using a perturbative renormalization-group analysis in a half-space, we show that Neumann and Dirichlet boundary conditions for the emergent gauge field lead to distinct boundary universality classes. We determine the boundary scaling dimensions of the fundamental fields and gauge-invariant operators that provide observable signatures. We further propose a fermion-gauge lattice model with tunable boundary interactions as a microscopic setting for realizing and probing these boundary universality classes.

AI.tldr: This paper studies boundary criticality in a (2+1)D U(1) Dirac spin liquid described by massless QED, showing that Neumann vs. Dirichlet boundary conditions on the emergent gauge field yield distinct boundary universality classes, and proposes a lattice model to realize them.
AI.motivation: An emergent gauge field can govern boundary critical behavior while leaving the bulk quantum spin liquid intact. Thus the boundary criticality of emergent-gauge-field systems is a distinct and physically relevant question.
AI.method: Perturbative renormalization-group analysis of massless QED in a half-space geometry; comparison of Neumann and Dirichlet boundary conditions for the emergent gauge field; computation of boundary scaling dimensions of fundamental fields and gauge-invariant operators; proposal of a fermion-gauge lattice model with tunable boundary interactions.
AI.result: Neumann and Dirichlet boundary conditions for the emergent gauge field lead to distinct boundary universality classes. Boundary scaling dimensions of fundamental fields and gauge-invariant operators are determined, providing observable signatures; the proposed lattice model offers a microscopic setting to realize and probe these classes.
AI.conclusion: Boundary criticality in the (2+1)D U(1) Dirac spin liquid is controlled by the emergent gauge field and splits into distinct universality classes depending on the gauge-field boundary condition, with observable scaling dimensions and a candidate lattice realization.

title: Exact anomalous current fluctuations in the strong-anisotropy limit of the XXZ chain
summary: We study spin-current fluctuations of the folded XXZ chain, which describes the strong-anisotropy limit of the XXZ chain. We obtain an exact expression for the moment-generating function of the time-integrated spin current at infinite temperature. A long-time asymptotic analysis establishes that the rescaled time-integrated current converges to a non-Gaussian distribution described by the M-Wright function. The derivation relies on a nonlocal map to the one-dimensional t-0 model and its exact spin-charge separation. By extending this approach, we also show that the dynamical correlation function of the spins summed over two adjacent sites exhibits a diffusive Gaussian profile at long times.

AI.tldr: Exact moment-generating function of the time-integrated spin current in the folded XXZ chain at infinite temperature; long-time rescaled current converges to a non-Gaussian M-Wright distribution.
AI.motivation: Spin-current fluctuations in strongly anisotropic (folded XXZ) chains are poorly understood, particularly the full distribution of time-integrated current beyond Gaussian approximations.
AI.method: Exact computation of the moment-generating function of the time-integrated spin current at infinite temperature, using a nonlocal map to the one-dimensional t-0 model and its exact spin-charge separation, followed by long-time asymptotic analysis.
AI.result: The rescaled time-integrated current converges to a non-Gaussian distribution given by the M-Wright function. The dynamical correlation function of spins summed over two adjacent sites shows a diffusive Gaussian profile at long times.
AI.conclusion: Non-Gaussian, M-Wright–type fluctuations govern spin transport in the folded XXZ chain, while adjacent-site spin correlations remain diffusive and Gaussian, highlighting distinct statistical behaviors within the same model.

title: Fabrication framework for three-dimensional colloidal particles with decoupled geometry and material composition
summary: Shape-programmable particles offer significant opportunities for microrobotic systems at the individual level and for hierarchical materials with emergent functionalities arising from collective particle behavior. However, fabricating shape-changing stimuli-responsive particles with complex three-dimensional geometries at colloidal length scales remains a major challenge. Here, we introduce a general fabrication framework that decouples particle geometry from material composition to produce free-standing three-dimensional colloidal particles with complex architectures. Our approach combines soft lithography, swelling-assisted extraction, and sacrificial adhesive transfer to fabricate particles with high geometric fidelity. We establish a predictive framework that defines the accessible design space for increasingly complex particle geometries. We further extend our framework to fabricate high-aspect-ratio pillar arrays with intricate three-dimensional architectures at colloidal length scales. To demonstrate material versatility, we fabricate particles from both liquid crystal elastomers and hydrogels. We show reversible shape-changing behavior of liquid crystal elastomer particles with cylindrical and chiral shapes under thermal and optical stimuli. In suspension, these particles display collective optical dynamic behavior arising from coupling between changes in the programmed liquid crystal organization within the particles and stimulus-induced geometric reconfiguration of the particles. Collectively, this work establishes a versatile platform for geometry-programmable colloidal particles with emergent collective functionalities, providing a route toward materials and fluids with dynamically programmable properties.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce a fabrication framework (soft lithography + swelling-assisted extraction + sacrificial adhesive transfer) that decouples particle geometry from material composition, enabling free-standing 3D colloidal particles with complex architectures from liquid crystal elastomers and hydrogels, showing reversible stimuli-responsive shape changes and collective optical dynamics.
AI.motivation: Shape-programmable particles are promising for microrobotics and hierarchical materials with emergent collective functionalities, but fabricating stimuli-responsive particles with complex 3D geometries at colloidal length scales remains a major challenge.
AI.method: Combines soft lithography, swelling-assisted extraction, and sacrificial adhesive transfer to produce particles with high geometric fidelity; establishes a predictive framework defining the accessible design space; extends the approach to high-aspect-ratio pillar arrays with intricate 3D architectures; fabricates particles from liquid crystal elastomers and hydrogels.
AI.result: Achieves free-standing 3D colloidal particles with complex geometries and high fidelity; demonstrates reversible shape-changing of liquid crystal elastomer particles (cylindrical and chiral) under thermal and optical stimuli; in suspension, particles exhibit collective optical dynamic behavior from coupling between programmed liquid crystal organization and stimulus-induced geometric reconfiguration.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a versatile platform for geometry-programmable colloidal particles with emergent collective functionalities, offering a route toward materials and fluids with dynamically programmable properties.

title: Rotational symmetry and common-mode phase drift in a counter-wound S-shaped Aharonov--Bohm interferometer
comment: 22 pages, 6 figures; submitted to Physical Review B
summary: We study common flux offsets in a three-dimensional InAs Aharonov-Bohm waveguide formed by two quarter-circle bends of opposite curvature. Each bend contains a through-opening that separates two conducting arms and encloses an independently specified flux. For a spin-independent, two-terminal model with ideal confined fluxes, microreversibility and a rotation exchanging the complete modules imply $\mathcal{T}(φ_1,φ_2)=\mathcal{T}(-φ_2,-φ_1)$. The counter-wound configuration is therefore stationary against common offsets, while the same-winding configuration is stationary against differential offsets. This constraint does not require cancellation of every interference phase, and it extends to a spatially uniform ambient field perpendicular to the plane of the guide, even though that field also penetrates the conductor. Three-dimensional scattering calculations at $R=350$ nm and $E_F\simeq 7.283$ meV retain three open orbital lead modes and strong reflection at the openings. The finest sampled counter-wound sweep has a visibility of approximately 3.56%; referring the grids to a common threshold gives an estimated continuum visibility of 2.6-2.9%. The response coefficients vary strongly with energy, while a 100 mK electron temperature retains about 98% of the visibility. For weak, purely common Gaussian phase noise, the leading transmission variance is quartic in noise amplitude, whereas the mean shift remains quadratic. Flux imbalance and asymmetric scalar potentials restore a linear response; symmetric scalar disorder preserves stationarity without guaranteeing high transmission. The proposed experimental test requires few-mode coherent transport, calibrated flux controls, and a magnetic-source design whose leakage fields and spin-dependent terms are assessed explicitly.

AI.tldr: A three-dimensional InAs Aharonov-Bohm waveguide with two counter-wound quarter-circle bends is shown to be stationary against common flux offsets, as required by microreversibility; the effect survives a uniform perpendicular ambient field and finite temperature, with a numerically estimated continuum visibility of about 2.6-2.9%.
AI.motivation: To identify a geometry in which transport is intrinsically insensitive to common (spatially uniform) flux offsets, and to establish whether this stationarity survives three-dimensional confinement, ambient perpendicular fields, finite electron temperature, and noise—thereby defining a viable experimental test.
AI.method: A spin-independent two-terminal model of a three-dimensional InAs waveguide formed by two quarter-circle bends of opposite curvature, each bend containing a through-opening that separates two conducting arms and encloses an independently specified flux. Symmetry arguments based on microreversibility and a rotation exchanging the complete modules yield T(φ1,φ2)=T(-φ2,-φ1). Three-dimensional scattering calculations are performed at R=350 nm with E_F≈7.283 meV, retaining three open orbital lead modes and strong reflection at the openings; the finest sampled counter-wound sweep is referred to a common threshold to estimate continuum visibility, response coefficients are studied versus energy, and weak common Gaussian phase noise, flux imbalance, and asymmetric/symmetric scalar potentials are analyzed.
AI.result: The counter-wound configuration is stationary against common flux offsets and the same-winding configuration against differential offsets; the constraint does not require cancellation of every interference phase and extends to a spatially uniform ambient field perpendicular to the guide plane even though that field also penetrates the conductor. The finest sampled counter-wound sweep gives a visibility of approximately 3.56%, with an estimated continuum visibility of 2.6-2.9%. Response coefficients vary strongly with energy, while a 100 mK electron temperature retains about 98% of the visibility. For weak purely common Gaussian phase noise, the leading transmission variance is quartic in noise amplitude while the mean shift is quadratic; flux imbalance and asymmetric scalar potentials restore a linear response, and symmetric scalar disorder preserves stationarity but does not guarantee high transmission.
AI.conclusion: Common-offset immunity in the counter-wound Aharonov-Bohm waveguide is a robust symmetry-protected property that survives three-dimensional effects, ambient perpendicular fields, and realistic temperatures. An experimental test requires few-mode coherent transport, calibrated flux controls, and a magnetic-source design whose leakage fields and spin-dependent terms are explicitly assessed.

title: Quantum Statistical Thermal Engine at the BCS-BEC crossover
summary: We propose a quantum heat engine based on a two-component Fermi gas with s-wave contact interaction, operating across the BCS-BEC crossover. The work is extracted from the statistical properties of the gas, which are controlled by the interaction, rather than relying solely on compression and expansion stages. Using the functional renormalization group formalism, we obtain the equation of state in a non-perturbative form along the crossover, encompassing the superfluid-normal phase transition. The cycle combines isentropic density strokes, isochoric thermalization, and isothermal interaction sweeps. This construction makes it possible to integrate features of both Otto and Carnot cycles, in which the system simultaneously saturates both efficiency limits without the net work vanishing. In the absence of density variations, the cycle reduces to a statistical Stirling-like engine, in which the work generated arises exclusively from the interaction, achieving efficiencies up to $38\%$. A pronounced asymmetry emerges through the crossover, giving rise to distinct operating regimes depending on the trajectory followed in the phase diagram. Consequently, the same architecture can be tuned to function as an engine, refrigerator, accelerator, or heater. These findings highlight pairing correlations as a versatile thermodynamic resource for quantum heat machines.

AI.tldr: A quantum heat engine based on a two-component Fermi gas across the BCS-BEC crossover is proposed, where work is extracted from interaction-controlled statistical properties of the gas. Using functional renormalization group, the equation of state is obtained non-perturbatively along the crossover. The cycle combines Otto and Carnot features, saturating both efficiency limits without vanishing net work, and can be tuned to act as engine, refrigerator, accelerator, or heater.
AI.motivation: Conventional quantum heat engines largely rely on compression and expansion stages for work extraction. This work is motivated by the idea of exploiting interaction-driven statistical properties of a strongly correlated Fermi gas, specifically pairing correlations across the BCS-BEC crossover, as an alternative and versatile thermodynamic resource.
AI.method: The authors employ the functional renormalization group (FRG) formalism to compute the equation of state in a non-perturbative form along the BCS-BEC crossover, including the superfluid-normal phase transition. The proposed cycle integrates isentropic density strokes, isochoric thermalization, and isothermal interaction sweeps.
AI.result: The cycle combines features of both Otto and Carnot cycles, simultaneously saturating both efficiency limits without the net work vanishing. In the absence of density variations, it reduces to a statistical Stirling-like engine with work arising exclusively from interaction, reaching efficiencies up to 38%. A pronounced asymmetry across the crossover yields distinct operating regimes depending on the phase-diagram trajectory, allowing the same architecture to function as an engine, refrigerator, accelerator, or heater.
AI.conclusion: Pairing correlations in a strongly interacting Fermi gas serve as a versatile thermodynamic resource for quantum heat machines, enabling multifunctional operation and high efficiency within a single tunable architecture.

title: Synthesis and modification of thin NaSICON solid electrolytes using ion beams
summary: Solid electrolytes (SEs) for sodium-based superionic conductors (NaSICON) were first introduced in 1976 and quickly recognized for their excellent ionic conductivity. While considerable effort has been made to develop thin electrolytes for all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs), only a few sodium-based SEs have been successfully fabricated as thin films. These thin films are particularly desirable for their reduced electrical resistance, which typically increases with the thickness of the SE. By reducing the thickness of the SEs to the nanometer scale, their ionic conductivity can be significantly enhanced. In this study, the NASICON composite was initially prepared in the form of pellets using the mixed oxide technique with a planetary ball mill and synthesized by the solid-state method at 1300 °C. The resulting pellets were used as sputtering targets in a low-energy ion facility to prepare continuous NASICON nanofilms. To explore the effect of ion implantation on the electrical properties of NASICON, the prepared films were bombarded with Ni ions at 1.1 MeV and varying fluences, using the Tandetron accelerator at the CANAM infrastructure (NPI Řež). The electrical properties of both the synthesized and implanted films were analyzed through electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS). The results, describing the impact of irradiation on NASICON's properties, are presented here.

AI.tldr: A NASICON composite was synthesized by solid-state reaction at 1300 °C, sputtered into continuous nanofilms, implanted with 1.1 MeV Ni ions at various fluences, and characterized by EIS to assess irradiation effects on electrical properties.
AI.motivation: NASICON sodium superionic conductors, known since 1976, show excellent ionic conductivity and are attractive for all-solid-state batteries, but only a few sodium-based solid electrolytes have been realized as thin films. Thinner electrolytes reduce electrical resistance and, at the nanoscale, can enhance ionic conductivity, motivating investigation of NASICON nanofilms and the influence of ion implantation on their electrical behavior.
AI.method: NASICON composite pellets were prepared by the mixed oxide technique using a planetary ball mill and solid-state synthesis at 1300 °C. These pellets served as sputtering targets for depositing continuous NASICON nanofilms in a low-energy ion facility. The films were then bombarded with Ni ions at 1.1 MeV and varying fluences using a Tandetron accelerator at the CANAM infrastructure (NPI Řež). Electrical properties of as-synthesized and implanted films were examined by electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS).
AI.result: EIS characterization of the synthesized and Ni-implanted NASICON nanofilms yielded results describing the impact of irradiation on the material's electrical properties.
AI.conclusion: Ni ion implantation at 1.1 MeV and varying fluences modifies the electrical properties of NASICON nanofilms, with the effects detailed via EIS in this study.

title: Multistate Torsion in Zitterbewegung
summary: We derive nonlinear Zitterbewegung velocity of electrons augmented by band torsion in crystals. The equation of motion with multistate quantum geometric tensors and torsion culminates in transient nonlinear photocurrent responses distinct from the recently measured resonant steady-state photovoltaic effects induced by circularly polarized light. Tomography protocols for measuring the multistate quantum geometric torsion tensors are proposed.

AI.tldr: The paper derives a nonlinear Zitterbewegung velocity for electrons in crystals that is modified by band torsion, using multistate quantum geometric tensors, and shows this yields transient nonlinear photocurrent responses distinct from steady-state circularly-polarized photovoltaic effects, along with tomography protocols to measure the torsion tensors.
AI.motivation: Recent experiments have measured resonant steady-state photovoltaic effects induced by circularly polarized light, which are governed by quantum geometric quantities. The authors aim to extend this geometric framework beyond the steady state by incorporating band torsion, which has been largely neglected, to uncover new nonlinear dynamical transport phenomena.
AI.method: They formulate an equation of motion for electrons that includes multistate quantum geometric tensors together with band torsion, from which a nonlinear Zitterbewegung velocity is derived. They also propose tomography protocols designed to measure the multistate quantum geometric torsion tensors.
AI.result: The torsion-augmented equation of motion produces transient nonlinear photocurrent responses that are qualitatively distinct from the previously measured resonant steady-state photovoltaic effects driven by circularly polarized light. Concrete measurement schemes (tomography protocols) for the multistate quantum geometric torsion tensors are provided.
AI.conclusion: Band torsion plays a nontrivial role in electron dynamics, giving rise to nonlinear Zitterbewegung and transient nonlinear photocurrents that go beyond steady-state geometric photovoltaic responses, and the multistate quantum geometric torsion tensors are experimentally accessible via the proposed tomography protocols.

title: Blind directions of linear response and the limits of finite-perturbation bounds on efficiency fluctuations
comment: 28 pages, 2 figures, 13 tables. Replication package: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23042372
summary: Thermodynamic uncertainty relations bound the fluctuations of time-antisymmetric currents. Stochastic efficiency is not one: a ratio of two odd quantities, it is even under path reversal, and for the conventional ratio $-W/Q_h$ no moment exists. We work with the exergetic ratio $η=W/(W+T_0S)$, whose moments exist, and ask how much of its variance a finite perturbation of the dynamics can certify when linear response cannot. The question is specific to nonlinear observables: for every current, and every observable linear in transition counts and residence times, the multiparameter Cramér-Rao bound over rate and site perturbations already equals the variance. For $η$ it does not. The Cramér-Rao bound vanishes on a hyperplane of perturbation directions, while the Barankin multi-point bound, applied to tilted path measures, stays positive there and recovers 75% of the variance of $η$ in a three-state motor model where every linear-response bound is zero. The Gram matrix of tilted Markov-jump path measures is a Feynman-Kac matrix exponential whose potential is the Hellinger integrand of the jump intensities, and the cost of a perturbation is its $χ^2$ divergence, which no dissipation bound controls. The bound captures 1.25-1.57 times the best linear-response bound, and the gain persists on networks of up to sixteen states. For an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process the construction is exactly solvable: the optimal tilt scales as $T^{-1/2}$ and three test points nearly reach the supremum. Two limits are established. The gain is a short-window effect that disappears as the counts become Gaussian, and the bound cannot be turned into inference: coarse measurements bound $χ^2$ only from below. The construction is a computational instrument for a model in hand, not an uncertainty relation.

AI.tldr: A multi-point Barankin bound on tilted path measures bounds the variance of the (even, nonlinear) exergetic efficiency η where linear-response and Cramér-Rao bounds vanish, capturing 75% of its variance in a three-state motor model.
AI.motivation: Thermodynamic uncertainty relations constrain fluctuations of time-antisymmetric currents, but stochastic efficiency is not antisymmetric: it is a ratio of two odd quantities and hence even under path reversal, and for the conventional ratio −W/Q_h no moment exists. Standard linear-response and Cramér-Rao bounds fail to certify variance of such nonlinear observables, so a new variance-certifying tool is needed.

The Gram matrix of these tilted measures is a Feynman-Kac matrix exponential whose potential is the Hellinger integrand of the jump intensities, with perturbation cost given by its χ² divergence. The construction is compared against multiparameter Cramér-Rao bounds over rate and site perturbations, and is exactly solved for an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process.
AI.result: For every current and every observable linear in transition counts and residence times, the multiparameter Cramér-Rao bound over rate and site perturbations equals the variance; for η it does not, vanishing on a hyperplane of perturbation directions. The Barankin bound stays positive there, recovering 75% of η's variance in a three-state motor model where all linear-response bounds are zero, capturing 1.25–1.57 times the best linear-response bound, with gains persisting on networks up to sixteen states. For the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process the optimal tilt scales as T^{-1/2} and three test points nearly attain the supremum. Two limits appear: the gain is a short-window effect vanishing as counts become Gaussian, and the bound cannot support inference since coarse measurements bound χ² only from below.
AI.conclusion: The multi-point Barankin construction certifies variance of the even, nonlinear efficiency η beyond what linear-response theory allows, but it is a computational instrument for a model in hand rather than a genuine uncertainty relation.

title: Evidence for Distributed Fault Energetics and Their Impact on Deformation in a Chemically Complex Alloy
comment: ~370 lines main text, 7 main figures, supplementary notes 1-9, supplementary figures 1-7, supplementary tables 1-2
summary: Chemically complex alloys feature intrinsically heterogeneous local chemical environments and, consequently, fluctuations in local fault energetics. However, experimentally quantifying their relationship remains challenging, leaving the role of this distributed energy landscape in deformation mechanisms incompletely resolved. Here, we develop a distribution based framework linking experimentally measured stacking fault widths to deformation relevant apparent fault energy, revealing a distributed local fault-energy landscape in CrCoNi. The framework reveals the stabilizing role of energy fluctuations and captures an upward shift in the apparent fault energetics, from negative values toward zero following heat treatment, which atomistic simulations associate with the emergence of L12 type chemical short-range order. Using one-dimensional kinetic Monte Carlo simulations, supported by electron microscopy observations, we further show that history-dependent changes in the local fault-energy landscape bias the competition among stacking faulting, nano-twinning and HCP transformation in CrCoNi. Our results provide an experimentally anchored, distribution-based framework for understanding deformation in chemically complex alloys as it evolves within a distributed fault-energy landscape shaped by local chemical order.

AI.motivation: Chemically complex alloys possess heterogeneous local chemical environments causing fluctuations in local fault energetics, but experimentally quantifying this relationship is difficult, leaving the role of the distributed energy landscape in deformation mechanisms unresolved.
AI.method: Development of a distribution-based framework converting experimentally measured stacking fault widths into deformation-relevant apparent fault energy; atomistic simulations to associate energy shifts with L12-type chemical short-range order; one-dimensional kinetic Monte Carlo simulations supported by electron microscopy observations.
AI.result: The framework reveals a distributed local fault-energy landscape in CrCoNi, shows the stabilizing role of energy fluctuations, and captures an upward shift in apparent fault energetics from negative values toward zero after heat treatment, attributed to L12-type short-range order. History-dependent changes in the landscape bias competition among stacking faulting, nano-twinning, and HCP transformation.

title: Multiscale modelling of nanoscaled FETs based on 2D ferroelectric materials
summary: Ferroelectric materials are highly attractive for low-power, high-speed electronics and emerging neuromorphic computing architectures. However, the severe physical scaling limits of conventional bulk (3D) ferroelectrics at the nanoscale have shifted attention towards two-dimensional (2D) ferroelectric monolayers. Accurate device-level performance predictions are essential to accelerate the experimental testing and screening of these novel materials. In this work, we present a multiscale simulation framework that bridges first-principles density functional theory with Non-Equilibrium Green's Function (NEGF) transport calculations. Using a 2D Indium Phosphide monolayer as a case study, our approach leverages a continuously interpolated, polarization-dependent Hamiltonian embedded within a self-consistent Poisson-NEGF solver. The model captures the dynamic interplay between ion movement and electronic transport, naturally reproducing macroscopic hysteresis loops and memory windows without empirical parameters. This predictive pipeline provides a computationally efficient tool to evaluate and optimize next-generation 2D ferroelectric field-effect transistors.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a multiscale simulation framework combining DFT and NEGF to predict device performance of 2D ferroelectric monolayers, demonstrated on an InP monolayer for FeFET memory applications.
AI.motivation: Bulk (3D) ferroelectrics face severe physical scaling limits at the nanoscale, prompting interest in 2D ferroelectric monolayers for low-power, high-speed electronics and neuromorphic computing. Accurate device-level performance predictions are needed to accelerate experimental testing and screening of these novel materials.
